name: Mississippi Today
title: Will the tobacco lawsuit settlement provide lessons for current leadership?
description: Mississippi House Speaker Pro Tem J.P. Compretta, D-Bay St. Louis, left, and Speaker Billy McCoy, D-Rienzi, applaud Republican Gov. Haley Barbour, who waves to spectators before delivering his State of the State speech to the Legislature at the Capitol in 2010.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
In a 2005 special session, the Mississippi Legislature was on the verge of selling a significant portion of its future annual tobacco lawsuit settlement funds for an immediate sum of money when a single phone call from the powerful House speaker stopped the process.
Then-state Treasurer Tate Reeves, a Republican who is now in his second term as governor, had explained to legislative leaders how the process to sell the future payments would work. Legislators initially bought into the concept of quickly getting a modest amount of cash rather than patiently waiting to collect a larger amount spread over decades.
Legislation “to securitize” a portion of the annual tobacco lawsuit funds passed the Senate. The bill was expected to pass the House Appropriations Committee and ultimately the full House when Speaker Billy McCoy made a phone call to Appropriations Chairman Johnny Stringer minutes before the committee met. 
One version of the story is that McCoy informed his money chairman that he was withdrawing his support for the proposal, and another version is that McCoy told Stringer point-blank not to pass the bill. The story further goes that McCoy made the pivotal phone call after a meeting with Gulf Coast Rep. Diane Peranich, one of his key allies, who voiced strong opposition to securitization.
At any rate, after that call, Stringer killed the bill.
The only problem was that the Legislature still had to deal with a whopping $268 million Medicaid deficit. Even by today’s inflationary standards, such a deficit would be significant. In 2005, it was near catastrophic.
There seemed to be no solution, and the Division of Medicaid was only days from being unable to pay medical providers.
The Democratic-controlled House wanted to increase the measly 18 cents per pack tax on cigarettes to address the deficit. The Senate aligned with Republican Gov. Haley Barbour, who had previously been a tobacco lobbyist, in opposing the cigarette tax increase. And to be honest, a cigarette tax increase on its own would not have generated enough revenue to solve the monumental Medicaid problem. Then, as now, most politicians considered a tax increase a nonstarter.
Seeing no solution, legislators left for the weekend on March 10. But before many of them got home, Barbour called them back in what was then a rare special session within the regular session.
In that special session, the securitization initially was viewed as both a smart business move and a way to solve the deficit.
Ultimately, instead of the securitization, legislators solved the deficit by making cuts to Medicaid and by withdrawing $240 million from the healthcare trust fund that was created with the tobacco lawsuit settlement funds.
The legislation included the caveat that the trust fund would be replenished.
That never happened. The trust fund no longer exists in any substantive manner.
Through a series of well researched stories and the “Black Box” podcast, Mississippi Today details how state and local politicians are starting to spend $430 million in opioid lawsuit settlement funds that the Mississippi will receive over many years.
Comparisons have been made to how the state has spent the tobacco lawsuit settlement money and how the state and local governments are currently spending the opioid lawsuit settlement funds. Both lawsuits were filed to obtain money from companies (tobacco and drug companies) for the harm they caused Mississippians. 
The 1997 tobacco lawsuit settlement  guaranteed Mississippi $4 billion over 25 years with annual payments, based on a formula, continuing forever. The most recent annual payment is about $90 million.
In 1999, the Legislature voted to place the annual settlement funds in a trust fund and use the earnings for healthcare initiatives. But not too long after the trust fund was established, a perennially cash-strapped Legislature and governor began to dip into it to deal with budget shortfalls.
Solving the Medicaid deficit in 2005 culminated that effort.
Many believe the end of the trust fund was a lost opportunity for the state to use the massive lawsuit to make a difference in healthcare.
It is hard to argue that it was not. But it also would be hard to argue in 2005 in favor of essentially shutting down the Medicaid program that provides healthcare for low-income people: children, pregnant women, disabled people and some of the elderly population.
For a Legislature afraid of tax increases, few other options existed.
The Legislature and governor are still adverse to tax increases and spend much of their time cutting taxes. But the opioid settlement comes on the heels of the state experiencing unprecedented revenue growth, thanks to a number of circumstances related to a massive influx of federal pandemic relief money.
While that growth has slowed, Mississippi’s financial situation is not nearly as bleak as it was in 2005, giving state leaders the opportunity to use the opioid settlement money for the intended purpose – to fight drug addiction.
If they do that, perhaps people won’t be talking about another lost opportunity a generation from now.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘The worst possible catch-22’: Fish and Wildlife struggles to combat bear rumors
description:
“What happens when you call us, 99% of the time, is that we give you advice on how to coexist with the bear,” said the department’s public information officer. “That’s what we want to be doing and that is what mostly happens.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘The worst possible catch-22’: Fish and Wildlife struggles to combat bear rumors.
text:
A bear enjoying a dumpster feast earlier this year in Eden, Vermont. Photo by S. Chambers, courtesy of Vermont Fish and Wildlife.
As bear-human incidents continue at record rates, the state Fish and Wildlife Department is encountering public misperception that is leading Vermonters to avoid reporting minor bear activity because they fear the bear will be killed.
This often leads to “the worst possible catch-22 for the bears,” said Joshua Morse, public information officer for the department: the situation not being properly addressed until it has escalated much further — so much so that it can be difficult, if not impossible, to de-escalate things without considering killing the bear.
“I wish people knew that what happens when you call us, 99% of the time, is that we give you advice on how to coexist with the bear,” Morse said. “That’s what we want to be doing and that is what mostly happens.”
Vermont has a large population of around 7,000 black bears, about one for every 100 residents, that reside in all areas of the state except the Champlain Islands.
The mammal’s sense of smell is 2,100 times better than a human’s and they have an excellent long-term memory, able to remember the location of food sources years after an initial visit. Black bears are “opportunistic omnivores” and will eat just about anything they find, especially during the spring and early summer when their highest-fat natural food sources (beechnuts and acorns) are not yet available and they continue to draw upon last year’s remaining fat reserves.
These biological factors mean the long-lived animals can locate human-created food sources like birdseed or unsecured trash from far away and, once they get a taste, will return for years in hopes the feast has replenished itself.
According to Jaclyn Comeau, the state’s black bear project leader and a wildlife biologist with the department, there have been a heightened number of bear-human incident reports for the past eight years, most of them minor. The department is on track to likely exceed 1,200 reports before the year is over, potentially hitting a new record, she said this month.
Not only are there more bear-human incidents being reported, but Comeau said the department is seeing an increase in more intense types of interactions: around 50 reports of home entries and around 40 reports of vehicle entries per year, often the same bear entering multiple homes or vehicles.
“If the department was able to intervene earlier, we believe it would help to reduce the number of more serious cases,” said David Sausville, wildlife management program manager with the department, in an email. “We would be able to help people before the issue elevated in concern.”
In situations where a bear is habituated to enter residences or vehicles, killing the bear does become a safety consideration, though Comeau notes that not every bear that enters a home needs to be killed. An average of about 35 bears per year are put down by the department, she said.
Comeau’s impression is that there are more severe bear reports happening and more bears needing to be killed: Six years ago, there were just a handful of home entry reports.
“As best we can tell, it’s a learned, escalated behavior where they’ve had enough positive food rewards from communities,” she said. “For some bears, this switch happens where they just become so bold that they are willing to take that risk of going right into someone’s house to get more food.”
While bears do need to be put down on a fairly regular basis, most of those cases do not make the news. Every so often, however, a highly visible case will occur, like last month in Stowe when a town police officer was authorized to shoot a bear after it repeatedly broke into a restaurant’s walk-in cooler.
Each time a bear killing does make the news, the rumor about reporting minor bear incidents leading directly to a bear being put down “bubbles up,” Morse said.
“It’s extremely frustrating. It’s this rumor with this really long life that pops up when you least need it,” he added. “It sounds really extreme, but it has real spreading power.”
Morse himself fields the department’s general inquiry phone and email lines a few days a week, and on occasion gets calls from people who say, “I was really anxious to call you. Please don’t kill the bear.”
“And I’ll say, ‘We’re so glad you called us. We’re not going to kill the bear,’” he recounted. “‘Our goal is to help you and the bear coexist, that’s what we want.’”
When should you report a bear sighting?
Vermonters should let the department know when they see bears in “places they probably shouldn’t be, or doing things they probably shouldn’t be doing,” Comeau said. The main way to do so is via Fish and Wildlife’s bear reporting form, though those needing immediate assistance for unsafe bear situations can call their local game warden.
When a report is submitted, the department follows up with an email full of detailed information relevant to the specific situation or, in medium-intensity situations, with a phone call. In either situation, Comeau said, they will offer a site visit to help people locate and secure bear attractants.
“Getting rid of bird feeders, putting up electric fences around chickens and finding a really good place to store your garbage can go a really long way,” the biologist said. “That’s the bulk of what we’re doing, and it proves to be most effective.”
In a new partnership with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, electric fences and electrified mats can be loaned out to Vermonters to help with bear situations for a few weeks until residents have a chance to purchase their own. Support staff help set up the equipment and get people comfortable with using it.
In more severe cases, the department has tactics to make the bear have a negative experience at a site to outweigh the positive food experiences. They catch the bear and release it on site with loud noises and use a paintball gun or rubber ammunition. Those efforts are very time-intensive, Comeau said, and are saved for situations where people have made all the right changes to secure food sources.

A bear exits a fenced but unsecured dumpster in Stowe on September 5, 2021. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger.

Despite their great sense of smell, memory and drive to locate calories, bears can definitely unlearn the association between a locale and a feast, the biologist said.
“It takes us being really diligent about it,” Comeau said. “We really have to make some of our own changes if we really want to see the light at the end of the tunnel for this situation.”
In some cases, though, when bears are consistently entering homes, businesses or vehicles, or acting aggressively and not responding to changed human behavior, they do need to be put down. Relocation is not an effective option, she said. Bears have an “amazing ability to navigate” and will eventually return to their original location, as well as likely causing problems for the humans or other bears living where they are relocated to.
“The public really likes that idea and I understand why they do, because it seems like the nicest thing to do,” Comeau said. “But I honestly feel like it is the most selfish way to handle this.”
‘We need people to step it up’
As the frequency and intensity of bear incident reports have increased, the department has amped up their bear coexistence outreach, Morse said, from workshops to social media and television ads to poster campaigns in conflict towns. Ten years ago, Morse said, the department wasn’t spending any marketing funds on bear coexistence.
Despite their best efforts, he said, the department seems to have “hit a wall” with the number of people they can reach and educate about bear coexistence, especially in places with chronic issues such as Stowe, Killington, the Mad River Valley and the Wilmington and Dover area.
“We are using every tool and every channel to try to give people the means to coexist with bears, and we need people to step it up,” Morse said.
“We need whole communities to be doing the information sharing and making the changes in lockstep,” he added. “Otherwise, it will just be whack-a-mole, and that’s not the scale of change that we need for the bears.”
To that end, the department is supporting a peer-to-peer nonprofit, Vermont Coverts, that helps residents educate their neighbors on what to do with bears using their own social networks or word of mouth. They also support grassroots community groups like the Mad River Valley Bear Initiative, as well as encourage towns to think about adopting ordinances to keep garbage contained.
Working to help Vermonters coexist with bears is a significant and overwhelming drain on the department, Morse said, even with the new partnership with the USDA. While all the outreach and education they do is to help make living with bears easier, the department is also discussing concerns that there are too many bears in the state.
“We are trying to help people expand their comfort level a bit, but we are also talking about making some changes to bring the population down a little bit lower to see if that will also help alleviate some of the pressure we’re all feeling,” Comeau said.
The best and really only way to do that is by increasing the number of bears killed in hunting season, a policy conversation the Fish and Wildlife commissioner’s office is currently having, she said.
To that end, the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Board announced Wednesday that it will be holding public hearings at the end of August on proposed changes to the state’s bear hunting regulations.
Currently, hunters can take one bear per year. The proposed changes would allow a second bear permit to be purchased for specific areas of the state, as well as slightly extend the bear hunting season.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas’ smoking ban just turned 20. Can the state find common ground on public health again?
description: Just 20 years ago, trying to avoid smoke in Arkansas was an onerous task. Going out to restaurants and bars often meant coming home reeking of cigarettes, even if you or your companions weren’t the ones smoking. Many employers had a smoke break room.  At my first newspaper job in Arkansas, that meant walking through […]
text:
A no-smoking sign on a doorway in Little Rock, Arkansas on Wednesday, July 22, 2026 (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)Just 20 years ago, trying to avoid smoke in Arkansas was an onerous task.
Going out to restaurants and bars often meant coming home reeking of cigarettes, even if you or your companions weren’t the ones smoking. Many employers had a smoke break room. 
At my first newspaper job in Arkansas, that meant walking through a thick, noxious cloud to buy a can of Diet Coke from the vending machine.
It wasn’t just a hassle navigating this environment. It was a serious risk, especially for a state that has regularly placed at the bottom or near-bottom of most major health indicators.
Last week marked the 20th anniversary of the state’s indoor smoking ban taking effect. The law is a testament to bipartisanship and the work of Arkansas public health leaders. It’s also a model for how Arkansas policymakers can address the state’s public health concerns today.



Let us know what you think...


 


Banning indoor smoking wasn’t the primary reason lawmakers were summoned to the Capitol in 2006. Republican Gov. Mike Huckabee, our current governor’s father, called the predominantly Democratic Legislature back into session to address a court ruling that Arkansas still hadn’t funded its schools adequately.
But the session gave Huckabee, who was term-limited and already laying the groundwork for a presidential bid, a chance to add policy wins to his resume. Trying to position himself as someone especially focused on health, reducing smoking became one of his signature causes.
To do so, he reversed course on his previous opposition to such a ban. The nonsmoking governor, who had received campaign contributions from tobacco companies, rejected a similar ban on smoking in restaurants in 2001.
But five years later, Huckabee argued forcefully for such a restriction and painted it as a matter of protecting workers’ health. 
“I think people are going to find out that there is an overwhelming number of people who really prefer a nonsmoking environment,” Huckabee said in 2006. “There may be some businesses who think they can thrive that way, but I think more often than not, I think they not only limit their customer base but they also do encourage additional hazards.”
The wide vote margins in the House and the Senate for the ban don’t reflect just how much resistance there initially was to a ban that’s now a part of everyday life in the state. The idea faced opposition from some restaurant owners who said it would hurt their business and from some conservatives who portrayed it as a form of government overreach.
The ban even cleared the way for the passage of another measure banning smoking in cars with small children inside. Health advocates embraced that restriction, even though many suspected it was introduced as a joke or protest to the indoor ban.
The smoke-filled restaurants and other workplaces aren’t the only things that feel bizarre 20 years later. The idea of bipartisan support on public health issues, in an increasingly polarized environment, also feels like a different world.
The smoking ban passed during a weeklong session where a Republican governor and Democrats passed a raft of progressive measures. The agenda included a major boost in school funding and an increase in the state’s minimum wage.
But the smoking ban still provides a model. It showed what happens when people of different political backgrounds trust health experts and work together to make a pragmatic argument for change. It required leaders to be willing to change their minds and to accept compromises.
It’s a model that may be more difficult to replicate in an environment where so many policy discussions turn into fierce partisan battles. And it’s complicated further by the demonization public health officials have faced and the easy spread of medical disinformation.
But obstacles like that can be overcome, and environments can change. Every smoke-free workplace and restaurant in Arkansas is proof that consensus can be found.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How a CT filmmaker’s first feature won at Sundance
description: Filmmaker Rashad Frett won an award for Best Directing at the 2025 Sundance Film Festival for the film "Ricky," which is based in Hartford.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

In Rashad Frett’s award-winning film “Ricky,” the audience is introduced to his titular protagonist as he walks home from work through a chain-link tunnel suspended over a Hartford highway.
Through another person’s eyes, that bridge might be an unremarkable hunk of urban infrastructure hovering on the edge of a city that has seen precious little attention from filmmakers. But to Frett, who grew up in Hartford, the bridge was a staple of its visual landscape that he knew he’d include in his first feature — a workaday vista from which his main character might regard the city skyline as he walks across the screen.
“When he’s walking to the right of frame, it shows that he’s trying to progress in his life,” Frett said. “It’s one of the subtle things we’re taught” in film school. 
That moment is one of thousands of tiny choices Frett crafted into “Ricky,” choices that added up to his win for Best Directing at the 2025 Sundance Film Festival. “Ricky” had a national theatrical release in April and is now available for streaming.
Frett’s own journey brought him from a childhood split between the U.S. Virgin Islands and Hartford, to the Army just out of high school, where he was a combat medic who responded on 9/11 and helped evacuate people from Manhattan. After he left the military, Frett wasn’t sure what he’d do next. There was the dream of being an actor. The pragmatic plan of going to business school. But his ambition of becoming a filmmaker was simmering in the background.

Rashad Frett attends the premiere of “Ricky” during the Sundance Film Festival on Friday, Jan. 24, 2025, at Eccles Theatre in Park City, Utah. Credit: Charles Sykes / AP

As he prepared to enroll at Central Connecticut State University, Frett visited the campus and met with Jeffrey Teitler, a professor there and Emmy-winning documentary filmmaker. It wasn’t a chance encounter —Frett had already been experimenting with film. He showed Teitler a comedic short he’d made with some family and friends.
The technique wasn’t there yet, and the nicest adjective Teitler could summon about the short was “quirky.” But Teitler came away from the meeting impressed by Frett and his commitment.
“Very rarely do you have a film student come in to meet with somebody, to talk to them about what it is that they want to do — and not only talk to them but follow up in really rigorous ways,” he said. “With Rashad, or with any student, it’s not about talent,” Teitler said. Once you master the use of a basic light, for example, a character on screen “can become luminescent and contrasting, and that could be beautiful. Rashad started to love these things. He started to embrace technique and love technique.”
Many of Teitler’s students dove in. They’d take the automatic settings off the camera, they’d experiment with pacing and cinematography. “All students can do this — all students can tell a story and use cinematic technique to speak to their interests,” Teitler said. But Frett? “He lived in the lab.”
“It was kind of like the sink or swim type of thing,” Frett recalled. “I felt like I wasted most of my 20s just trying to figure out my life. By the time I got here, I was like, ‘This is what I’m doing.'”
Teitler connected Frett with a Hartford police officer named Mark Manson, who had come up with a TV show idea called “The Second District” along with Felix Soto, a “career criminal” he met while in the field. Manson and Soto were both fans of “The Wire,” the celebrated series about the Baltimore police and local gangs. “The Second District” follows a struggling Hartford police department trying to rid the streets of drugs. Manson funded the pilot, which Frett directed and edited.
“He was really the type of person I was looking for,” Manson recalled — someone with the energy to take on the project who was also deeply rooted in Hartford.
The trailer for the pilot went viral, and the prospect of a series attracted media attention, yet efforts to produce the show fell through. Manson said he was naive to the industry at the time, and trusting of every contact who showed interest in the project. 
Rashad Frett, a film director from Hartford, gives direction on the set of the pilot for “The Second District” in 2010. Credit: Allan Vega / Contributed photo
But making the pilot would cement a long-term working relationship: Manson was a co-producer of “Ricky” and has a small part the film, as does Soto. Manson has since left a career in policing to be a full-time filmmaker and is currently working on a documentary and his first feature.
Frett’s effort on the pilot for “The Second District” convinced Teitler, more than ever, that Frett needed to go to graduate school at New York University’s prestigious Tisch School of the Arts, a program Teitler attended.
“He just needed to be at the highest place of storytelling,” Teitler said, to learn from icons like Spike Lee and Todd Solondz, who were then teaching in NYU’s graduate program.
To Frett, NYU seemed like a pipe dream. From his military days, though, Frett had learned to prepare for a mission. Only this time, he had Teitler’s help. For nearly a year, teacher and student got together weekly at a sandwich shop to work on the application: a personal statement, resume, letters of recommendation and a sample script.
Frett interviewed for the program.
“Normally when I get nervous, I start cracking jokes,” he recalled. When he left the interview, he was convinced he’d blown it. 
A month later, while he was watching a play in Hartford, a call came into his cellphone from a New York area code. The department chair left him a message. Instead of returning her call, Frett, still in the audience, called Teitler.
“I was like, ‘Jeff, they called me to tell me I didn’t get in,'” Frett whispered into the phone. Teitler was confused: why would they call him to tell him he didn’t get in? Another call beeped in: it was the department chair again. This time, Frett picked up. The whispered phone calls got him kicked out of the play, but he’d been admitted to NYU. “It was unreal.”
Rashad Frett gives direction on the set of “Ricky,” his first feature film, which shot in and around Hartford in 2024. Credit: Jeremy Gumener / Contributed photo
“Ricky” is based on a short Frett co-wrote with classmate Lin Que Ayoung during his final year at NYU. The lead character has spent half his life incarcerated since being convicted of a crime as a teenager. The film begins as he is tenuously starting his life again in Hartford, still under the watch of a parole officer.
That scenario was one Frett grew up witnessing.  
“I knew a lot of people that went through the criminal justice system, and I saw how they were stunted when they came back home,” he said. Ricky has made it out of prison only to find that freedom is fragile, contingent and terrifying. The narrative tracks the question of whether Ricky will be able to hang on to that freedom. Played by Stephan James, Ricky often wears a wounded, wary expression as he goes to work, negotiates rides and tries to steer clear of trouble. At times, as when he meets a love interest, the raw hope in his eyes is shattering.
Ricky is a sympathetic character; his journey reveals many of the obstacles, small and large, that can unravel a person’s chance of starting life again after incarceration. But Frett also dares to make him flawed: he lies, steals and makes bad choices.
The character is still stuck, as Frett says, in the immature mindset of a younger man. In Hartford, he is surrounded by people with varying degrees of desire to help him, but who are also motivated by their own struggles and goals and frustrated by the strain of the character’s need.
The film is rooted in a city that Frett knows well. But to make the world of the film believable, Frett and Ayoung “sat in arraignments, spoke to judges, spoke to parole officers,” Frett recalled. Frett also drew on his work on “The Second District.”
One critic described what distinguishes Frett’s directing as “a sixth sense for where to place the camera, so that the film is always drawing in your eye with a weaving, bobbing, voyeuristic intimacy.”
Frett’s intuitive sense of where the camera belongs is based on a confluence of experience: as an editor choosing the best cuts in post-production, as an actor who understands how to capture the nuances of performance and from working as a cinematographer composing the frame.
“When I’m directing, I’m mashing all of that,” he said. “I’m like, ‘wait, dip here,’ because when you dip here it could be an editing point. That’s how my brain works.” Before shooting, Frett and his cinematographer create a shot list as a backup, but he rarely references those plans on the day. “For the four weeks we shot, we looked at the shot list twice.”
Rashad Frett gives direction on the set of “Ricky,” his first feature film, which shot in and around Hartford in 2024. Credit: Jeremy Gumener / Contributed photo
“Ricky” has proven his abilities as a filmmaker. But Frett also wants the film to spark conversation about the perils and potential for formerly incarcerated people.
“There’s a lot of opportunities, depending on where you are. What I’ve learned is some prisons have great programs to help formerly incarcerated people, and there’s a lot of others that aren’t,” he said. 
Though Frett never did time, he can relate to the feeling of being spit back out into the world and having to shift your mindset: “When I went to boot camp and I went to training and I came back to the civilian world, I was still on high alert. I was in soldier mode. It took me some months to readjust to being outside.”
Frett lives in New York City now and teaches film at Brooklyn College, where he tries to pay forward the mentorship that Teitler provided him. Thanks in part to that relationship, and to his own relentless drive, he has the world at his doorstep.
The directing award at Sundance has opened up a vast range of filmmaking opportunities, and his time at NYU has given him a circle of friends that spans the globe. But he’s still interested in the possibility of reviving “The Second District” in some form, putting Hartford back on the screen.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The distance between the police and public is literally widening. So is the accountability gap.
description: Not long ago every newsroom had a police scanner. I’m not talking about the days when ashtrays overflowed with cigarette butts and a bottle of scotch was kept in a desk drawer to toast special occasions. Like Thursday. But sometime between the pandemic and now, everything changed. Reporters used to work with the damned thing […]
text:
The author's now largely useless police scanner. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)Not long ago every newsroom had a police scanner.
I’m not talking about the days when ashtrays overflowed with cigarette butts and a bottle of scotch was kept in a desk drawer to toast special occasions. Like Thursday. But sometime between the pandemic and now, everything changed.
Reporters used to work with the damned thing squawking in the background because they knew that all of the important breaking news stories would come across that box. Every murder, every fire, every chemical spill. So would the routine calls, the domestic disturbances and the petty larcenies, but after a while you learned to tune out the background noise and listen only for the 10-codes that mattered.
A 10-40 was a fatality. A 10-32 was a chase. A 10-99 was a jailbreak.
You used the radio traffic, which was sometimes inaccurate because of misunderstandings or stress, as an alert to start asking questions. You didn’t report the scanner traffic, you verified it. There was no substitute to being on the scene, and some of my best reporting was based on my observation.
In covering a storm once, I described how a man stood in the doorway of his upside-down mobile home and described “what it feels like to shake hands with a tornado.”
If you were a police reporter, you likely had a scanner in your car or a handheld unit to slip in your pocket. Years ago I left my handheld scanner on a table at Otto’s Café in Pittsburg. The manager of the restaurant rang me at the Morning Sun newsroom and begged me to come get it, because the constant chatter was driving him crazy and he didn’t know how to turn it off.
The press — and the public — have been listening to police calls since Bayonne, New Jersey, installed a two-way radio system in 1933. For most of the 93 years since, police dispatch calls were considered public because they used a shared medium — the airwaves. The 10-codes and related signals (Signal One, for example, meant armed and dangerous) developed as a kind of shorthand and as, perhaps, a way to confuse the casual listener. And there have been plenty of average citizens who relied on police scanners to know what was going on in their neighborhoods.
“Although no one knows exactly how many Parsons homes are equipped with scanners,” Hurst Laviana wrote for the Parsons Sun in 1982, “estimates from law enforcement officers indicate anywhere from 10 to 40 percent.”
The story is a neat bit of enterprising reporting, with Laviana calling local telephone numbers at random to ask if they had a police scanner. Some did. One man said he didn’t use the scanner much, except when “something was going on.” A police officer Laviana spoke to said you’d think crooks would make scanners an essential tool, but that he’d never found a criminal who had one.
That may have been because the police didn’t use radio traffic for truly sensitive material, such as coordinating to execute a search warrant. For that and many other things, you’d often hear a request for the officer to contact dispatch via “public service,” meaning a telephone call.
Laviana, who would go on to become an investigative reporter for the Wichita Eagle and broke the story of the BTK serial killer’s return, died of cancer in 2023. He was 72. I didn’t know him, but I had a few phone conversations with him, and I remember once he called me and generously said “hats off” for a story I’d done about a local candidate running for governor who hadn’t voted in a general election for years.
When Laviana wrote the scanner story, the transition to programmable scanners was taking place. Instead of opening up the radio and inserting a crystal house inside a little metal canister about the size of a Chiclet for each channel, you could just punch a series of numbers into a keypad to select any frequency you wanted. At the Morning Sun at Pittsburg, my boss sent me down to Dick’s Electronics to get a new scanner for the newsroom, and I came back with one of the new programmable models, which cost about five times what he wanted to spend. It was probably the closest I came to being fired, at least over a piece of equipment.
A couple of decades later, in the 2000s, many agencies made the switch to trunked radio systems. It was more difficult to program a trunking radio, but if you had the patience (or you paid somebody else to do it) it was still possible to listen in to police dispatches. I have a trunked police scanner here in our house on Constitution Street, and I used to turn it on whenever red and blue lights painted the neighborhood. Most of the time it was the police pulling somebody over for going the wrong way down our one-way street.
From traffic violations to major disasters, journalists have used police scanners to monitor, in real time, news of all sizes. Even the most storied bit of reporting in memory began when an editor listening to a police scanner in the Washington Post newsroom heard that an open door to the Watergate complex was being investigated.
Now the police scanner is no more.
Law enforcement in Kansas and across the country have largely moved to encrypted communications for all calls, when formerly encryption was reserved for tactical channels. Oh, there are scattered departments that have not yet made the switch, but the move to secrecy is all but complete. You couldn’t listen on your old scanner if you wanted to, and even if you had a new radio capable of listening in and the decryption key to go with it, you’d be committing a felony under federal law.
Police nationwide are citing guidelines from the U.S. Department of Justice regarding sensitive information as the excuse to move to encryption. The Wichita Police Department, for example, went to encryption in April.
“The change is being made to comply with the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Security Policy, which requires (such information) be protected during transmission outside of secure environments,” according to a press release from Sedgwick County. “Because radio communication is not inherently secure, encryption is necessary to meet this federal requirement.”
Fire and emergency medical service calls would remain unencrypted, according to the press release.
“Media partners can continue to contact Sedgwick County Emergency Communications with time-sensitive inquiries,” the statement said. “Residents are encouraged to follow official department pages for local law enforcement agencies for safety alerts and notifications.”
Similar messages have gone out to communities across the country, citing a federal mandate that requires FBI Criminal Justice Information Services data to be protected by encryption. The 461-page policy includes not just radio traffic, but all  CJIS data stored or transmitted, and the deadline for compliance is Oct. 1, 2027. It does not cover all dispatch traffic, but most agencies are opting to go all-in with encryption. Officer safety often is cited as a rationale.
The result is not only to silence journalists’ primary source of breaking news, but to control the flow of information to news outlets through public information officers, PR professionals who know how to spin a story. It also encourages the public to monitor law enforcement social media accounts, which by nature offer an uncritical accounting of an agency’s activities.
“Police like to think they are protecting officers by encrypting radio, but in reality, they are endangering the public,” Tara Puckey, the president of the Radio Television Digital News Association, told me via email. “People need to be informed in emergencies, and journalists and the public have always used police radio to share vital information at critical times.”
The public has a right to know what is happening in their communities, she said, and “restricting the flow of information does not serve the greater good.”
There have been so many stories of national significance in the past year or so that the law enforcement migration to encryption hasn’t gotten the coverage or the public attention it deserves. It’s also an issue that’s difficult to explain to the public. But a reporter for LoudounNow, a nonprofit news site in Virginia, recently managed to do it.
The reporter, Patrick Lewis, in reporting on a planned move to encryption, quantified how news would be lost.
“Loudoun Now analyzed the Sheriff’s Office’s public notifications for 27 incidents that have happened in 2026,” Lewis reported, “including every robbery, shooting, stabbing, and active incident involving a firearm that Loudoun Now has reported on this year.”
Most of those incidents were first discovered by monitoring radio traffic or when information showed up in court filings. When the local sheriff’s department sent out public statements or posted about the incidents, it was typically hours or days later, and some incidents weren’t mentioned at all.
In Kansas, the press and the public face another burden, the HALO Act.
Patterned after proposed federal legislation meant to give ICE and other federal agents greater authority, the Kansas act creates a 25-foot buffer zone around law enforcement officers while engaged in official duties. Senate President Ty Masterson, a GOP hopeful in the GOP gubernatorial primary who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump, said the law would keep “radical protestors” at bay and keep officers and bystanders safe. He promised Kansas wouldn’t become like Minnesota, referring to the immigration raid protests that rocked Minneapolis early this year. In that unrest, two American citizens were killed by ICE agents.
The HALO law has been roundly criticized by the Kansas Press Association and free speech advocates as being unconstitutional. The GOP-controlled Legislature overrode a veto by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly to pass it into law, effective July 1.
It was used July 11 by ICE agents to move back a Lenexa woman who was recording video from her car, as reported by Kansas Reflector intern reporter Baya Burgess. An agent shouted “25 feet, 25 feet.” The woman wasn’t arrested, but the incident is representative of how the law is changing the way the public is documenting interactions with ICE agents.
It will also change the way reporters cover news, because it’s difficult to ask questions from 25 feet away.
If you’re having trouble visualizing just how far that is, imagine you’re standing on the sideline of a basketball court. Twenty-five feet is the center circle in the middle of the court, where the tipoffs happen.
The Kansas HALO law is bound to be challenged sooner or later because it hampers a journalist’s First Amendment right to gather news. But until that happens, a reporter’s rights — and your right to free speech as an average citizen — are being suppressed by lawmakers who choose to shield the actions of federal agents and other law enforcement officers from scrutiny.
In a just world, our lawmakers would be protecting citizens from the abuses of ICE officers, who have shot at 23 people since last year, killing six, according to research by the New York Times. Instead, the quisling majorities in the Kansas Statehouse are falling all over themselves to increase the distance between the public and its servant, the press, to protect the beer-bellied thugs in balaclavas.
It’s enough to make one reach for that bottle of scotch.
But for the record, I never drink while practicing journalism. Not while interviewing, not while writing, not while editing. The idea of having that bottle in my desk meant more to me than actually drinking it. Ah, those days are gone, like my Radio Shack PRO-70 scanner.
What the rush to encrypt police radio traffic and the craven passage of Kansas HALO has done is create an accountability gap between unbridled authority and the public’s right to know. Twenty-five foot buffer zones make it harder for the public, armed with smartphone cameras, to document abuses. The encryption of radio traffic is not about protecting the personally identifiable information of victims of crime and others, but is an excuse for agencies to clamp down on the sharing of real-time knowledge to journalists and the community. The FBI directive was to protect CJIS data, and some states — including Minnesota — concluded that it didn’t require blanket encryption of all dispatch traffic.
A democracy can be judged on how freely information flows to the public.
As a country, we’re backsliding.
The United States has dropped to 64th in press freedom, as calculated by Reporters Without Borders, between Botswana and Panama. In 2020, the U.S. was ranked 45.
“After a century of gradual expansion of press rights in the United States,” according to Reporters Without Borders, “the country is experiencing a significant and prolonged decline in press freedom, with Donald Trump’s return to the presidency greatly exacerbating the situation.”
Norway is ranked No. 1 in press freedom, as it has been for eight years.
An informed electorate is essential to democracy, and you can’t have that without a free and vigorous press — nationally, regionally, locally. If your town is still lucky enough to have a local newspaper, like mine does, support it by subscribing. If it doesn’t, start one. Donate to nonprofit news sites like Kansas Reflector. And the next time you meet a reporter, one who might even have a difficult question for you, tell her how much you appreciate the time and dedication good journalism takes.
She might be the one who breaks the next Watergate.
Police scanners aren’t coming back, but a reporter’s curiosity remains their most valuable asset.
Meanwhile, we’ll be left to ponder if the next set of red and blue lights on our block is for a traffic stop or a serial killer. In Kansas, we can’t even approach to ask the question.

Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: P.T. Barnum’s Bridgeport was no circus
description: Barnum helped build Bridgeport into an industrial powerhouse.
text:
When you think of P.T. Barnum your first thought is probably about his circus, or maybe his museum of oddities in 1840’s New York City.
What you may not know was that Barnum lived in Bridgeport and was once a state representative in Hartford and, in 1875, Bridgeport’s mayor.  His real genius wasn’t just in filling circus tents.  It was understanding logistics… how to move goods, people and opportunity efficiently.



Barnum was truly a city builder, especially because he understood that Bridgeport’s future depended on its railroads.
When the New York and New Haven Railroad reached Bridgeport in 1849, most people saw a passenger line.  Barnum saw the foundation of an industrial empire. He invested accordingly, donating land for Seaside Park, backing Bridgeport Hospital and subdividing his 30-acre Waldemere estate into neighborhoods that attracted Bridgeport’s industrial elite.  But most importantly he knew those civic amenities couldn’t survive without an economic engine.
That engine was the New Haven and Housatonic Railroads.
The railroads gave Bridgeport something neither Hartford nor New Haven could match: direct coastal access plus rail connectivity to New York, Massachusetts, and the entire Northeast.  Manufacturers could ship south to New York markets, north to New England, and worldwide via Long Island Sound.
Bridgeport manufactured everything: sewing machines, buggies, machine tools, munitions, every product imaginable.  But by the 1880s, there was a problem.
Bridgeport’s railroad tracks used to run at street level right through downtown… trains competing with pedestrians, horses, carriages.  It was constant gridlock.  For local factories trying to move freight 24/7, those grade crossings were a productivity killer.

P.T. Barnum was not only a circus operator but a Bridgeport mayor and state representative. Credit: Wikipedia

As mayor in 1875-1876, Barnum pushed hard for grade separation, elevating the tracks above street level.  Though he didn’t live to see it completed, the New Haven Railroad spent $5 million in the 1890s ($183 million in today’s inflated dollars) to build that viaduct.
Think a kind thought of Barnum the next time you ride Metro-North through Bridgeport, high above the streets.
Once those tracks were elevated, something remarkable happened. The Railroad Avenue industrial district exploded.  No more street-level bottlenecks.  Freight trains moved around the clock. Factories adjacent to the viaduct could load and unload directly onto rail cars.  Bridgeport boomed, eventually becoming one of Connecticut’s largest cities, filled with skilled immigrants making good money.
What Barnum understood better than most modern planners was that you can’t build a thriving city on civic projects alone.  Parks and hospitals matter.  But they’re all built on an economic foundation.
Today we’ve got it backwards. We debate roundabouts and bike lanes while underinvesting in regional rail connectivity.  The New Haven Line still runs through Bridgeport.  It still carries passengers and could still be an economic engine… carrying freight.  
Why no freight trains today along the coast?  Stay tuned.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Democratic candidates focus on ag future at Iowa Farmers Union forum
description: ELKHART — Nearly 100 Iowa Farmers Union members from across the state came out Saturday to learn how several Iowa Democratic candidates plan on leading change — especially for the ag industry and the struggling farm economy. The event at Big Oak Barn in Elkhart kicked off with Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democrat who is […]
text:
Nearly 100 Iowa Farmers Union members from across the state attended the annual barn party on July 25, 2026 at the Big Oak Barn in Elkhart, Iowa. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)ELKHART — Nearly 100 Iowa Farmers Union members from across the state came out Saturday to learn how several Iowa Democratic candidates plan on leading change — especially for the ag industry and the struggling farm economy.
The event at Big Oak Barn in Elkhart kicked off with Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democrat who is running for U.S. House District 3 against incumbent Republican Rep. Zach Nunn. She focused on how the farm bill is a viable way to address declining farm income.
“In the farm bill, we have tremendous opportunity to really incentivize the practices that we know make a difference, cover crops, no till. But in order to do those things, farmers have to invest in some new technology and they have to be prepared for a decrease in their productivity for a period of time,” Trone Garriott said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
State Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, Democratic candidate for U.S. House District 3, speaks July 25, 2026 at the Iowa Farmer Union’s annual barn party. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“We have to help them through it,” she continued. “We’re (farmers) under a lot of pressure right now and it’s really hard to make changes when you’re so stressed.”
She explained that during the Nixon administration, there was a huge investment in water quality and that priority cleaned up the country’s water.
“We can do that again,” Trone Garriott said. “I believe that we have the resources, we have the answers. We just need to direct that support and make it the priority. And we can make a huge positive impact for our state.”
Muhlbauer cites farm bankruptices, high input costs
Dave Muhlbauer, a fifth-generation farmer from Manila, Iowa, running for lieutenant governor on Democrat Rob Sand’s ticket, said he has prioritized agriculture and rural communities as part of his campaign.
Dave Muhlbauer, running for Iowa lieutenant governor on Rob Sand’s ticket, speaks during the Iowa Farmers Union annual barn party July 25, 2026 in Elkhart. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“If it’s a good idea, it doesn’t matter where it comes from,” Muhlbauer said. “It’s not right versus left but right versus wrong and we’re going in the wrong direction. I gotta say, people are very frustrated and upset with the direction of our state.”
Muhlbauer said many farmers are facing a fourth consecutive year of losses and last April farm bankruptcies hit a six-year high. He cited a recent report that found farm incomes have dropped 53% in the last three years. He said causes include the tariffs and high input prices like fuel and fertilizer as a result of the ongoing Iran conflict.
“This isn’t sustainable to our family farms and it’s further driving our state economy into the ditch,” Muhlbauer said. “You know, I’m a farmer. I’m a real farmer. That’s my livelihood and what I’ve done all my life, so I think it’s fitting for me to say it’s time to rotate crops.”
Jones calls for diversifying crops
Chris Jones, Democratic candidate for Iowa secretary of agriculture, speaks to Iowa Farmers Union members July 25, 2026 in Elkhart. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Chris Jones, Democratic candidate for secretary of agriculture, who spent his career monitoring water quality and high nitrate levels, agrees. He noted that Iowa is a two-crop state (corn and soybeans) and it’s time to diversify crops with a focus on crops that would thrive in Iowa. Diversifying crops, he said, would help reduce nitrate levels in Iowa’s water.
“It’s time to stop making incremental change and focus on structural change. It came to me that if we want to improve agriculture, if we want to create a resilient and a humane and a sustainable system that delivers good environmental outcomes, we need structural change,” Jones said.
To do this, Iowa needs diverse farming systems where farmers are growing oats, forage crops, vegetables and fruits,  Jones said. He is advocating for locally grown food to be served in local schools and his campaign is releasing a local food policy that will position Iowa to be the number one state in the country for access to local food.
“We can’t be saying we feed the world when we can’t feed Polk County,”  Jones said.
He is running against incumbent Republican Mike Naig.
Turek emphasizes need for change
Josh Turek, Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, speaks July 25, 2026 to Iowa Farmers Union members in Elkhart. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Josh Turek, Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, said Iowa needs candidates who are going to fight for Iowa and Iowans. “Fighting for social and economic justice, not just fighting for the billionaires and the large corporations. That’s the opportunity all of us have this year – working together.”
Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs who is running against Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson,  stressed that Iowa should not be leading the country in farm foreclosures. He made the promise if he is elected, he will fight to pass policies that support farmers, including enabling farmers to repair their equipment. He also promised to pass a farm bill that works for farmers. “I will not let Congress leave D.C. with a passive farm bill.”
He ended the evening highlighting what Iowans have been saying to him as he travels across the state speaking with Iowans:  “This is not the state I know. This is not the state I love. We need change. I voted for Ernst. I voted for Trump. Enough is enough.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: El-Sayed, Warren court McMorrow supporters at Ferndale rally
description: After Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in her campaign for U.S. Senate, just a few major endorsements remain up for grabs. While former state Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak) has not weighed in since suspending her campaign, former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed is hoping a rally in her district with […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen during a rally in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)After Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in her campaign for U.S. Senate, just a few major endorsements remain up for grabs.
While former state Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak) has not weighed in since suspending her campaign, former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed is hoping a rally in her district with one of her top endorsers might help win over some of her voters.
U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) endorsed El-Sayed last week after initially backing the campaign of McMorrow.
Warren said in an interview with the Michigan Advance that El-Sayed and McMorrow both ran without taking corporate PAC money, which she says has “swamped” the race to succeed retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters (D-Bloomfield Township).
“It’s corporate money hiding under a veil of neutrality,” Warren said. “Not a single one of these ads really tells us what the underlying agenda is all about: Stop Abdul from lowering the cost of drugs, stop Abdul from putting some curbs on crypto, stop Abdul from pushing back against arming Israel.”
U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren speaks at a rally for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal also spoke at the event. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) joined Warren and El-Sayed for a rally Saturday in Ferndale.
Van Hollen, a former Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, told reporters after the event that he views El-Sayed as the more electable candidate.
“How is it that somebody who needs $60 million just to convince voters in the primary is going to somehow be the stronger candidate in the general election,” Van Hollen said. “It just doesn’t compute.”
Peters, another former DSCC chair, has endorsed Stevens, saying she “will be ready on day one to fight for Michigan” and calling her a “workhorse.”
Whitmer said Stevens would do “whatever it takes to get things done for the people of Michigan.”
But El-Sayed said part of getting things done is “being able to communicate big ideas.”
“That’s what the fight is,” El-Sayed said. “They will discount speeches as, ‘Ah, look, you’re just one for speeches, they’re getting stuff done.’ But how do we get stuff done in politics if it’s not persuading people about what we can have and fight for, especially against the corrupting power of $60 million in this race?”
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a rally in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal also spoke at the event. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
El-Sayed said during the rally that he was outspent by both Whitmer and U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar during his 2018 campaign for governor but still earned 340,000 votes.
“We were two-to-one more efficient than the governor, three-to-one more efficient than a guy who’s currently in Congress,” El-Sayed said.
El-Sayed said outside spending in the U.S. Senate race, much of which comes from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, is a “$30 million down payment on the vote to send $3 billion somewhere else.”
Referring to outside donors, El-Sayed added, “They don’t give it to you because they think you’re nice. There is a pro quo at the end of the quid.”
El-Sayed at one point looked to the row of broadcast news cameras and addressed AIPAC directly.
“I know you’re watching,” El-Sayed said. “You ought to burn your damn money.”
He said tax dollars should be spent in the U.S., not to support “a foreign government that’s done genocide and apartheid, and now has taken us to a war for the goal of annexing southern Lebanon.”
El-Sayed was referencing Israel’s actions against Palestinians in Gaza, which have been labeled as a genocide by both Amnesty International and a United Nations independent commission. Israeli officials have also called for annexing portions of Lebanon.
“We’ve got potholes that need to be filled here in Michigan,” El-Sayed said, referencing Whitmer’s central campaign promise without naming her. “Eight years later, still need to be filled here in Michigan.”
Oak Park resident Renee Thornton attended the rally. Thornton said she, like Warren, supported McMorrow before the Democrat from Royal Oak suspended her campaign. Now, Thornton said she plans to vote for El-Sayed in the Aug. 4 primary.
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a rally in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal also spoke at the event. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Nan Shilts also attended Saturday’s rally as a former McMorrow supporter.
She said the endorsements of Warren, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders are helping to sway her toward El-Sayed because her granddaughters support the national progressives.
“They’re the future, so if that’s what they want, I’ll go with that,” Shilts said.
Shilts said while Whitmer endorsing Stevens could be a blow, her political influence is waning.
“I don’t think anybody’s paying attention to Governor Whitmer anymore,” Shilts said. “I like Governor Whitmer a great deal, but I think she’s become irrelevant.”
Her husband, John Shilts, said “a lot of Democrats think Gretchen turned her back on Michigan Democrats.”
“I don’t think she’s a Democrat anymore,” he said. “Gretchen Whitmer is Gretchen Whitmer. She’s running for herself.”
But Shilts said there’s no need for McMorrow to endorse after suspending her own campaign, adding that if McMorrow endorsed Stevens, he would wonder who got to her.
Warren, who some progressives have criticized for not endorsing Sanders for president in 2020 after dropping out, said she would “leave her the space to make her own decision.”
“It’s tough, and the dynamics are very different from one race to another,” Warren said.
El-Sayed said he would welcome McMorrow’s support but understands she has a lot to think about.
“You know, I’ve been in that position before where I ran a big campaign and it didn’t work out the way I wanted, and there’s a lot to figure out on the back end,” El-Sayed said. “That’s for her and her family to figure out together.”
Warren said El-Sayed is building a grassroots campaign where any one endorsement isn’t as important as it might be in a top-down approach.
“There are two issues in this campaign. One is cost, and one is corruption,” Warren said. “And the way you fight that fight and mean it is from the grassroots up.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: I led efforts to increase primary care spending in Rhode Island. Here are the things Massachusetts must get right.
description: High-quality primary care must be a common good for all Massachusetts residents. It is the most important part of a health care system, and it needs to be treated as such.
text:
THE PASSAGE BY the Massachusetts Senate of S-3116 at the end of June marks a milestone in efforts to strengthen Massachusetts’s vital but fragile primary care sector. The bill’s detractors are now furrowing their brows and defending the status quo. Their arguments should not carry the day.  
I know because I confronted and refuted those same arguments 15 years ago as Rhode Island’s health insurance commissioner when we started down the same path. 
Primary care is essential to a high-performing health system. It is the only health care service where an increased supply results in longer lives and more equitable outcomes. Hospitals, specialists, and the pharmaceutical industry cannot say the same thing. Yet because of political power and explicit public policy, we have funneled more and more money into those services, resulting in an ever-weakening primary care system, in Massachusetts and the country.  
The solution is clear but requires persistence. We must spend a greater portion of our health care dollar on primary care and pay for it in ways that allow primary care teams to improve access and coordination. This is exactly what S-3116 would do.  
The bill would require increasing the share of health care spending directed to primary care from the current level of less than 7 percent to at least 15 percent. It would phase in this shift over three years, starting in 2028, and require that the change have no net impact on health care spending, insurance premium prices, or cost sharing paid by patients.  
It recognizes that the current model of private rate negotiation between health insurers and providers advantages large systems, which use their size to negotiate high rates for their profitable medical services, leaving primary care clinicians with crumbs and patients without access.  
Faced with the prospect of change, insurers and health care providers have started wringing their hands. Insurers raise the prospect of increased insurance premiums. Providers, seeing a threat to their revenues, point to increases in the number of uninsured resulting from Medicaid cuts stretching their budgets.       
I have heard these arguments before, and they need to be recognized for what they are — a defense by entities invested in the current ways of doing things. This is the status quo that created this mess. 
In Rhode Island, 15 years ago, we saw the value and the impoverished state of primary care.  Confronted with the evidence, a consumer and business advisory council told the Office of the Health Insurance Commissioner, which I led, to increase primary care spending for commercial health insurance without adding to premiums. We used the annual rate review process to do just that, holding insurers accountable for increasing primary care spending without contributing to premium increases. 
And insurers did their part. It turns out when only 5 percent of health care dollars goes to primary care, to increase that portion you don’t have to take money away from anybody. You just have to give everybody else lower increases each year than they might like. After some initial resistance, insurers liked having a bad guy they could point to when they offered lower increases to specialists and hospitals.    
As for the costs of uninsured, those expenses are indeed significant for large health systems, but only as they are currently configured. While Massachusetts needs to continue its nation-leading efforts to keep everybody covered, it must also find cheaper ways to pay for that coverage.  
That means these large health systems — as the state Health Policy Commission has regularly articulated — must rebalance themselves to be more primary-care-oriented, so that uninsured people need not wait for expensive and wasteful emergency room care.  
With employer support and comprehensive rate review, provider and insurer handwringing did not carry the day in Rhode Island, and enforceable primary care spend targets were implemented. Subsequent premium increases have been significantly lower than in Massachusetts, and hospitals somehow managed to stay in business. However, overall primary care spending in the Ocean State has not increased in the last 15 years, and the state of primary care is no better than in Massachusetts.  
There were three major reasons for this: 1) our measures only affected commercial insurance — a small portion of the health care dollar — not Medicaid or large employers who self-insure and are not subject to state regulation; 2) we did not address how primary care got paid; and 3) we did not follow through with monitoring and oversight. 
The bill passed by the Massachusetts Senate — informed by the deliberations of the Primary Care Task Force established last year by the Legislature — learns from our efforts in Rhode Island and addresses all those shortcomings. It holds large health systems as well as insurers accountable for increasing primary care spending, thus covering the self-insured population. It prepares for a change in how primary care gets paid by facilitating the broad adoption of MassHealth’s highly acclaimed primary care payment model, where they have defied insurers’ concerns and raised primary care spending without contributing to increased overall Medicaid costs. And it establishes an office of primary care policy in the Health Policy Commission to keep the state’s collective eye on the ball.  
The bill’s architect, Sen. Cindy Friedman, and Senate President Karen Spilka have done the Commonwealth a great service in advancing this legislation. Attention now turns to the House, where “the assassins of progress,” as one Rhode Island advisory council participant memorably labeled industry soothsayers, will no doubt focus their efforts to defeat the bill. Those calls need to be ignored.  
High-quality primary care must be a common good for all Massachusetts residents. It is the most important part of a health care system, and it needs to be treated as such.  
Christopher Koller was the country’s first health insurance commissioner, serving in Rhode Island from 2005 to 2013. He is now a senior advisor at Ariadne Labs in Boston.

text:
A sign next the the grounds for the annual Fancy Farm Picnic thanks visitors for coming to the West Kentucky town. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Days after launching his bid for governor, Democrat Rocky Adkins will join the lineup of speakers at the upcoming Fancy Farm Picnic, a Kentucky political tradition. 
Meanwhile, the state’s top Democrat, Gov. Andy Beshear declined to speak this year.
Organizers announced the latest lineup Friday evening. The annual barbecue picnic, a fundraiser for the St. Jerome Catholic Church in Graves County held the first Saturday in August, has become a longstanding Kentucky tradition for elected officials and campaigning hopefuls. The 2026 picnic is scheduled for Aug. 1 in the West Kentucky town of Fancy Farm. 
Adkins kicked off his campaign Tuesday. He is currently facing  Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman, who launched her campaign in April and has previously said she will attend the picnic. 
Republicans Auditor Allison Ball and Treasurer Mark Metcalf also confirmed their attendance. 
The latest list of speakers attending are: 

State Sen. Jason Howell, R-Murray
State Rep. Kim Holloway, R-Mayfield
U.S. Sen. Rand Paul, Republican
U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, the Republican running for U.S. Senate
Former state Rep. Charles Booker, the Democrat running for U.S. Senate
U.S. Rep. James Comer, the Republican seeking reelection in the 1st Congressional District
John “Drew” Williams, the Democrat challenging Comer
Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman, Democrat running for governor in 2027
Rocky Adkins, Democrat running for governor in 2027
Attorney General Russell Coleman, a Republican seeking reelection 
Treasurer Mark Metcalf, Republican
Auditor Allison Ball, Republican 
Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell, Republican

Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams’ attendance was still pending, according to picnic organizers. However, he recently told the Lexington Herald-Leader that he was considering launching a run for governor at the Fancy Farm Picnic or after it. 
Another Republican, U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell has been invited but has yet to decline or accept. He was hospitalized last month and has since moved to a rehabilitation center.  
Typically, only politicians who hold office or are seeking office in general elections to represent the Western Kentucky region speak at Fancy Farm. However, that’s changed with the addition of Adkins to this year’s lineup. Last year, three Republican candidates for U.S. Senate spoke. 
Steven Elder, the political chairman of the picnic, said the committee for the event “wants to ensure that the Fancy Farm Picnic remains relevant. By continuing to include primary candidates for upcoming elections, we can ensure a dynamic event.” 
“For Rocky Adkins, we felt that current officeholders will likely speak about their future candidacy or plans,” Elder added. “Since this is the last picnic before the primary, we felt that because of his name recognition, fundraising ability to compete, and electability, he should be given the opportunity to address the crowd.” 
The general election is in November and the primary is in May.

title: Sen. Ted Cruz calls for regulating kids’ use of AI chatbots at Hinson campaign event
description: ANKENY — U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz said Saturday Congress needs to find a balance between regulating artificial intelligence chatbots and incentivizing the growth of the country’s AI industry as he joined U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson at a roundtable in Ankeny. Hinson aims to join Cruz in the Senate through her 2026 campaign to fill the […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson was joined by U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz July 25, 2026 in Ankeny at a campaign event for her 2026 Senate run where the Republicans spoke with Iowans for a roundtable focused on children's online safety. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)ANKENY — U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz said Saturday Congress needs to find a balance between regulating artificial intelligence chatbots and incentivizing the growth of the country’s AI industry as he joined U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson at a roundtable in Ankeny.
Hinson aims to join Cruz in the Senate through her 2026 campaign to fill the seat currently held by U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst, and is running against state Rep. Josh Turek, D-Council Bluffs, in the 2026 general election. At Faith Baptist Bible College Saturday, she and the Cruz spoke with Iowa parents about what lawmakers in Washington D.C. can do to help better protect children in online spaces.
Cruz pointed to measures already passed by the U.S. Senate to address these concerns — like the “TAKE IT DOWN Act,” led by him and Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, to criminalize both real and “deepfake” revenge pornography. He also pointed to the Kids Off Social Media Act, known as KOSMA, which sets the minimum age for social media platforms to 13, requires schools receiving federal funds to block social media on campus and bans companies from algorithmic boosting of content for users under age 17.
Cruz said there was a “generational divide” in the U.S. Senate on these issues — a majority of the sponsors of KOSMA, he said, were senators in their 40s and 50s, while older senators were not as involved.
“That’s one of the many reasons why why I’m excited for Ashley to come join us, because I think bringing the perspective of a mom dealing with these challenges every day when you go home at night,” he said. “That’s real, and we need that kind of urgency to understand why we need to be doing what we do.”
Members of the roundtable also brought up concerns about children interacting with predators or other bad actors on gaming platforms. Hinson said her sons play games like Roblox, which involve interaction with others online, and that could be an area where the government could set age restrictions or put other protections in place for children.
“You think about all the different places where we may need to be looking at these protections — it’s not just social media; it’s any place there may be a social interaction, and technology is that intersection,” Hinson said. “So whether it’s a big tech company or a gaming company, we may need to have conversations about what age limits are appropriate.”
The federal government has taken some steps to address concerns about social media, but members of the roundtable said there’s a new major concern about regulating digital spaces for minors: the use of artificial intelligence. Cruz said he’s working on a bill that he is calling “chatbot KOSMA” that he said would give parents control over whether their children interact with chatbots, like ChatGPT or Claude, and allow parents to see their children’s conversations.
Hinson said there were some chatbot protections included in the Kids Internet and Digital Safety Initiative passed by the House that regulate when an AI bot is “masquerading as a professional” or counseling a minor on issues like suicidal ideation or medical advice. But she said there was more work to be done.
“We want to make sure that the chatbots are also in their own lane, right?” Hinson said. “Because I think that’s the new frontier dealing with AI and the challenge that we are frankly struggling to keep up with on the policy side, because it’s moved so fast and advanced so quickly. Trying to figure out how we rein that in so that we’re not limiting everything, but we make sure we protect our kids from nefarious actors.”
Though the politicians said they want to put guardrails on AI, Cruz said it was also important to keep in mind that the U.S. was competing with China to become the “dominant standard” in the field — a competition he said it was vital for the U.S. to win.
“I very much want America to win that race, both because trillions of dollars of investment and millions of jobs are going to flow to whoever wins that race — and so I want them to come to America and not go to China — but equally important, whichever country wins that race, the values of that country are going to suffuse AI,” Cruz said. “So if China wins, the values of the Chinese Communist Party will suffuse AI. You will have surveillance and espionage and propaganda and control throughout AI. I very much want American values of free speech and individual liberty and free markets and individual rights, those values to suffuse AI.”
State Rep. Ryan Weldon, R-Ankeny, who joined the panel, said regulating chatbots has been a serious discussion in the Iowa Legislature as well. When state lawmakers were considering measures to restrict minors’ access to interact with chatbots — primarily large language models — concerns came from the private sector about these measures inadvertently impacting businesses that use “closed loop” AI chatbots for customer service or other specific purposes.
Weldon also said Congress should consider ways to encourage businesses to develop AI and other technologies that fall in line with their safety standards.
“We talk a lot about restrictions and I think those are good conversations,” he said. “In the private sector, we talk a lot about, ‘you get what you incentivize.’ And so I just wonder if there’s some some ways that we can incentivize our innovative companies to create products and services that will be safe for all of us to use without without these scary things. I’m a big believer in the free market and getting government out of the way so that people can do what they do, but just on the incentives, I wonder if there’s maybe some options.”
