name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Democrats say they’ll consider fate of ’28 caucuses after midterm elections
description: Iowa Democratic Party Chair Rita Hart said the party will “have more to say after November” about its path forward in the 2028 presidential nominating cycle after the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee denied Iowa a waiver to hold an early contest. Members of the Rules and Bylaws Committee voted Friday in Washington, […]
text:
Iowa Democratic Party Chair Rita Hart did not rule out defying the national party when scheduling the Iowa caucuses in 2028. Here, she is shown speaking to reporters at the party's headquarters in Des Moines on March 5, 2024. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Democratic Party Chair Rita Hart said the party will “have more to say after November” about its path forward in the 2028 presidential nominating cycle after the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee denied Iowa a waiver to hold an early contest.
Members of the Rules and Bylaws Committee voted Friday in Washington, D.C., to have South Carolina lead Democrats’ 2028 nominating calendar, with the state’s primary set to kick off the nominating process Jan. 22, 2028.
The panel also approved waiver requests from five other states to hold their nominating contests before Super Tuesday, with a tentative order set for Nevada’s contest on Feb. 1, New Hampshire, Feb. 8; New Mexico, Feb. 15; Michigan, Feb. 22 and Virginia Feb. 29.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Notably absent from the 2028 calendar is Iowa, the state which held its “first in the nation” status leading the presidential nominating cycle for both parties for several decades. This changed beginning in the 2024 presidential nominating cycle, after the DNC approved a new calendar that started with South Carolina, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, Georgia and Michigan.
Because there were issues with Georgia and New Hampshire implementing the new calendar during the 2024 cycle, the DNC decided to restructure its nominating calendar once again ahead of 2028.
Iowa Republicans continued to hold first-in-the-nation caucuses in 2022 and are expected to be first again in 2028.
Scott Brennan, an Iowan serving on the DNC and a former member of the Rules and Bylaws Committee, said in a news conference Friday he expected Iowa would not be chosen in the early window once again. Brennan lost his spot on the RBC in 2025, after the election of DNC Chair Ken Martin earlier that year.
“Look, I’m not surprised by this decision,” Brennan said. “It was probably decided 18 months ago when the new members of the Rules and Bylaws Committee were appointed by Chair Martin. … When we lost the White House, we did make a good faith effort to share our concerns, but clearly, our case was not heard by this committee or Chair Martin.”
The panel approved four states to represent the Eastern, Midwest, Southwest and Southern regions of the U.S. in the early window, alongside granting waivers to two additional states — New Mexico and Virginia. In the current calendar set up, Michigan is set to be the only state in the “Midwest” region to hold an early contest, which is set to be the fifth of six in the early window.
Iowa Rep. Ross Wilburn, D-Ames, one of the Democrats who presented before the RBC earlier this year, said he shared Hart’s “frustration and disappointment” about the panel’s decision Friday. He said the proposed calendar “signals to voters here in the Midwest that their voices don’t matter.”
“As I told the committee in May, if we want to build lasting, sustainable majorities, then enact real change, Democrats need to invest in Iowa and the Midwest — not leave us behind, like they did today,” Wilburn said. “We can’t win the White House without the Midwest, and we can’t afford to continue to let Republicans have a spotlight in Iowa and Middle America.”
While the DNC did not give Iowa approval to hold a contest in the early window, the state party still has the ability to “go rogue” and hold a contest out of compliance with the DNC calendar. This decision would result in penalties — the DNC would not seat state delegates at the 2028 national convention, and the state party would incur a $270,000 fine. Candidates campaigning in Iowa, if the state holds a rogue contest, would be banned from earning delegates in early states, and would not be allowed to appear in DNC-approved debates.
Despite these sanctions, Iowa Democrats are still considering this path in 2028. The discussion comes after New Hampshire defied the DNC calendar in 2024, which resulted in the state initially having their delegates stripped but later restored by the DNC. New Hampshire also gained an additional seat on the RBC after the 2024 election.
With South Carolina given the starting position again in 2028, Brennan said, “New Hampshire’s not gonna stand for this calendar” and expected similar conflicts to occur. He also said “Nevada was all in on being first” and were unhappy with the RBC decision, which he said means “all bets are off” on the calendar approved Friday standing.
Iowa GOP chair pushes for rogue Democratic contest
In 2024, the state complied with the DNC calendar. Iowa GOP Chair Jeff Kaufmann told reporters Friday he believed this decision was “an abrogation of duty on the part of the Iowa Democratic Party” and led to the DNC disregarding Iowa in the 2028 process.
“The bottom line is, the time when you should have stood up to the Democratic National Committee was at the last caucus,” he said. “… You don’t have to be a political sage to realize what was occurring and what was going on here, and the Iowa Democratic Party let it happen by not pushing back. And now we’ve got the situation where, exactly what I’ve been saying all along, is the coasts, the progressive wing, has literally targeted the state of Iowa and yanked them out.”
Kaufmann said he wants to see Iowa Democrats give a “clear, decisive reaction that says, ‘we are going first, and we are going to comply with state law and hold a caucus.'”
“And at the same time, they’re saying that, I’d like to see follow up, follow up promises from their political leaders that they will stand with them,” Kaufmann said. “… That’s what I would do. Will that work? I don’t know. Seems to have worked pretty well with New Hampshire.”
While Hart did not say if the state would hold an unsanctioned contest in 2028, she said Iowa Democrats are in a difficult position and that she had received many comments from people encouraging the state party to not comply with the calendar.
“I had this conversation with Ken Martin and with some of the members of the RBC, that it’s pretty hard to defend any kind of situation that we’re in right now,” Hart said. “When we got slapped last time, when we worked in cooperation with the DNC and lost our representation on the RBC, in comparison to other states that did not cooperate and got rewarded. So it’s really hard to make a case to these people that say, you know, ‘why work with the DNC going forward?’ But I would say that that is a conversation that is not doesn’t need to be taking place right now. As we, when we get to November, and we have some newly elected Democratic officials, they’re gonna have some things to say about that, along with the rest of our Democrats.”
Iowa is expected to have many competitive races in the 2026 general election, including the race for Iowa governor between State Auditor Rob Sand, a Democrat, and businessman Zach Lahn, as well as races in Iowa’s 1st and 3rd Districts where Democratic challengers hope to unseat GOP incumbent Reps. Marianette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn. Iowa’s U.S. Senate race, where GOP U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, D-Council Bluffs, has also gained national attention.
Hart expressed frustration with the DNC moving forward with setting the 2028 nominating calendar before the 2026 midterms, saying it could have an impact on Democratic candidates’ ability to win in states like Iowa.
However, Brennan offered optimism, saying, “frankly, by doing this, it allows us to just purely focus on these elections in November.” He said Democratic victories in Iowa in the midterms would put the state party in a stronger position on future conversations about the 2028 nominating cycle.
“I think after the election, when it goes well, then I think we will just tell the national folks that, you know, we are ready to participate in the ’28 process on our terms,” he said. “… I’m not worried about them. We focused here, because we’re gonna win elections here, and then, we’ll go tell them what we’re gonna do.”

title: Suit alleges Homeland Security targeted people observing, protesting immigration agents
text: Three people who observed federal immigration enforcement during the Trump administration’s sometimes-violent surge said in a federal lawsuit filed Friday the Department of Homeland Security illegally recorded them and revoked their status in the department’s trusted traveler programs.The suit, filed in the Southern District of California, says the administration violated a federal privacy law, administrative law and the First Amendment by targeting people who observed and protested aggressive immigration enforcement, including during the deadly operation in Minneapolis in January. The Electronic Privacy Information Center, a legal group that advocates for privacy issues related to technology, is also a plaintiff in the case.Amid a nationwide surge of immigration enforcement that has included federal agents shooting and killing protesters, observers and immigrants, opponents “did what anyone is supposed to do when they disagree with government action: They exercised their First Amendment rights” by assembling, protesting and recording DHS agents’ activity in public, the suit says.“In response, DHS decided to record the Americans who were peacefully observing its agents,” the suit says.Officers with the DHS agencies Immigration and Customs Protection and Border Patrol killed two observers, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis in incidents 17 days apart in January. ‘Driven home by ICE’ICE and Border Patrol agents used facial recognition technology, license plate readers and other technology to identify protesters and observers. The agents would then use that information in efforts to intimidate and retaliate against protesters, the suit says. Federal immigration officers addressed many legal observers by name, despite having never spoken to them. In Minnesota, legal observers tailing DHS agents in a car would commonly be led back to their own home addresses, according to the suit.“The experience … is so widespread that Minnesota residents have coined a term for it: being ‘driven home by ICE,’” the suit said.The practice shows that DHS is no longer following its own 2023 policy on facial recognition, the suit says. The department quietly removed the policy from its website — omitting it even from a set of archived pages — during President Donald Trump’s first month back in office, the suit says.The complaint argues that amounted to a policy change, which DHS did not conduct through the process agencies must follow under the Administrative Procedure Act. The department also retaliated against protesters and observers by revoking their status in DHS trusted traveler programs TSA Precheck and Global Entry, the suit says.Nicole Cleland, a Minnesota woman who is one of the individual plaintiffs in the suit, said Global Entry status was revoked three days after an encounter with a Border Patrol agent whom she was following at a safe distance, according to the suit.Chilling rightsThe suit alleges DHS’ actions have had a chilling effect on First Amendment-protected activity. Cleland has stopped observing DHS operations for fear of further retaliation, according to the suit.The two other individuals who brought the suit, Jacquelyn Ivey of South Carolina and Anna Walker of California, said they experienced “fear, anxiety and emotional distress” following their interactions with DHS officers.The suit also mentions activity in Maine, North Carolina and Chicago.DHS responseIn response to a request to DHS for comment, a spokesperson for Customs and Border Protection, which administers Global Entry, said trusted traveler status can be denied for “inability to demonstrate low-risk traveler status.”“Global Entry or other CBP Trusted Traveler Program memberships are not revoked because someone exercises their First Amendment rights,” the spokesperson wrote. “Membership may be denied or revoked for reasons such as criminal activity (including pending charges or warrants), violations of customs or immigration laws, or inability to demonstrate low-risk traveler status.”The spokesperson added that travelers whose Global Entry is denied or revoked can ask for additional review. A Global Entry ombudsman provides “additional oversight” of some cases, the spokesperson said. A denial of Global Entry is not an impediment to travel, they wrote.DHS did not respond to questions about its policies for recording or using facial recognition on observers.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: League of Women Voters, Law Forward sue elections commission over absentee counting
description: The League of Women Voters of Wisconsin filed a lawsuit Thursday against Wisconsin Elections Commission guidance that bars people who request an absentee ballot from casting an in-person ballot if the mail ballot will not arrive by the time polls close on Election Day.  The lawsuit was filed as officials in Wisconsin, and the commission […]
text:
Chief Inspector Megan Williamson processes absentee ballots at the Hawthorne Library on Madison's East Side. (Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)The League of Women Voters of Wisconsin filed a lawsuit Thursday against Wisconsin Elections Commission guidance that bars people who request an absentee ballot from casting an in-person ballot if the mail ballot will not arrive by the time polls close on Election Day. 
The lawsuit was filed as officials in Wisconsin, and the commission itself, have warned voters about potential delays in the mail system ahead of this year’s August and November elections. 
But commission guidance states that once voters mail their absentee ballots back to the clerk, they cannot be issued new ballots at the polls on Election Day. This means that if voters realize their ballots will not arrive in time after early in-person voting closes the Sunday before an election, they will not be able to vote. 
“Once a voter has placed their ballot in the mail, it is considered mailed,” the WEC guidance states. “They cannot be issued a new ballot at the polling place on Election Day, even if their absentee ballot will not be returned to the clerk’s office in time to be counted.”
The lawsuit seeks to allow voters who believe their ballots will not arrive to the clerk in time to go in person to cast a provisional ballot that would be set aside and only be counted if the initial ballot does not arrive by the deadline. 
Hundreds of voters did not have their votes counted during the state’s April elections because their ballots did not arrive in time. A WEC survey of clerks following the April election reported that hundreds of the state’s election officials believed delays in the mail had caused problems in the spring election. 
“Every voter in Wisconsin that puts an accurately requested absentee ballot in the mail on time expects their vote will be counted. Delays in mail delivery prevent that. It is time to have a remedy for these eligible voters,” Debra Cronmiller, executive director of the League of Women Voters of Wisconsin, said. 
The League is represented in the lawsuit by Law Forward and the Fair Elections Center. The lawsuit argues that the commission understands the problem but is not taking advantage of an obvious solution to the potential mail delays. 
“The right to vote protects Wisconsinites from baseless disenfranchisement on Election Day. But WEC wants to turn these voters away. That’s just wrong,” Law Forward attorney Scott Thompson said. “We shouldn’t punish Wisconsin voters just because the mail is late. They must have the opportunity to vote on Election Day.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Ruiz family wants charges against officer, body cameras for Madison cops
description: Family members  of Corey Ruiz, who was shot and killed by a Madison police officer on the city’s east side Wednesday, said at an emotional press conference Friday afternoon they want charges filed against the officer who fired the shots and for Madison cops to be equipped with body cameras.  Speaking from the Assembly parlor […]
text:
Corey Ruiz's daughter, Kah'liyah, wipes away tears while speaking at a press conference about the police killing of her father. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Family members  of Corey Ruiz, who was shot and killed by a Madison police officer on the city’s east side Wednesday, said at an emotional press conference Friday afternoon they want charges filed against the officer who fired the shots and for Madison cops to be equipped with body cameras. 
Speaking from the Assembly parlor in the state Capitol building, Ruiz’s mother, two sisters, brother, daughter and daughter’s mother spoke of a man who loved to crack jokes, make music and work in construction. 
The family was joined by state Rep. Shelia Stubbs (D-Madison) and Ben Crump, a national civil rights attorney who has frequently represented the families of people of color killed by police. 
Orchestrating the press conference, Crump noted Madison’s policy against high speed chases for property crimes — Ruiz was first chased by police on his bike after officers responded to reports that someone in the area was looking into parked cars. Crump also raised questions about whether  the other officers on the scene believed deadly force was necessary and if Ruiz actually brandished the knife police have said he used against the officer who shot him. 
“We saw an execution, and it shocked our conscience,” Crump said. “People all over Wisconsin were shocked when they saw the execution of Corey Ruiz. People all over America are shocked when they see the execution of Corey Ruiz, because they understand when they see that video that it was so unnecessary to execute him. It was unnecessary, unjustifiable, and unconstitutional how they executed Corey Ruiz.”
Crump also said he wants officials to be transparent about the investigation, which is being conducted by the Wisconsin Department of Justice under a state law that requires officer-involved shooting investigations to be led by  an outside agency. Crump added that he believes the officer responsible should be charged with a crime. 
Marjorie Ann Aliomar, the mother of Ruiz’s 13-year-old daughter, Kah’liyah, said the tragedy was especially painful because the shooting took place at a busy intersection in their own neighborhood. 
“This place is two blocks up the street from our home, two blocks away from her school,” Aliomar said. “Every day she has to walk to school … she would have to walk past her dad’s memorial, where he was murdered by people we’re supposed to trust and depend on.”
While wiping away tears, Kah’liyah addressed the police. 
“How can I call you knowing you shot my father?” she said. “How are you going to have four policemen on one Black man? On top of that, how are you going to get scared of us if you’re supposed to save us?” 
Several times, Ruiz’s family said they wanted the city to equip Madison cops with body cameras. 
For years, city and police officials have requested body cameras for all Madison police and a body camera pilot program is currently underway on the city’s north side. 
Last fall, the common council voted against allocating money in the budget for a citywide body camera program, instead sending that money to the city’s Office of the Independent Monitor — the civilian oversight body that tracks the police department. 
Ripple effects 
Protests over the killing of Ruiz continue to make waves across the city. 
Two days after the shooting, activists still control the intersection of Baldwin and Williamson Streets where the shooting occurred, with makeshift barricades of garbage bins, mattresses and scrap metal blocking off the streets in every direction. 
Organizers of Atwood Fest, a popular annual street festival that takes place a few blocks east of the shooting’s location, was canceled. 
“Our community and our Marquette neighbors witnessed another horrific officer-involved shooting just blocks from our festival grounds, leaving us in deep pain and justified anger,” organizers wrote on the festival website. “AtwoodFest’s core values have always centered on building community, using each festival’s proceeds to support the groups doing important work right here in our neighborhood. Now it is vital to support our neighbors, particularly those who have borne the brunt of this pain and injustice, by taking time to mourn and reflect on our role in these broken systems, so we can create a community that truly lives up to our values.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Feds sue Milwaukee over ordinance against law enforcement masking
description: The U.S. government filed a lawsuit against the city of Milwaukee Thursday, arguing the city has no authority to enforce its ordinance preventing law enforcement from wearing masks while interacting with the public.  The lawsuit, filed against the city as well as its mayor, city attorney and police chief, argues that cities and states are […]
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer watches a crowd of protesters at Delaney Hall in Newark, New Jersey, on May 25, 2026. (Photo by Ben Ackman/New Jersey Monitor)The U.S. government filed a lawsuit against the city of Milwaukee Thursday, arguing the city has no authority to enforce its ordinance preventing law enforcement from wearing masks while interacting with the public. 
The lawsuit, filed against the city as well as its mayor, city attorney and police chief, argues that cities and states are unable to regulate federal government action. 
“For centuries, the Supreme Court has reaffirmed that States have no authority whatsoever to regulate the Federal Government,” the lawsuit states. “Despite that well-established principle, Milwaukee recently enacted an ordinance that purports to do exactly what constitutional law says it cannot: regulate how federal law enforcement officers carry out their official duties in that City.”
Initially enacted in April, the Milwaukee ordinance prohibits law enforcement officers performing their duties from covering their faces and requires that their names and the agency they work for be easily identifiable on their uniform. 
“The use of facial coverings and disguises by law enforcement officers significantly affects the public’s perception of law enforcement, officer-community interactions, and accountability,” the ordinance states. “Persons reasonably may experience fear or intimidation when approached by officers whose faces are obscured. Such reactions can heighten defensive behavior and unnecessarily escalate the tension inherent in many interactions between law enforcement officers and members of the public.”
Last week, City Attorney Evan Goyke wrote in a letter to U.S. prosecutors  that federal officers wouldn’t be exempted from the ordinance, prompting the lawsuit. 
“the City and the public have a right to know if masked, armed, and unidentified men seizing people on our streets are who they say they are,” Goyke wrote, objecting to the federal government’s insistence that immigration officers be allowed to conceal their identities “at their discretion.”
“Unfortunately, in the case of federal immigration officers, in particular, that unbounded discretion, coupled with guns and a lack of accountability, has had tragic consequences in cities across the country,” he wrote. Goyke disputed the federal government’s claim that the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution makes ordinances such as Milwaukee’s illegal, citing previous and ongoing litigation on the matter.
Federal immigration officers across the country have worn masks while carrying out  President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigrants. Federal officials have argued the masks prevent officers from being doxxed. 
“State and local leaders cannot tell Federal officers how to do their job,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. said in a news release. “And they certainly cannot prohibit them from ensuring their own safety in safeguarding our communities and enforcing federal law. We will never tolerate the doxxing or harassment of federal officers, or any law like Milwaukee’s that enables violent behavior against law enforcement officers and their families.”
The lawsuit argues that federal officers should be able to make decisions about covering their faces on a case-by-case basis. 
“Denying federal agencies and officers discretion in these areas would chill federal law enforcement, threatening the safety of communities in Milwaukee,” the lawsuit states.
Brad Schimel, the former conservative Supreme Court candidate who is now an assistant U.S. attorney, said that the ordinance pits federal and local cops against each other. 
“Not only is this ordinance an affront to the Constitution, but it jeopardizes the safety of our courageous sworn law enforcement officers,” Schimel said. “Further, it puts local and federal law enforcement officers at odds with each other when they should be working together on the common goals to enforce the rule of law and keep our communities safe.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bronin campaign, Iran war votes, TPS holders: CT politics news
description: Plus: Work stacks up for Congress post-recess, a report condemns "extorded compliance," and CT puts $10M towards rural infrastructure.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more news about the 2026 legislative session, campaigns, elections and more, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Bronin gets help promoting campaign
Impact CT, an independent-expenditure group chaired by former New Haven Mayor Toni Harp, is running digital ads and paying for direct mail in support of former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin’s campaign to unseat Congressman John B. Larson in the 1st Congressional District.
The ads and mailer are positive pieces, making the case for generational change in the days before the Democratic primary on Aug. 11. Neither mention Larson, the 78-year incumbent seeking a 15th term. Impact typically focuses on General Assembly campaigns, but it did spend money promoting U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, in the general election two years ago.
— Mark Pazniokas, Capitol Bureau Chief
CT delegation supports more war power votes
The House and Senate took separate votes this week on war powers resolutions to rein in the war in Iran. Democrats have forced votes multiple times since the start. Most have failed, though recent attempts have been more successful, albeit mostly symbolic.
For a second time, the House voted to end the hostilities as the U.S. ramps up strikes and oil prices surge. All Democrats backed it, including Connecticut’s delegation, and four Republicans. But later that day, the Senate blocked consideration of its own war powers vote. Speaking from the floor, Sen. Chris Murphy argued that the administration “has not achieved a single war goal.”
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
Work stacks up for Congress post-recess
The House left town Thursday for its monthlong recess — and the Senate will follow in early August. They’ll return to a lengthy to-do list of must-pass bills.
House Republicans passed a short-term government funding bill well before the deadline. Most Democrats were opposed, including Connecticut’s delegation. Rep. Rosa DeLauro warned there are issues regarding Border Patrol in the current version.
They’ll also need to tackle compromise legislation on the annual defense policy bill. The House passed its bill and attached the SAVE America Act to it. That led Democrats like Rep. Joe Courtney to oppose it, though he noted the wins for Connecticut’s defense industry.
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
As protective status expiration looms, Haitian TPS holders could be pulled out of CT workforce
On Monday, work permits and legal status expires for some 350,000 Haitian Temporary Protected Status program holders in the U.S. — including roughly 5,000 living in Connecticut. The expiration will impact a significant portion of Haitian communities in Bridgeport, New London and Norwich.
The end of Temporary Protected Status, which provides a lifeline for immigrant populations fleeing political violence and environmental disasters, could also affect the state’s economy more broadly, pulling people out of the workforce as unemployment rises and Connecticut’s labor force continues to shrink. Estimates suggest that some 100 Haitian caregivers could be affected by the decision, reducing the number of nursing home workers amid larger struggles to support aging communities in the state.
A 2025 report from DataHaven found that immigrant workers are vital to the state’s economy, helping offset population declines and working in several key industries, including agriculture, healthcare, and early childhood education.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Report condemns “extorted compliance”
The Trump administration has developed a reputation in higher ed: It withholds federal funding from universities for alleged discrimination, then extracts wide-ranging concessions.
The practice is what the American Association of University Professors called “governance by extortion” in a scathing report released Wednesday. They argued the administration uses civil rights compliance as a pretext for taking government control over higher education.
The report comes weeks after news broke that Yale University is considering a settlement with the Trump administration. Students and faculty have called on university to reject any agreement that involves concessions like those made at peers like Columbia.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
CT puts $10M towards rural infrastructure
The Lamont administration is pouring $10 million into rural transportation infrastructure, providing funding to projects that are often ineligible for money from the federal government.
The money, announced on Thursday, will come from the third round of the state’s Transportation Rural Improvement Program (TRIP). Established in 2022, the program is administered by the Department of Transportation and has awarded $30 million to 27 projects.
Nine projects will get funding in this round, including more than $1.9 million for road intersection drainage and surface reclamation in Chaplin; $1.85 million for community access corridor rehabilitation in North Canaan, and more than $850,000 for sidewalk and trail construction in Haddam.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont doesn’t need political parties to get things done
description:
Vermont could set a national example by replacing party politics with merit-based elections and ranked-choice voting.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont doesn’t need political parties to get things done.
text:
Dear Editor,
Since Vermont has a political landscape that is probably less partisan than most states and, without a doubt, far less partisan than Washington, maybe it can set an example for how to move away from partisan politics. We urgently need cooperative, nonconfrontational efforts to mitigate the host of critical problems we face.
It seems that political parties often foster irrational noncooperation. What if Vermont eliminated political parties and candidates ran on their individual merits? We could have an open primary season in which candidates would provide, on a statewide website, their photos, appropriate personal information, what they would like to accomplish, how they would achieve those goals by working with others and any other information they deem appropriate.  

READ MORE

There should probably be a comments and suggestions section for each candidate. They would not bear a party label. No campaign funding would be allowed, but organizations and individuals could endorse candidates on the Vermont website. Candidates would be free to campaign in person and through media appearances, but not pay for advertising.
On primary day, voters would choose from a list of candidates who have met the residency and informational requirements for the Vermont website using ranked-choice voting. This tends to foster constructive debate among candidates and makes it more likely that voters will cast their ballots for candidates they think are best, since their vote is not wasted on a long shot.  
Assuming a primary attracts multiple candidates, the top two in each race would stand for election on the November ballot. Neither would have a party label. Campaign spending and advertising restrictions would stay. Voting in the November general election would be like it is now: Whoever gets the majority of the votes wins.
For those elected to go to Montpelier, more leadership and committee choices would be based first on merit rather than party affiliation.
We don’t have time to waste putting better ideas into practice.
Gerry Hawkes
Woodstock, Vt.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Engling campaign says it returned $60K donation from dark money group
description: A complaint to Indiana election officials alleges that Republican secretary of state candidate Max Engling violated state law by accepting a $60,000 campaign contribution from a dark money group associated with U.S. Sen. Jim Banks.
text:
Max Engling speaks with reporters after winning the Republican secretary of state nomination on June 20, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A complaint to Indiana election officials alleges that Republican secretary of state candidate Max Engling violated state law by accepting a $60,000 campaign contribution from a dark money group associated with U.S. Sen. Jim Banks.
The Engling campaign said it had already returned all of that money before the complaint was filed Friday by Knox County Clerk David Shelton, who finished second to Engling in seeking the Republican nomination during last month’s state party convention.
The complaint pertains to a $60,000 contribution on June 30 to Engling’s campaign from Hoosier Leadership for America, which is registered with the state as a nonprofit corporation with a post office box address in the Allen County community of Huntertown.
US Sen. Banks takes an unusually active role in attacking anti-redistricting lawmakers

Shelton’s complaint asks the Indiana Election Commission to take action against the Engling for violating state law that limits corporations and labor organizations to a maximum of $5,000 a year in contributions to statewide office candidates.
Those limits don’t apply to individuals, limited liability corporations and political action committees that are required to disclose their sources of money.
The Engling campaign said Friday that the $60,000 was refunded on July 14 after being flagged during an internal review. The return will appear on the next report due in October. 
“We determined its entity type was unclear and thus refunded out of an abundance of caution. The donation was made via wire. Once a wire is made, we can’t stop it,” campaign spokeswoman Chloe Anagnos told the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
Shelton said in the complaint that Engling wrongly recorded the Hoosier Leadership for America contribution as coming from a non-corporate source.
“Hoosier Leadership for America, Inc. has never registered as a political committee with the Election Division or the Federal Election Commission,” Shelton’s complaint said. “Any contention by (Hoosier Leadership) that it is not subject to the corporate contribution limit is therefore an admission that it operated as an unregistered political action committee — a status that would require it to register with the Election Division and publicly disclose all of its donors, past and present.”
Knox County Clerk David Shelton, left, speaks with a delegate at the Indiana Republican convention on June 20, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Engling was the central Indiana regional director for Banks’ U.S. Senate office when he launched a late challenge in May with an endorsement from Banks against current Secretary of State Diego Morales.
The ad-tracking firm AdImpact reported Hoosier Leadership for America spent $5.2 million on broadcast advertising during this year’s primary campaign against Republican state senators who opposed President Donald Trump’s demands for Indiana congressional redistricting.
Hoosier Leadership’s status as a nonprofit organization allows it to keep the sources of its money secret, which is why such groups are commonly referred to as dark-money groups.
The $60,000 from Hoosier Leadership is the largest contribution that Engling reported to the state Election Division.
The next largest is $50,000 from former U.S. House Speaker Kevin McCarthy’s campaign committee. Engling worked for about five years as an aide to McCarthy in Washington before moving back to Indiana in 2023 for an unsuccessful run for Congress.
Democratic candidate Beau Bayh ended June with about $2.3 million in the bank ahead of what is expected to be an expensive fall campaign.
Engling’s late start gave him little time for fundraising and his campaign had about $150,000 as of June 30, according to Election Division reports.
Former GOP Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard is running as the Lincoln Party candidate and Libertarian Lauri Shillings will also be on the ballot.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Gap in federal grant money threatens North Dakota’s only fair-housing organization
description: The only fair-housing organization in North Dakota faces a grim outlook with the delay of a major federal grant.  The Grand Forks-based High Plains Fair Housing Center has been in a funding gap for two months. The center, which has one part-time and seven full-time employees, will likely furlough four of its staff on July […]
text:
Michaela Ficek, a fair housing specialist for the High Plains Fair Housing Center, is pictured July 24, 2026, near apartment buildings and homes in Bismarck. She is at risk of being furloughed due to a gap in federal funding. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)The only fair-housing organization in North Dakota faces a grim outlook with the delay of a major federal grant. 
The Grand Forks-based High Plains Fair Housing Center has been in a funding gap for two months. The center, which has one part-time and seven full-time employees, will likely furlough four of its staff on July 31 if the $425,000 Fair Housing Initiatives Program grant doesn’t show up, Center Executive Director Michelle Rydz said.
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development awarded the three-year grant in 2023 but hasn’t released the third installment. The second-year grant ended in May. The center expected the third-year grant to start the day afterward, but still hasn’t received the funds, Rydz said.
“We have no idea if it will be tomorrow or if it will be in a year or more,” she said. 
Everyday people will keep contacting the center because they face housing discrimination, need a disability accommodation or are at risk of losing their housing because of a miscommunication about a reasonable accommodation, Rydz said.
“These problems don’t stop because the funding stops,” she said.
A spokesperson for HUD did not return a request for comment Friday. 
The fair housing center has been in touch with North Dakota’s congressional delegation. The offices of Sen. John Hoeven and Rep. Julie Fedorchak, both R-N.D., have inquired with HUD about the grant’s status. Fedorchak’s office also contacted the White House. Hoeven’s office said HUD has committed to giving an update. 
The center could probably hang on with half staff for another year before being reduced to almost no staff or volunteers, Rydz said. With reduced services, fewer people would know about their civil rights and be helped in their housing situation, said Nicki Green, the center’s associate director and director of intake.
“To be honest, we’re going to do the best we can because the seven and a half of us are super passionate about this work, and we already work as hard as we can for our clients, but it’s going to be tough,” Green said.
The center, started in 2016, assists people within the scope of the federal Fair Housing Act, which prohibits people from being treated differently because of a protected characteristic, such as race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status or disability, Green said.
The center investigates, mediates and resolves housing discrimination complaints, and assists with accommodations such as closer parking spaces, changes in rent due dates and adjustments to heavy doors and mailboxes for people with disabilities.
Bismarck-based fair housing specialist Michaela Ficek is one of the employees who will be furloughed if the grant does not come through in time. She has helped people get their assistance animals approved, receive assigned parking spots and get out of their leases due to domestic violence situations. Her clients would have to be passed along to somebody else who will likely have to take on caseloads of three people. 
“It’s just kind of day by day, we’re taking it as it comes,” Ficek said. 
In 2025, the center fielded 958 total calls, more than one-third of which related to allegations of housing discrimination. The others related to landlord-tenant matters or general inquiries, Green said.
The center reached 204 resolutions for clients, about half of which were done without having to file a complaint, she said. Resolutions can be helping someone file a complaint or giving advice for how to ask for a reasonable accommodation or referring someone to legal services. 
“We always help provide something or help in some way, even just education,” Green said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura can be reached at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Unaffiliated candidate critical of Melat Kiros makes November ballot for Denver congressional seat
description: An unaffiliated candidate who launched a last-minute campaign to represent Denver in Congress will be on the November ballot.  Shimon Blau submitted more than enough valid signatures to qualify for the ballot, the Colorado secretary of state’s office announced Friday. Blau submitted about 2,200 petition signatures after three days of collecting signatures ea[...]
text:
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)An unaffiliated candidate who launched a last-minute campaign to represent Denver in Congress will be on the November ballot. 
Shimon Blau submitted more than enough valid signatures to qualify for the ballot, the Colorado secretary of state’s office announced Friday. Blau submitted about 2,200 petition signatures after three days of collecting signatures earlier this month, and just over 1,900 were verified by the secretary of state’s office. Candidates must submit 1,500 valid signatures to qualify for the ballot.
Blau, a doctor, announced his candidacy in a now-private Facebook post. He said in a video on his Facebook that he is a “true independent” who leans left on social issues and right on fiscal issues. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Concern for what he views as antisemitic rhetoric from Democratic nominee Melat Kiros is what motivated Blau, who is Jewish, to run for Colorado’s 1st Congressional District, he said in the Facebook post. Maintaining a strong alliance with Israel is a priority of his campaign, as well as healthcare and childcare reform. 
How democratic socialist Melat Kiros stunned Colorado politics with congressional primary win

Kiros was fired from her job as a corporate attorney in late 2023 after she posted an open letter defending students protesting Israel’s war in Gaza from charges of antisemitism. Throughout her campaign, she has been critical of Israel’s military operation in Gaza, which U.N. bodies and human rights groups say amounts to a genocide. She faced criticism for an interview in which she declined to call the deadly June 2025 firebombing attack in Boulder an act of antisemitism.
In the June Democratic primary election, Kiros, a 29-year-old democratic socialist, defeated U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette, a 15-term incumbent who took office four months before Kiros was born, by more than 20,000 votes. Her upset victory followed progressive wins in New York congressional primaries. 
Blau filed a statement of candidacy with the Federal Elections Commission on July 21. He has not responded to attempts from Newsline to contact him by phone and email since he announced his candidacy. 
The general election is on Nov. 3. Republican Christy Peterson is also running for the seat. The district heavily favors Democrats.

name: Michigan Advance
title: ‘More than a bridge’: Canada celebrates Gordie Howe bridge as Trump looms over Monday’s opening
description: WINDSOR, Ont. – The Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority and Canadian government officials gathered Friday for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the planned opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge between Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, which is scheduled Monday. The bridge had been scheduled to open in mid-June, but that was scrapped after President[...]
text:
Murray Howe, surrounded by other family members of NHL star Gordie Howe, speaks at a ribbon cutting ceremony for the Gordie Howe International Bridge. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. WINDSOR, Ont. – The Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority and Canadian government officials gathered Friday for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the planned opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge between Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, which is scheduled Monday.
The bridge had been scheduled to open in mid-June, but that was scrapped after President Donald Trump asserted that the deal for ownership, financing and bridge tolls — negotiated in 2012 between the Canadian government and the administration of then-Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder, with federal approval under President Barack Obama — was a “bad deal” for the United States.
Trump again threw plans into disarray when he announced 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods on Monday — after which an intended joint U.S.-Canada celebratory event scheduled for Friday was cancelled and rescheduled without any American officials present or speaking. 
“Given the recent tariff action from the U.S. we felt that we should focus today on celebrating here in Canada, on the workers who put in all the work to build this bridge, the many Canadians and Americans who did the hard work on it,” Gregor Robertson, the Canadian Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, told reporters following the ribbon-cutting. “We felt it’s inappropriate to have a big joint celebration when we’re working through those challenges.”
The Gordie Howe International Bridge, seen from Windsor, Ontario. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford emphasized in his speech at the event that only through cooperation between Canada and the United States can the economic growth and legacy of the bridge actually be seen — and that Trump has challenged that cooperative relationship through his overall foreign policy, including the most recent round of tariffs.  
“Team Canada has never been more united,” Ford said. “Ontario will be ready to respond to any new American tariffs, will not back down, and will negotiate from a position of strength as a top trading partner, more than half of the United States, because I know that both Canadians and Americans are better off when we work together instead of standing apart.”
The economic benefit of the bridge was the spotlight of Friday’s event, with Robertson noting that the increased number of toll lanes and inspection lanes, as well as the easy connectivity to major highways on both the Canadian and American sides of the bridge, are estimated that they will save carriers 850 thousand hours annually in a heavily used corridor for truck transportation. 
“It was time to fight for the future,” he said in French. 
Mark Wiseman, the Canadian ambassador to the United States, added that the bridge stands as a symbol of promise to future generations in both Ontario and Michigan. 
“What was once a small fur trading settlement has grown into one of the busiest border crossings and most important trade routes in the world,” he said. “This achievement, having one of the most fluid and secure, high-volume border crossings in the world, is a testament to the long-standing partnership between Canada, the United States, and the state of Michigan. 
Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens further emphasized the industrial corridor between Windsor and Detroit, which are both major manufacturing regions in their respective countries, especially in the automotive sector. 
“We want more trade, not less. We want more jobs, not fewer, and an abundance of opportunities, not a scarcity of potential,” he said. “We’re standing against uncertainty, against threats, against bullies. We’re united as Windsorites. We’re united as Ontarians, and we’re united as Canadians.”
While the bridge is planned to open for traffic on Monday, American officials have not confirmed any details of that on their end, including what time the border crossing on the American side of the bridge will become operational. However, Canadian officials remain confident that it will, in fact, open as scheduled. 
“Our understanding is we’re opening the bridge on Monday,” Robertson said. “The systems are all go here on this side of the border, and we understand on the U.S. side as well.”
During the event in Windsor, Trump posted on Truth Social to highlight what he sees as the changes in the deal from what had been initially negotiated. 
Mark Wiseman, the Canadian Ambassador to the United States, speaks at a ribbon cutting ceremony for the Gordie Howe International Bridge. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Windsor, Ontario Mayor Drew Dilkens speaks at a ribbon cutting ceremony for the Gordie Howe International Bridge. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Doug Ford, the Premier of Ontario, speaks at a ribbon cutting ceremony for the Gordie Howe International Bridge. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Gregor Robertson, the Canadian Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, speaks at a ribbon cutting ceremony for the Gordie Howe International Bridge. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Processing lanes at the Canadian border entry at the Gordie Howe International Bridge. “Canada disinvited the United States of America to the opening of the Gordie Howe Bridge, which is fine, considering they are paying substantial TARIFFS to the United States, but the original Deal on the Bridge, which was terribly negotiated by a previous Administration, no longer stands,” he posted. “We changed the terms of the Deal so that the United States of America now gets 50% of the Profit.”
Trump’s role in the bridge opening is complicated due to his campaign ties to the Moroun family, who own the Ambassador Bridge — the only other bridge operating between Ontario and Detroit. Matthew Moroun is a major Trump donor, and met privately with U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick earlier this year to lobby the Trump administration regarding the Gordie Howe crossing. 
Dilkens, however, emphasized the importance of the “redundancy” of having two bridge crossings, in case something should happen to one of the bridges. 
“Although we will probably see a shift in traffic from one bridge to the other over time, people will get back to crossing at the crossing that best suits them,” he said. “Probably the one from a trucking perspective, the one that gives them a direct highway-to-highway connection with the fastest clearance processing time, which would be the Gordie Howe Bridge.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Steve DeWitt, the CEO of ACS Infrastructure and Bridging North America, the private-sector partners on the bridge, further called the bridge — the longest cable-stayed bridge main span in North America — a “modern engineering marvel.”
The legacy of Gordie Howe, the Canadian-born Detroit Red Wings NHL star, for whom the bridge is named, was used as a parallel to the bridge by a number of speakers. 
“This bridge is a game changer, just like Gordie Howe was in his day,” Robertson said. 
Murray Howe, Gordie’s son, who was joined by around 30 members of the Howe family at the ceremony, further spotlighted how his father’s ties to both Canada and Detroit are honored by making him the bridge’s namesake. 
“Our parents loved life, and they loved people,” he said of Gordie and his wife Colleen. “They dedicated their lives to building bridges between people, between families, between communities, and between nations. This bridge will serve as an unmistakable symbol of the priceless bond and true friendship between the people of Canada and the people of the United States.”
Gordie Howe died in 2016, two years before construction on the bridge began. 
“We are so grateful that our father was able to experience such a profound expression of love, reverence, and gratitude in the twilight of his life,” Murray Howe said. “We are truly humbled by the immensity of this bridge, and even more so by the immensity of this honor.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Fraternal Order of Police latest group to oppose property tax constitutional amendment
description: The Florida chapter of the Fraternal Order of Police is the latest public safety organization to oppose Amendment 3, the proposed constitutional amendment designed to provide property tax relief to homeowners but which critics allege could radically reduce revenues for local government essential services, including public safety. “The Florida State Fraternal[...]
text:
Fraternal Order of Police Pinellas Lodge  (via Florida Fraternal Order of Police Facebook page).The Florida chapter of the Fraternal Order of Police is the latest public safety organization to oppose Amendment 3, the proposed constitutional amendment designed to provide property tax relief to homeowners but which critics allege could radically reduce revenues for local government essential services, including public safety.
“The Florida State Fraternal Order of Police believes Florida taxpayers deserve meaningful property tax relief,” the organization said in a written statement Friday. “We understand the financial pressures facing homeowners, and we support thoughtful, responsible reforms that provide relief while protecting the essential services our communities depend on.
“However, we oppose the current Amendment 3 because it creates far too much uncertainty about how local governments would continue to fund law enforcement, fire rescue, emergency medical services, and other critical public safety functions. Public safety should never become collateral damage with uncertain fiscal consequences.”
If approved, the proposed amendment would increase homestead exemptions for Floridians who own primary residences by the end of this year to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Further increases would be tied to the Consumer Price Index.  The amendment would cap assessment increases on other property to 5% a year.
Last week, the Florida Fire Chiefs’ Association became the first major statewide public safety organization to formally oppose Amendment 3, saying providing tax relief and reliable emergency services “are not mutually exclusive, but both require responsible long-term planning.”
According to state economists, the proposed amendment would reduce local government property tax revenues by an estimated $5 billion in its first year and $11.8 billion per year after five years.
The Florida Democratic Party announced its opposition to the measure earlier this week, while the Republican Party of Florida has yet to take a public stance.
Gov. Ron DeSantis campaigned on providing major property tax reduction for homestead property owners over the past year, but didn’t unveil his own plan until less than a week before he called the Florida Legislature to convene for a special session in June.
After it was approved with some changes to his plan, he has said that, while he will vote yes on the amendment, he is not as enthused about it and will not head any political group championing the measure. That’s a noticeable difference from 2024, when he formed a political committee and actively campaigned against proposed constitutional amendments that would have legalized recreational cannabis and enshrined abortion rights into the Florida Constitution.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Attorneys for death row inmates file legal objections to block executions next week
description: Attorneys fighting to prevent two Florida death row inmates from being executed by the state filed a joint lawsuit Friday in federal court. James Aren Duckett and Dominick Occhicone are scheduled to be executed Tuesday at Florida State Prison near Starke. If the executions take place as scheduled, it would be the first time in […]
text:
Credit:  YouTubeAttorneys fighting to prevent two Florida death row inmates from being executed by the state filed a joint lawsuit Friday in federal court.
James Aren Duckett and Dominick Occhicone are scheduled to be executed Tuesday at Florida State Prison near Starke. If the executions take place as scheduled, it would be the first time in 62 years the Sunshine State had executed two individuals on the same day.
The Florida Supreme Court earlier Friday denied Duckett’s motion for a stay of execution and said it would consider no motion for rehearing. Duckett is on death row for the 1987 rape and drowning of 11-year-old Teresa McAbee in 1987. His attorneys have now filed a petition in federal court asking to stop his execution and order additional DNA testing on the victim’s clothing. He is scheduled to be executed Tuesday at noon.
Dominick Occhicone, 80, would be the oldest inmate executed by the state ever (and second oldest in U.S. history) and is scheduled to be executed Tuesday at 6 p.m. for the 1986 murder in Pasco County of Martha Artzner, the mother of his girlfriend. He received a life sentence for the simultaneous murder of Raymond Artzner, the father of his girlfriend.
Attorneys for the two death row inmates argued in a court filing in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida Friday that their federal constitutional right against cruel and unusual punishment would be violated if the state proceeds with his execution as planned — arguing executing two men on the same day would cause them pain and suffering in violation of the Eighth Amendment.
“By combining Mr. Duckett’s execution day with Mr. Occhicone, the risk of a botched execution is exponentially increased due to factors including the impact of the prison and execution teams not being prepared to conduct two executions on the same day and the risk of errors with the lethal injection drugs,” their attorneys write in the filing.
“Additionally, by creating two separate classes of individuals who are treated differently in their execution proceedings, the Defendants have violated the Plaintiff’s right to equal protection. This arbitrary treatment burdens the Plaintiffs’ right to be free of cruel and unusual punishment.”
Executing two men on the same day ‘seems especially callous’
Michael B. Sheedy, executive director of the Florida Conference of Catholic Bishops, wrote to Gov. Ron DeSantis earlier this week asking for a stay of execution for both men and to commute their sentences to life imprisonment without parole.
If Duckett and Occhicone are executed Tuesday, they would be the 30th and 31st prisoners on Florida’s death row executed since January 2025, and the 10th and 11th executed this year, respectively.
“To punish with lifelong imprisonment is not to minimize the heinousness of these men’s crimes. It is rather to recognize with awe that God is the author of life, and to reserve to him the taking of human life except where it is otherwise impossible to maintain the common good,” Sheedy wrote. “Moreover, requiring state officers to kill two men on the same day seems especially callous.”
“These are very different cases but it all comes to this same reality that Florida continues to expand the use of capital punishment practically and legislatively despite mounting evidence that this is not what Floridians want,” said Grace Hanna, executive director of Floridians For Alternatives to the Death Penalty. 
“Last year there were five new death sentences handed down in Florida. In 2011, 14 people were sentenced to death. So juries are moving away from the death penalty and aren’t seeing it as necessary even though our state leaders are accelerating executions.”
Florida leads the country in exonerations of people sentenced to death with 30. Attorneys and advocates for Duckett maintain there are too many questions regarding his guilt to execute him.
Duckett, a former police officer from the city of Mascotte in Lake County, has maintained his innocence since the day he was arrested in the killing of Teresa McAbee. The jury that convicted him in 1990 was split about the case, finding him guilty on an 8-4 vote.
Duckett’s attorneys say the case against him has been based entirely on circumstantial evidence and that several pieces of evidence have since come under doubt.
The only witness who claimed to have seen the victim leave in Duckett’s car was then-16-year-old Grace Gwendolyn Gurley. She did not come forward until five months after the crime. She later recounted her testimony in a sworn statement to Duckett’s death row appeal team.
But in 1997, when she was brought before a court, she refused to say whether she lied when she testified that she saw the victim in Duckett’s car, as reported by the Orlando Sentinel.
Other witnesses testified in that same court hearing that she’d been coached by sheriff’s investigators to accuse Duckett of the crime by memorizing a script in return for preferential treatment at the Lake County Jail.
The prosecution also relied on forensic evidence from an FBI analyst.
DNA testing
Duckett’s attorneys requested DNA testing for years regarding the biological material found on the victim’s clothing. Some items were tested and yielded no results. But after DeSantis signed a warrant for him to be executed on March 31, a judge did grant his attorneys’ request for DNA testing.
The results were deemed inconclusive. Duckett’s attorneys argued the testing should have been conducted by a lab in Texas that uses a method known as whole genome sequencing, which they said would be more likely to extract usable results.
The state objected to testing in Texas, insisting on keeping the sample in Florida. It was “consumed” or destroyed in the testing process.

text:
The North Dakota Capitol building. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)The accounting director for the North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality will serve as interim director of the agency, Gov. Kelly Armstrong announced Friday.
Beth Jacobson, a 29-year state government employee, will begin leading the department on Aug. 1 after DEQ Director Dave Glatt retires at the end of the month, according to the governor’s office.
Glatt has served as director of the department since it became a standalone state agency in 2019. He has worked for the state for more than 40 years.
As accounting director, Jacobson has supervised the department’s financial operations, budgeting, federal grant management, procurement and fiscal compliance operations.
Armstrong’s office said the search for a permanent director is ongoing.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT officials say ICE is active at Bradley International Airport
description: CT officials acknowledged the presence of federal ICE agents at Bradley Airport but had no details about the agency's long-range plans.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont and his top public safety official acknowledged Friday the presence of federal ICE agents at Bradley International Airport without being able to say if it signaled a new emphasis on immigration enforcement by the Trump administration in Connecticut.
“We were made aware that they are at the airport, and if someone goes through TSA, that they may be checked. And if in fact there’s a violation, that they’re pulled out of the line,” said Ronnell Higgins, the commissioner of emergency services and public protection. “But that’s the extent to what I know right now.”
The media offices of ICE in New England and nationally did not respond to a request for comment.
Connecticut is one of the blue states where immigration enforcement is a source of chronic conflict, given the passage of revisions to Trust Act that set explicit limits on the circumstances in which local enforcement can cooperate with the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.
“Connecticut State Police is assigned to Bradley Airport. They are not involved in any way” in the immigration enforcement there, Higgins said. 
Higgins said ICE officially notified the state of its presence without sharing details on long-range plans. The federal agency does not routinely notify state police of arrests at the airport, a state-owned facility with federal oversight.
“I have no reason to believe that they’re going to not be there tomorrow or the next day or the next day,” Higgins said.
Lamont on Friday repeated the message he has been articulating since the opening of the General Assembly session in February.
“Leave us alone. Leave these people alone,” he said. “These are maybe people who want to go for a long weekend and see the aunt in Chicago, instead of getting picked up by ICE, the TSA at Bradley, maybe sent away to a detention facility. I don’t want to jump to conclusions. We’ll see what’s happening.”
State authorities could not confirm if anyone was arrested and detained at the airport by ICE.
TRAC, the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, reported that more than 65,000 people were in immigration detention nationally as of July 11 and that 70% were individuals without criminal convictions.

text:
Michigan Board of State Canvassers discuss the MMOP ballot petition. July 24, 2026 | ScreenshotValid signatures for the Michiganders for Money Out Of Politics ballot petition were determined to be sufficient on Friday after a close call by the Board of State Canvassers. However, the board must still determine if the wording of the proposed petition meets legal standards.
It was still a key victory for the ballot initiative, which faced a steep initial challenge from an opposition group, Protect MI Free Speech, which effectively reduced Michiganders for Money Out Of Politics’ signature cushion to a little more than 20 signatures. That was significant because organizers for Michiganders for Money Out Of Politics turned in more than 562,000 signatures to the Bureau of Elections in May, well over the 356,958 valid signature threshold — 8% of the votes cast for governor in 2022 — needed to qualify for the November ballot.
A staff report released late last week said that despite being pared down, the Michigan Bureau of Elections determined that the petition narrowly cleared the signature threshold, with 657 valid signatures found in a 1,000-signature sample after review and a challenge.
A second challenge was lodged to the canvassers ahead of Friday’s meeting to determine the sufficiency of Michiganders for Money Out Of Politics’ signatures by Protect MI Free Speech. Yet after a morning full of opening arguments from either side, and a line-by-line examination of signatures the opposition said were still faulty, the canvassers ultimately voted 3-1 to approve the signature threshold. Republican Paul Cordes was the lone no vote.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Michiganders for Money Out of Politics, which aims to ban utility companies and government contractors from making campaign contributions. The initiative would create a new state law saying as much.
If the board ends up approving the petition language, the canvassers-approved initiative would then head to the Michigan Legislature, which would then have 40 days to either accept the proposal language as written — in effect approving the new law — or reject it by voting it down. If the Legislature were to reject the measure or allow it to sit past 40 days, the language would automatically go to the next general election ballot for a statewide vote.
Michigan voters, in that case, would decide whether the state’s regulated utilities like Consumers Energy Company and DTE Energy Company can continue to make campaign contributions.
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.
