name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Statewide EMS task force faces shutdown amid funding crisis
description: NJ's EMS task force, a statewide backup for local responders and preparedness planning leader, needs additional funding to operate beyond September.
text:
New Jersey's EMS Task Force outside MetLife Stadium preparing for the World Cup matches. (Photo courtesy of the task force)Members of New Jersey’s Emergency Medical Services Task Force spent July 4th evacuating a Voorhees nursing home of more than 200 people after the facility’s air conditioning failed during a heat wave that would lead to a record 29 deaths statewide.
Other members were deployed to help local responders at fireworks events in five counties and America250 celebrations along the Delaware River, to track wildfires in South Jersey, and to standby at World Cup matches in East Rutherford, an assignment that would eventually involve 8,500 personnel hours over five weeks, its largest undertaking ever.  
The nonprofit task force, which was founded to manage large-scale emergency medical responses in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, serves as a statewide backup for local emergency services, coordinates emergency preparedness for large-scale events, and leads regional emergency response planning. But as of August, it has just 60 days of funding left, according to its president, Michael Bascom.  
“We have zero funds to sustain, repair, or replace any of our equipment,” Bascom told the New Jersey Monitor, let alone money to continue to pay its handful of staff.
The task force had pushed Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Democratic leaders in the Legislature to include $500,000 for its work in the most recent budget, but the $60.7 billion budget she signed in late June did not include it. Bascom said it is now requesting at least $8 million in one-time capital funding while it searches for sustainable revenue.
“If our organization fails to maintain — there IS NO OTHER backup. Local EMS cannot absorb the work scope. Hospitals cannot replace it,” Beau Huch, a longtime EMS advocate and director of government affairs for the law firm Porzio, wrote in a funding request to lawmakers this spring. 
“This is not a warning bell ringing. This is an emergency siren blaring,” he added.  
Senate Democrats declined to comment on the request.  
A spokeswoman for Sherrill said she is grateful to the first responders, including the EMS task force, who have worked hard to protect public health during high-profile sporting events, extreme heat and summer celebrations, an “especially demanding period.”  
“Federal partnership has been essential to supporting New Jersey’s preparedness for health threats. As certain funding comes up for renewal and as other COVID-era federal funding streams end, the State remains committed to exploring ways to sustain key preparedness work. At the same time, no state can fully absorb the fiscal impact of expiring federal funds and broader federal policy changes,” Sherrill spokesperson Maggie Garbarino told the New Jersey Monitor.  
Sen. Declan O’Scanlon (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Sen. Declan O’Scanlon (R-Monmouth), a sponsor of a bill to codify the task force, said it’s the state’s responsibility to protect residents and that failing to fund the organization “could be a life-or-death thing.” 
“It’s just a continued demonstration that this administration, like the previous one, doesn’t give a damn. It would have been easy if they cared,” O’Scanlon told the New Jersey Monitor.  
Most of the task force’s 200 members work full-time for other emergency response organizations, which cover the cost of their deployments with the task force. 
It maintains equipment valued at $70 million, Bascom said, including 19 medical ambulance buses that can transport ten times as many patients as a regular ambulance, oxygen generators, field hospital shelters and more, all available for use by local responders in the state’s 21 counties. Repair needs are estimated at close to $30 million, he said.   
Bascomb said its funding needs were amplified over the Independence Day weekend, when several ambulance buses malfunctioned. Severe thunderstorms swept through the state that Saturday, causing extensive flooding and damage.
“We learned a lot from Saturday, lessons we’ll take on the road to the next mission and beyond,” Bascom wrote in an email to task force members, thanking them for their work.  
The state Department of Health is tasked with maintaining and coordinating the activities of the task force under the 2017 law that formalized the group. But the $1.1 million in federal funding the department provided last year to ensure the task force could operate through the World Cup will soon be gone, Bascom said.  
The soccer matches are now history, but Bascom said the task force’s work continues, including its mandate to staff all events at MetLife Stadium. In 2025 alone, task force members deployed at least 225 times to evacuate nursing homes or hospital facilities and assist with major emergencies and led 1,500 hours of emergency preparedness training, according to task force data.
Members of New Jersey’s EMS Task Force attend a briefing before the final World Cup match in the Meadowlands on July 19, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the task force)
Once funded as a function of the state Department of Health, Bascom said the task force was pushed to become a nonprofit under Gov. Phil Murphy, but the grant money officials said would be available has not yet materialized. The group played a key role in the state’s COVID-19 response, setting up testing sites, vaccine clinics and field hospitals, but funding has been sporadic and unreliable, he said. 
The Department of Health did not respond to a request for comment.
O’Scanlon took a swipe at Democratic legislators for focusing too much on pork, a Trenton-insider term for money that legislative leaders add to the budget for pet projects, during this year’s budget process.
“Emergency preparedness should come before one dime of pork, and it didn’t,” he said. “The priority was pork over preparedness.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Our safety net was already full of holes. They’re only getting bigger
description: Back when I was growing up, it seemed a bit easier to get by on next to nothing. People could afford food and shelter on a working-class wage and get a little help from safety net programs when needed. But since the 1990s, the cost of housing and healthcare has increasingly exceeded wage growth. We’re […]
text:
The Missouri Capitol Building in Jefferson City on May 12 (Jason Hancock/Missouri Independent). 


Back when I was growing up, it seemed a bit easier to get by on next to nothing.
People could afford food and shelter on a working-class wage and get a little help from safety net programs when needed. But since the 1990s, the cost of housing and healthcare has increasingly exceeded wage growth. We’re also paying a larger share of our income on food now.
Even as recently as 2021, an expanded Child Tax Credit, stronger unemployment insurance, and health care programs were keeping people out of poverty — even slashing child poverty in half. But spending hawks in Congress refused to renew these pandemic-era social programs, and poverty spiked right back up.
Under this administration and Congress, things are even worse. Already thin assistance programs have been slashed to fund tax cuts for billionaires and more endless wars.
Even before these latest cuts, it was clear we needed a stronger safety net with less red tape.
Years ago, when I stepped out on my own as a mother, I had to apply for SNAP (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamps). It helped my kids get the best start in life with good, adequate nutrition, even living in an area where well-paying jobs were scarce and child care was expensive.
In search of better-paying work, I moved to St. Louis. I found better pay, but the rent was at least double. Even with a bigger paycheck, I had to live in my car and apply for Section 8 housing assistance. My son had to go live with his dad. I was devastated.
I found some subpar housing while I spent three years stuck at number 2,000 on the waitlist. But eventually I fell off the list altogether. It turns out the form they sent me to remain on the waitlist was returned as “undeliverable.” They had entered my address incorrectly. The error was theirs, not mine.
The Department of Housing and Urban Development doesn’t track how many people lose their place in line for housing assistance. Still, the estimated number of losses due to administrative error is in the tens of thousands each year.
And this is on top of the 7.2 million unit deficit in affordable housing stock, so millions who are eligible for housing assistance can’t receive it at all. According to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, over 50 percent of public housing agencies keep their voucher waitlists closed to new applicants at any given time. The figure can run even higher in urban areas.
The system disadvantages the very people it is meant to help.
According to the National Low Income Housing Coalition, no state in the country has adequate affordable rental housing available to meet the needs and eligibility criteria. Nationally, only 35 affordable units are available for every 100 high-need, low-income applicants.
In short, we need more affordable housing units, better staffing to reduce administrative errors, and less red tape for applicants.
Meanwhile, the so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” cut over $1 trillion from Medicaid and SNAP over the next decade. It doesn’t just reduce benefits, it adds red tape and “work requirements.” Most able-bodied recipients already work, but failure to file the right paperwork to prove it can cost you your benefits even if you’re eligible. And of course, without housing, how are we going to get good jobs?
Already, millions have lost health coverage, and millions more have seen their SNAP benefits cut. But the worst could be yet to come, with steep Medicaid cuts scheduled for after this year’s midterms.
Our national priorities are upside down. We need to tell our lawmakers to ensure that our tax dollars go where they are actually needed: affordable, accessible basic human needs. Not for more wars or tax cuts for billionaires.
Lift your voice.

This op-ed was distributed by OtherWords.org.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: In rare Idaho state audit of a city, report finds major procedural shortcomings in Kamiah’s spending
description: Amid a rapidly declining cash balance and a half-a-million dollar public pool renovation project that isn’t yet complete, Idaho state auditors are referring a report on spending by the city of Kamiah to the state’s chief legal officer.  The audit report, published Thursday, included information on employee pay raises, vacation time, large vendor payments for[...]
text:
The Kamiah city pool seen last month. The city spent more than $500,000 on a renovation project that is not yet complete. (Photo courtesy of Idaho County Free Press) Amid a rapidly declining cash balance and a half-a-million dollar public pool renovation project that isn’t yet complete, Idaho state auditors are referring a report on spending by the city of Kamiah to the state’s chief legal officer. 
The audit report, published Thursday, included information on employee pay raises, vacation time, large vendor payments for candy, and a nearly $455,000 over-spend on a contract for the pool renovation — all with little to no documentation to justify the expenses and seemingly with little input from the City Council. 
“The level of missing documentation across all financial transactions reviewed is very concerning,” the report said. “We were unable to determine if the missing documentation was due to incompetence or fraudulent activities, but it does call into question the integrity of many transactions.” 
The financial audit largely looked at activity between 2020 and 2024. The city has since changed leadership and has implemented policies to try and address many of the findings, according to its response to the report. 
The city’s response said that there was no evidence fraud took place. Current Mayor Genese Simler and current legal counsel Geoffrey Schroeder wrote the response. Simler was not mayor and Schroder was not legal counsel during the time period reviewed in the audit. 
Simler and Schroeder wrote the city had a new mayor, new city attorney, and city council voted to remove the prior city clerk and hired an accounting firm to perform treasurer and in-house accounting reconciliation.
The Kamiah mayor could not be reached for comment.
Many of the findings in the report were based on the lack of documentation to justify certain expenses and policies that lacked safeguards against fraud. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Kamiah signed a $43,700 contract for pool renovations. It paid nearly $500K, and the pool still isn’t renovated. 

In October 2020, Kamiah entered a contract with Idaho Stage Construction to renovate a municipal pool. Several change orders were made and largely attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic, the report said. The city has paid Idaho Stage Construction $498,453.22 in total, including around $40,000 to close out the contract with no documents provided to indicate services provided for the last payment, the report said. 
The city has paid an additional $54,634.75 to two other vendors on the pool renovation project. 
“Current Kamiah staff could not explain why Kamiah paid over $500,000 and the pool was still inoperable,” the report said.
Photos of the pool depict the “dilapidated state” auditors found it in when they visited the pool last year. 
Last September, a citizen asked Kamiah City Council members about the opening of the pool, the Idaho County Free Press reported. 
Former deputy city clerk Mike Tornatore responded, “It is going to take $1.5 million to repair the pool correctly.” He said it may take as long as two years, the newspaper reported. 
According to the city response, Idaho Stage Construction is no longer in business. The city wrote there were “no indications of fraud or even suspected fraud” in previous communications related to the project failure. 
The city decided that “pursuit of purported overpayments would be fruitless given the potential cost of pursuing them,” the response said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Audit found unusual vendor payments with no supporting documents 

The 30-page report included examples of a number of unusual payments that lacked documents to justify their business purpose. 
The lack of documentation itself required auditors to refer the audit report to the Idaho attorney general, who has the authority to investigate potential fraud or misappropriation of public funds, State Auditor April Renfro told the Idaho Capital Sun. 
“If you don’t have the support and you can’t prove that (expenditures) were for business purposes, then it becomes questionable whether or not that’s a misappropriation or an illegal use of public funds,” she said.

The following are expenditures that were highlighted in the reported: 

Then-interim city Fire Chief Jared Silvis personally paid a vendor $6,893.72 for tires and then was reimbursed by the city. Auditors couldn’t determine if the charge was for a city vehicle or why the city didn’t directly pay the vendor instead of reimbursing the employee. Auditors also couldn’t identify the vendor that sold the employee for tires.  
Then-Deputy City Clerk Mike Tornatore was also hired as a contract grant writer for the city. He was paid directly $2,842.70 instead of through his business, MFT Inc. Costs covered include candy, postage, and food. 
Tornatore’s business MFT Inc. was also paid $39,972.31 for grant writing fees as well as for candy for a barbecue, snacks for a meeting, and utility billings. The city “could not provide an explanation as to why the contractor was paid for items outside of grant writing,” the report said. 
Kamiah paid itself as a vendor $9,277.52, and auditors were “unable to determine the purpose of the payment or payments.”
The city made an automated clearing house, or ACH money transfer, in May 2021 for $19,252.23 that “appears to have been paid to either a fake vendor or for ransomware,” the report said. The city had no documentation on the payment other than a handwritten note by an unknown author. The City Council did not approve the payment. 

The state auditors tracked Kamiah’s declining cash and investment balance. (Screenshot from audit report)
 Kamiah employee credit card usage wasn’t documented while cash reserves declined 

The city’s cash and investments declined by 94% between 2020 and 2023, the report said. All withdrawals were initiated by city employees. Credit card usage by employees at the time didn’t require supporting documentation, the report said, making it not possible to determine “if purchases had a legitimate business purpose.” 
Auditors reviewed 59 credit card purchases that totaled $35,994 from 2021 to 2024, with vendors that included electronic stores, specialty clothing retailers, gym outfitters, grocery outlets, hotels, convenience stores, and large commercial equipment supplies. 
Several purchases appeared to be travel-related, the report said, but without documentation of what the travel was for. One purchase was for the medical flight operator Life Flight in Oregon with no reason provided as to why. 
“While all the purchases may have a legitimate purpose for city business, there was no way to verify that without supporting documentation,” the report said. “The accounting system included some abbreviated notes, but nothing definitive for the transactions.”  
 Some payroll, sick leave, vacation records don’t’ include documentation of City Council approval

In 2021, the city provided most long-term employees a $2 per hour pay raise using federal pandemic relief funds through the American Rescue Plan Act. However, those funds were time-limited, and auditors suspected that permanent raises using temporary funding “could contribute to future declining cash balances.” 
Some employees in 2022 were given a $1 an hour cost of living adjustment, while two employees — former clerk Brenda Taylor and the former deputy clerk Tornatore were given a $2 adjustment. Tornatore is now the temporary interim city clerk as the city looks to replace him with a permanent city clerk, according to the city response to the report.  
“They appear to be the only employees that received the increased amount,” the report said. “None of these wage increases had supporting documentation showing the mayor and City Council’s approval, as required by city policy.” 
Tornatore was first employed by the city at an hourly rate of $13 in 2020, the report said. His pay increased three times until it was set at $22 per hour in 2022. However, Tornatore asked to switch from full-time to part-time, and had his pay cut to $12.50 an hour, and he entered a contract to be an outside grant-writer for the city. 
As a contracted grant writer, his contract was for $1,200 a month along with 3% of grants he obtained,  provided those grants had terms allowing the payment. He provided the mayor and City Council a memo in 2023 detailing more than $3.5 million in grants secured. Auditors were not able to verify that amount, the report said. 
None of the grants allowed him to receive the 3% cut, so he requested a new contract for $2,400 a month for grant-writing services. Auditors found no evidence of approval of the new contract by City Council, but there were signed contracts provided to auditors showing the new terms. 
Taylor, the former clerk, on four occasions was paid for sick time in addition to 80 or more hours of regular, holiday or overtime pay in a single pay period, which is contrary to federal labor laws, the report said. In a pay period that only included one holiday, Taylor was paid for two holidays. 
Silvis, the former interim fire chief, was offered the temporary position at a rate of $2,500 biweekly. He was paid $3,000 biweekly in late 2022 into 2023, and the city provided no documentation of the reason for the increase or that it was approved by City Council. 
Based on city vacation policy, Tornatore maximum vacation accrual should have been 120 hours between Oct. 1, 2020, and Dec. 31, 2022, the report said. Between October 2022 and December 2022, he received payment for 240 hours of vacation. 
“When asked about the discrepancy, Mike Tornatore indicated that Kamiah kept paying so he kept asking,” the report said.
 Some discrepancies occurred in utility billing 

As deputy city clerk, Tornatore was the only city employee with access to utility information with the ability to make changes, the report said. Auditors found some discrepancies when tracing amounts billed to billing rates provided by Tornatore. 
In some cases, rates charged to cover the cost of city bonds did not match the appropriate bond year, the report said. In one case, an account was over-billed by 56 cents, and another account was under-billed by $60.72. 
“The lack of segregation of duties in the utility revenue process significantly increases the risk that fraud could occur,” the report said. “Given the current process, the deputy city clerk could intentionally enter incorrect rates, meter readings, and adjustments.” 
The city wrote in its response there was no evidence fraud took place. “While there had been occasional forbearance of nonpayment shutoffs in some instances, all amounts due and payable for utility usage appear to be appropriately recorded.” 
The city has changed its practices for utility billing. 
 Why did the state audit a city?

It’s not common for the state to audit a city, Renfro said. The Legislature’s auditing office does have the authority to audit any entity that is authorized or funded by the Legislature, which includes cities, but it needs approval to do so from the Legislative Council. The council, comprised of legislative leaders, rarely approves these requests, Renfro said. 
Idaho State Police had been investigating the city after complaints were initially made to the Lewis County Sheriff’s Office. The sheriff contracts with the city for law enforcement, so it asked state police to take over. 
State police asked the audit office to assist in 2024, and the Legislative Council provided the authority to move ahead with the audit at a June 17, 2024, meeting. The report was sent to Idaho Attorney General Raul Labrador’s office. 
Damon Sidur, spokesman for the attorney general’s office told the Sun in an email Thursday,   “Our office has received the audit and is reviewing it to determine whether any additional investigation or action is necessary.”  
Special Report City of Kamiah-1

name: WyoFile
title: Rep. Allemand’s DUI case surfaces previous domestic battery, trespass charges
description:
The GOP representative, who is running for reelection, faced misdemeanor domestic violence and harassment charges when he lived in Kansas in the 2000s.
The post Rep. Allemand’s DUI case surfaces previous domestic battery, trespass charges appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Midwest Republican Rep. Bill Allemand on July 15 pleaded guilty to driving under the influence of alcohol following his arrest in Buffalo in December. 
A review of court documents shows the lawmaker also faced two separate sets of criminal charges for domestic battery and violating a protection order — allegations which included trespassing and “harassment by telephone” — in Kansas during the 2000s.
The domestic battery charge stemmed from a Feb. 27, 2001 incident in which Allemand allegedly did “unlawfully, willfully and intentionally cause physical contact with another person … in [a] rude, insulting or angry manner,” according to court documents.
Allemand agreed to a pre-trial diversion program, which suspended the criminal proceedings for 12 months, during which he had to abide by all laws, abstain from the use of alcohol or drugs and attend domestic violence education classes. The charge was dismissed after Allemand completed the one-year program, according to court documents. 
“It never happened,” Allemand told WyoFile on July 16. “It was dismissed because it didn’t happen.”

Rep. Bill Allemand, R-Midwest, during the Wyoming Legislature’s 2026 budget session. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)

The protection order violation accusation followed a Dec. 5, 2009 incident in which he was charged with criminal trespass for allegedly appearing at an address prescribed by court order as off limits to him, and with harassment for allegedly calling the victim 27 times the same day, according to court records obtained by WyoFile. 
WyoFile was unable to make direct contact with the victim, but was told by the victim’s family they did not want to comment.
He pleaded no contest to the violation of a protection order and was sentenced to six months in jail and a $200 fine. The other charges were dropped. Instead of serving jail time, he was granted 12 months of “non-reporting” probation requiring him to avoid contact with the victim, to obtain a domestic violence assessment and to follow any resulting recommendations, the plea deal states.
“I know nothing about that,” Allemand told WyoFile, referring to the 2009 incident and charges.
Both sets of Kansas charges were mentioned by Johnson County Deputy Prosecuting Attorney Josh Stensaas during Allemand’s Dec. 29 arraignment when he initially pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence of alcohol, according to an audio transcript of the hearing.
DUI conviction
Johnson County Circuit Court Magistrate Judge Jeremy Kisling sentenced Allemand to 90 days in jail with credit for two days served following his Dec. 28 arrest. Kisling suspended the jail time in place of one year of unsupervised probation and ordered him to pay a $500 fine plus $270 in court fees. 
The court ordered that, during his probation period, Allemand must refrain from alcohol and controlled substances and not enter bars or liquor stores where alcohol is the main item of sale, according to court documents. He is subject to random testing — one to two times per month for the first six months — of blood, breath, urine “upon reasonable articulable suspicion of use.” He must also complete an alcohol/substance abuse evaluation.
A WyoFile review of Wyoming court records found no prior DUIs on Allemand’s record. 
In Wyoming, a first DUI conviction is punishable by up to six months in jail and a $750 fine, according to the Governor’s Council on Impaired Driving. A driver with a non-commercial driver’s license is considered drunk with a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.08%. A first DUI conviction with a blood-alcohol content of 0.15% or higher requires the offender to install an ignition interlock for six months, according to the council and state statute. 
The Wyoming Department of Transportation is notified about all DUI convictions and determines whether license suspension and/or interlock installation is mandated, based on state statutes.
Rep. Bill Allemand, R-Midwest, listens to a Johnson County sheriff’s deputy as he is asked if he can perform a field sobriety test on Dec. 28, 2025, after being pulled over for suspected drunk driving in Buffalo. (Johnson County Sheriff’s Office)
The state’s test showed Allemand, who runs an oilfield trucking company, had a blood-alcohol content of 0.24%, according to court documents. Allemand and his attorney disputed the accuracy of the test results.
While his blood-alcohol content exceeded 0.15%, according to the state, it’s unclear whether Allemand will be required to install an ignition interlock. WYDOT told WyoFile that information about interlock installation is confidential under the Driver Privacy Protection Act.
Allemand didn’t respond to WyoFile’s inquiry about whether there were any restrictions applied to his driving privileges.
Allemand initially pleaded not guilty in December, and maintained that position until July 15. Reached by WyoFile on July 16, Allemand said he had no comment about his change of plea.
It comes after months of maintaining his innocence, alleging the traffic stop was unjustified and that body camera footage of the arrest “shows that I was not drunk,” Allemand told WyoFile in June.
Political implications
Allemand, a Wyoming Freedom Caucus member who has served House District 58 since 2023, is running for a third term. He faces a primary challenge from one of his former supporters, Peter Boyer, who is wrapping up a term as mayor of Bar Nunn. The winner of the GOP primary, to be decided on Aug. 18, will face Democratic candidate Keenan Morgan in November.
Allemand frequently touts his status as a member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, which proclaims to “plan together, work together, and pray together in pursuit of policies that promote truth by protecting life, private property rights, and Judeo-Christian family values.” Freedom Caucus Chair Rachel Rodriguez-Williams has declined WyoFile’s request for an official comment on Allemand’s legal entanglements.
Gillette Republican Rep. John Bear, the former Freedom Caucus chairman, told WyoFile in June, “As an individual, I would tell you that everybody deserves their day in court, and we’ll see how that comes out.
“If he has a problem, I hope he gets help. And if it turns out that, you know, that wasn’t the case, then I hope justice is served.”
Gillette Republican Rep. John Bear is joined by other members of the Wyoming Legislature including Rep. Bill Allemand, center,  as the Wyoming Freedom Caucus hosted a press conference on the opening day of the 2026 budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
In the body camera footage released by the Johnson County Sheriff’s Office last month, Allemand appears to tell a detention officer during a search, “If you were a woman, I would like this.” 
Moments later during the search, Allemand tells the officer, “Look at that belt buckle.” 
“Oh, that’s a nice buckle,” the officer responds.
“What does it say?” Allemand asks. 
The officer responds, “Honor Wyoming. I like it.”
Honor Wyoming, a conservative political group in Wyoming that touts “integrity” among its core mission, scores Allemand as a “top hand” in its online “Integrity Index.”
“Honor Wyoming doesn’t have a perspective on the personal life of any lawmaker unless it was some sort of conflict of interest related to legislation they were voting on,” John Guido of Honor Wyoming told WyoFile via email. Honor Wyoming’s “Political Integrity Index scores each lawmaker’s votes to see if they are in alignment with the most basic and agreed-upon responsibilities all Wyoming voters expect them to uphold.”
WyoFile’s editor, Tennessee Watson, and reporter, Maggie Mullen, contributed reporting.

name: WyoFile
title: Cheatgrass is invading the best sagebrush left in the West. How can Wyoming hold the line?
description:
Mapping cheatgrass-dominated landscapes is easy: Satellite photos do the trick. Now, scientists are taking on a tougher task of finding the invasive grass along its leading edge.
The post Cheatgrass is invading the best sagebrush left in the West. How can Wyoming hold the line? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
SOUTH PASS—Corinna Riginos planted her feet among shin-high sagebrush that stretched out of sight. The ecologist, who leads the science team for The Nature Conservancy-Wyoming, was trying to verify if noxious cheatgrass also grew nearby.
Walking along the 7,500-foot-high rolling tableland, not a single blade could be found.
“When we think about ‘defending the core,’ here we are at ground zero,” Riginos said on a still early July morning. “We have this real opportunity to try to keep it that way. Practically speaking, how do we get there?” 
“The core” refers to the best sagebrush remaining on Earth. Sagebrush is the backbone of an ecosystem in decline everywhere, including Wyoming. Still, places like South Pass and the Green River Basin are home to, by far, the largest and healthiest sagebrush tracts that are left. 
“There’s 16 million acres of core sagebrush area in Wyoming,” Riginos said. “That’s half of what there is across the whole western sagebrush ecosystem.”
Corinna Riginos and Lauren Marsh take notes in the Sweetwater Canyon during a July 2026 cheatgrass surveilance outing. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Cheatgrass poses perhaps the gravest threat to the shrinking habitat’s long-term persistence. Riginos and fellow TNC scientists Courtney Larson and Charlotte Cadow are embarking on a yearslong mission to get ahead of that threat. They’re trying to find cheatgrass before it takes over.
Where cheatgrass grows in thick, there’s no mistaking it. The landscape’s very color is the telltale sign.
“Cheatgrass has a nice seasonal signature,” Larson said. “It greens up early, then it turns kind of purpley-colored. And then it dies off earlier than other grasses.” 
As a result, heavily invaded areas can be easily mapped using satellite imagery. 
But predictive models don’t do so well when cheatgrass accounts for less than 15% of the groundcover. The Nature Conservancy crew knows that from experience. In summer 2025, they went to 200 survey plots where they found no cheatgrass. Yet, their modeling predicted 88% of those sites would have some trace amount.
“They overpredict, at low levels of cheatgrass,” Larson said. 
Low densities of cheatgrass grow amid bitterbrush in the Sweetwater Canyon in July 2026. When the invasive grass is intermixed with another species, like this, it often becomes undetectable in satellite imagery. Wyoming scientists are developing strategies to better detect trace levels of cheatgrass. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
One of the crew’s goals is to dial in the predictive models. Verifying what’s growing where takes a whole lot of fieldwork. 
“We’re going to try to get 400 random points,” lead sagebrush technician Lauren Marsh said while en route to one of them. 
During the 2025 field season, TNC’s techs found the invasive annual species in unlikely corners of Fremont County — deep into the Wind River Range up St. Lawrence Basin and on the high slopes of Green Mountain. 
“We’re seeing it at 9,000 feet,” Riginos said. “Someone else saw it at 10,000 feet last year.” 
There have even been patches documented along forested, north-facing slopes, she said.
“It’s heartbreaking and mindblowing at the same time,” Riginos said. “The models of habitat suitability don’t really end: 78% of Wyoming is suitable habitat.”




Click to enlarge: Cheatgrass mapping is accurate when the invasive grass exceeds about 15% groundcover. At trace levels, however, researchers have lots of room to improve predictive models. (The Nature Conservancy-Wyoming)
Teton County’s also seeing signs of invasion into landscapes that land managers once thought immune. 
“We found cheatgrass at 8,000 feet in the Gros Ventre,” Cadow said. 
The Jackson Hole crew has even been observing little patches in the conifers where elk are bedding down, she said, and also where elk manure is especially prevalent.
“In Teton County, we’re really seeing wildlife as a vector,” Cadow said. “Cheatgrass is getting a foothold higher and more remotely than we anticipated.” 
Dropping into Sweetwater Canyon during the early-July outing, Riginos, Larson, Marsh and Joey Friedman descended toward several survey plots where they were confident they’d find cheatgrass. 
On the steeper, south-facing slopes, it was everywhere. Riginos grabbed a pile of cured, tinder-dry seeds and stems that accumulated atop the soil in the canyon.  
“Super good fire starter,” she said. “There’s a reason they call it grassoline.” 
As cured strands of cheatgrass break down, they form a layer of especially flamable duff on the surface of Wyoming rangelands. This pile of duff from the Sweetwater Canyon is sitting in Corinna Riginos’ palm on July 8, 2026. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
One of cheatgrass’ most harmful traits is that it speeds up the wildfire cycle. When an infested area burns, the cheatgrass grows back even thicker. Then the landscape’s even more prone to burn yet again, creating an ecologically devastating feedback loop.
Wildfire-scarred landscapes from the 2024 House Draw Fire and 2025 Red Canyon Fire have become top priorities for keeping cheatgrass from taking over. Funding to pay for the pricey herbicide that’s the most effective at keeping cheatgrass at bay is hard-fought. 
“A lot of the energy and intention and money goes to those [post-wildfire] situations,” Riginos said. “My fear is that we’re not putting enough focus on these places where we have this opportunity to hold the line.”
Currently, land managers who steward the least-invaded reaches of Wyoming have a tough argument for funding when they’re competing for limited dollars with weed and pest districts losing their cheatgrass fights. 
The Nature Conservancy’s research could help make their case.
“An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” Riginos said. “How do we do that intelligently?”

name: WyoFile
title: Letter to a future ancestor
description:
Writing 250 years into the future, writer Dawn Stagner reflects on Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho history since America's birth.
The post Letter to a future ancestor appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
To a future ancestor,
With my eyes shut, I hear the pop and crackle of far-away fireworks. I open my eyes and squint into the darkness, seeing the colors explode and disappear. They look like distant birthday candles.
Above, the clear night reveals thousands of stars and a bright but waning moon. It’s America’s 250th birthday, and July Fourth has never looked so small to me. Just matchsticks in the sky.
I’m at Arapaho Sundance, and the drums and singing drown out the pops of colorful light. From now on, when I think of America, I will think of two things: a tiny light in the distance and you. 
My thoughts keep returning to you, future ancestor, on this night. I dream of who you might be 250 years from now.
Perhaps you will be majoring in Indigenous Studies at the University of Wyoming, learning the struggles and triumphs of our peoples. Or you might live in another town, far away from the reservation but speaking either Shoshone or Arapaho as you pray, offering tobacco and burning sage. Maybe you will stand where I’m standing, waxing poetically in the moonlight. 
Generations from now, will you still be fighting the same battles for land, water and wildlife? There is a hope you will have already won protections for your plant and animal relatives. And perhaps even yourself.
In this future, long gone are the days of fighting for our rights, our languages and our cultures. The United States has finally lived up to its broken promises and has a good relationship with the Tribal nations who call this place home. I see it all so beautifully.
My greatest dream is that this information is so ingrained in you and all your non-native friends that it’s boring. I hope you whine, voice heavy with exasperation, “Please don’t make me read this! I’ve learned it thousands of times already.”
Don’t let this old ghost bore you.
But if the need to fight remains, we must begin long ago in a place now called Wyoming: the Equality State. 
The Eastern Shoshone’s ties here on Wind River date back 12,000 years, according to petroglyphs, artifacts and villages. The area that would eventually become the Wind River Indian Reservation was the preferred wintering grounds for the Eastern Shoshone. They called it “yu’paakatete,” or the Warm Valley. A good place to be during the cold and windy winter months of the high plains. The Wind River Mountains continue to be a place of respite and reconnection for Tribal locals. I hope you have visited them often and for long periods of time.
(Taylar Dawn Stagner)
Buffalo nations, like the Eastern Shoshone, followed herds across the plains for thousands of years. They filled the continent — millions from Canada to Florida. The horse also made hunting Buffalo easier on the plains, and the Shoshone were some of the first tribes to adopt them in hunting Buffalo — called “boy-zhan.” I capitalize Buffalo to show the importance of the relationship.
The Eastern Shoshone are matriarchal, meaning women held important cultural power and political positions. The word in English comes from the Greek noun “māter” meaning “mother” and the Greek verb “archein” meaning “to rule”.
From this perspective, matriarchy could be seen as the foil to patriarchy, with women ruling over men. But this is not so. Our matriarchal societies were built on community care and kinship systems, guided by the mothers and their families in conjunction with the men. They showed leadership not through domination and control, but through community responsibility and generosity. There was conflict, of course, but it was a far cry from the patriarchal structure the United States lives under now.
Matriarchy is the sibling of patriarchy, not its twin. Like brothers and sisters, they do not mirror each other, but have distinct personalities and priorities. 
As the United States built the railroad westward, and settlers slowly started to show more interest in this area, conflict grew, until eventually the United States struck a deal with Chief Washakie and the Eastern Shoshone. The Fort Bridger Treaty of 1863 facilitated a heck of a deal — around 44 million acres, plus food, medicine and safety. It was called the Eastern Shoshone Reservation. 
Then five years later, in the Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868, a trend started to emerge. The United States began to rewrite the original deal they had signed, and the Shoshone Reservation shrunk as settlers arrived. 
And on it went. The Brunot session reduced the reservation by a third and opened portions for white settlement, the McLaughlin agreement helped establish the town of Riverton, and the Homesteading Act further sold off lands north of the Wind River that bisects the reservation. 
During this time, the Eastern Shoshone could not leave their dwindling reservation land and their traditional hunting, fishing and foraging dwindled as settlers closed in. The food provided by the United States government was notoriously poor in quality, and the attempts to make farmers out of a nomadic Buffalo nation were not well funded, as the main goal was to assimilate them into settler society. The settlers killed the Buffalo indiscriminately, policed water use and arrested or attacked Native people who left the reservation. 
Treaties are important documents. While it might feel like ancient history to you, it’s important to remember that we gave up land to secure a future where the U.S. government would provide adequate healthcare and food. Around 370 of these promises were broken by the United States. 
The Northern Arapaho faced injustices of their own. In 1864, the U.S. military killed around 230 Cheyenne and Arapaho people, mostly women, children and elders of both the northern and southern bands of Arapaho. Both tribes still recognize the Sand Creek Massacre to this day, and I hope you, future ancestor, have been to an event or two.
(Mike Vanata)
They had been promised a reservation in the Front Range of Colorado, but gold was found. The Arapaho were evicted from their traditional homelands. It took 14 years after the events at Sand Creek, but in 1878 the Northern Arapaho were brought to the Wind River Indian Reservation. 
That’s how we got here. Stolen land and people taken before their time for no reason other than that they were Native. Not the story people want at their July Fourth barbecue, but it’s important for everyone to know. 
The story of Indigenous peoples and the story of settlers. It feels like you are describing two different realities. Disparate histories that don’t sit well together. Do you make the reality more palatable, or do you throw your heart onto the page? I hope you know the answer for yourself. 
In 1869, Wyoming’s first territorial Legislature passed a bill that allowed white women the right to vote. Indigenous women, who occupied a space of great respect and leadership, were losing more of their rights by the year. A year before this, the U.S. government kept around 2,500 Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho on the Wind River Indian Reservation like prisoners. A cruel irony for a nomadic people used to foraging and hunting, now relying on subpar rations from the federal government to survive, while the new Wyoming government built itself upon stolen old hunting grounds. 
Non-Native women had received a small leg up while our women ancestors were confined to the reservation.
The Buffalo by this time were close to extinction on the continent. Settlers killed them indiscriminately as the railroad made its way west. This was no accident, but rather a targeted attack on our food, on our self-reliance.
The Buffalo are also matriarchal, and both the Arapaho and Eastern Shoshone mirror Buffalo social systems in our own lives. Buffalo are often led by females that decide where to eat, when to bed down and when to go. They do all this while having a baby almost every year and often outlive their male counterparts by almost a decade. 
I hope it’s not lost on you that the near extinction of Buffalo coincides with Indigenous women losing power and status in settler society. Today, Indigenous women are attacked and killed at higher rates than almost any other demographic. Our pain is not seen, and our voices are unheard. 
Cattle replaced Buffalo on the plains, and extractive mining and oil operations moved in. Gone were the stewardship practices that protected the Bridger Teton and Medicine Bow forests, and Yellowstone National Park was purged of Indigenous presences in favor of a “fortress conservation” that erased the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho relationship with the area.
Yes, Wyoming became the first state to give settler women the right to vote 21 years before becoming a state, but it’s hard to hold that fact alongside our removal. This was a political act employed by a conquering nation, so it’s hard for me to celebrate. So I don’t. Not when I see so many persistent issues on the Wind River Indian Reservation. 
If we went into all the bad things that happened during this time, we would have room for nothing else. The government made our ceremonies and traditional ways illegal, and the boarding school system tried to strip us of our languages and traditional ties to our lands. Our languages are now endangered and might disappear in the span of a generation. 
These facts magnify everything else.
(Ryan Dorgan)
“Equality” did not exist for us here in Wyoming, and we would not gain the right to vote until 1924 with the Indian Citizenship Act. Voting power, while important, is hard to compare with our own societies, where women held considerably more political power. Settlers brought with them patriarchy and the dominance over women, and we now must learn to live alongside and within that power structure. 
Maybe you feel different. And maybe you are less bitter than me, and you have moved forward, hand in hand, with this place now called Wyoming. I pray that you use this clarity to do good for the Shoshone and Arapaho peoples.
You are of this land. Your bones know the soil. Your blood and the Wind River flow with the same memory. 
The problems on the Wind River Indian Reservation will not be fixed in one or two lifetimes. True equality demands a hard look at the past. I hope you already reside there, in that idyllic future, where our people, water, lands and wildlife are cherished and protected. 
Where all this is common knowledge.
I hope you are happy and healthy. Our history is longer than a firework. It’s as enduring as our most precious ceremonies. When I see the brilliance of the night sky and its blazing moon, the explosions don’t seem as big and bombastic. In a forest full of teepees, what is a birthday candle to the moon?

title: On the eve of Colorado statehood in 1876, two men were lynched by a Cañon City mob
description: The official canvass of the Colorado Territory’s referendum approving a state constitution was completed at Gov. John Routt’s office on July 24, 1876. The final tally was 15,443 votes for the constitution and statehood, and 4,030 votes against. Routt, the Civil War infantry captain appointed territorial governor by President Ulysses S. Grant the previous yea[...]
text:
A view of a street in Cañon City in a photograph dated between 1871 and 1874.
(Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, Z-6637)The official canvass of the Colorado Territory’s referendum approving a state constitution was completed at Gov. John Routt’s office on July 24, 1876.



← July 16–22
July 23–29 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

The final tally was 15,443 votes for the constitution and statehood, and 4,030 votes against. Routt, the Civil War infantry captain appointed territorial governor by President Ulysses S. Grant the previous year, affixed his signature to the canvass and dispatched it to Congress and the White House.
“Mr. Reigart, private secretary to Gov. Routt, will leave for Washington tomorrow as the bearer of the official vote,” reported the Denver Times.
Seventeen years on from the start of the Pikes Peak gold rush, and roughly 30 years since the Hispano settlers of the San Luis Valley became Colorado’s first non-Indigenous permanent residents, Colorado was on the verge of becoming the 38th state admitted to the union.
“Closing out all our TERRITORIAL goods,” read an ad from Salomon’s grocery store, at 15th and Larimer streets in Denver, “so as to fill up with now at STATE prices.”
The story leading many territorial newspapers that week, however, wasn’t Grant’s imminent proclamation of Colorado statehood but a brutal act of vigilante justice in southern Colorado.
A horse trader named Newman had traveled to the Colorado Territory earlier in 1876 and was seen with two other men in the Wet Mountain Valley, in present-day Custer County, in early July. A party of cattle herders discovered Newman’s dead body a week later, and his wagon and team of horses were missing.

Suspicion immediately fell on his two companions, and two men were captured and accused of the murder in the days that followed: Jose Talmage, identified as the son of a Mexican mother and a Hungarian-Italian father, and Felipe Salazar, both “well known” residents of Cañon City, the Pueblo Chieftain would report.
Newspaper accounts show considerable confusion about the two men’s identities in the aftermath of Newman’s killing. At least one of the dead man’s companions was first reported to be an “American” — that is, white — man, possibly named Jim, but when caught, Talmage and Salazar were branded as the “two Mexican murderers.” Talmage was initially characterized as having been “always considered a quiet and steady young man,” but after his arrest the Chieftain declared he had “heretofore born(e) a bad reputation, and that of his father is no better.”
The “shocking murder … has cast a gloom over the whole valley,” wrote the paper’s Wet Mountain correspondent, “and the persons who committed the horrible deed, if caught, had as well be a thousand miles from land, in an open boat, with sails of lead and oars of iron and purgatory his nearest port.” Among the valley’s ranchers, there was little doubt as to who the killers were.
“It is the general opinion among those who understand the facts in the case, that Talmage and (Salazar) murdered Mr. Newman,” reported the Chieftain.
That was all a mob needed to storm the Cañon City jail where the two men were being held on the night of July 21, and bring them “before Judge Lynch’s court,” as the Chieftain put it. They purportedly confessed to killing Newman, and were promptly hanged. As was often the case in such acts of vigilantism, a subsequent coroner’s inquest said the two men had “come to their death from hands unknown.”
“Cañon City is not a place where we would expect mob law would be enforced, and the people there have the reputation of being among the most law-abiding in the state,” the Chieftain observed. “In our eight years experience in southern Colorado, we have never known man to be lynched there.”
Vigilantism on the frontier
The Chieftain and other Colorado newspapers were mostly supportive of this act of mob justice, albeit with some throat-clearing ambivalence about lynchings in principle. They were quick to blame the act on territorial criminal statutes that barred capital punishment in the case of a guilty plea, as in the case of several Italian-American men convicted of murder in Denver earlier that year.
“However much we may deprecate the exercise of lynch law, the very peculiar statutes which we have regarding murder is the direct father of this affair at Cañon City,” said the Golden Globe.
In Denver, the Rocky Mountain News was even more direct in excusing the extralegal executions: “The atrocity of the Wet Mountain murder was such as to call for swifter and surer retribution than is commonly reached by legal process,” declared an editorial. “The News has no sympathy to waste on the hardened wretches who met their fate at the hands of men who, in the absence of a law adequate to the punishment of the crime committed, framed an admirable substitute.”
“It is, perhaps, unfortunate that the law was not permitted to take its course with these culprits,” allowed the Chieftain. “But so many murderers have escaped their just dues of late in Colorado, and the jails are so exceedingly leaky, that some allowance must be made for a little extra haste and zeal on the part of the citizens in punishing these cut-throats.”
A portrait of Colorado Gov. John Rout, taken sometime between 1875 and 1895. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, Z-1971)
“The Mexican population of Cañon City are the only people in that section who are not pleased with the action of the vigilantes,” the Chieftain added in passing.
At least 19 of the 175 documented lynchings that occurred in Colorado between 1859 and 1919 targeted Hispanic people, according to historian Stephen J. Leonard. Hispanos accused of crimes were especially at risk from vigilantism in Arkansas River Valley towns like Cañon City, where the diverging demographics of northern and southern Colorado clashed.
“At those points of contact, where Anglo Americans held the power, Mexican Americans were more likely to be lynched on a per capita basis than they were in Trinidad and other heavily Hispanic places south of the Arkansas,” writes Leonard. “In Trinidad, where Mexican Americans could elect sheriffs and other officials, Anglos could not kill with impunity.”
By the mid-1880s, pro-lynching attitudes “rapidly fell out of favor” in Colorado, Leonard writes. Shortly after being appointed territorial governor in 1875, Routt had dealt with a plague of deadly feuds and extrajudicial violence among settlers in the frontier region of Lake County, which included the murder of a county judge who had issued arrest warrants for members of a vigilance committee. In his message to the final territorial Legislature in January, he called for the funding of a standing militia in part “to check mob violence, and to enforce the civil authority when resisted.”
Though widespread in 1876, the Colorado Territory’s approval of the lynchings of Talmage and Salazar — rooted in a belief in the “frontier justice” of its Wild West days — wasn’t unanimous. The Colorado Springs Gazette was among those unafraid to say, in a July 29 editorial, that the act was a “disgrace” to the soon-to-be state of Colorado.
“There is no security for any, in person, rights, or property, except under a vigilant, impartial, firm administration of the law, and it is the duty of good citizens to obey and to aid in enforcing it,” wrote the Gazette. “The act of this lawless mob, although with different motives, was just as much murder as the act they assumed authority to punish.”



Selected sources

The Rocky Mountain News, July 25, 1876
The Pueblo Chieftain, July 11–23, 1876
Leonard, Stephen J. “Lynching in Colorado, 1859–1919”

description: Idaho state election officials are asking the public to weigh in on a proposed ballot initiative to end the state’s strict abortion ban. The Idaho Secretary of State’s Office will feature some arguments in favor and against the ballot initiative on a voter pamphlet that it mails to all Idaho households ahead of the Nov. […]
text:
Volunteers pass boxes of signatures supporting a ballot initiative to end Idaho's strict ban on abortion on July 2, 2026, outside the state Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho state election officials are asking the public to weigh in on a proposed ballot initiative to end the state’s strict abortion ban.
The Idaho Secretary of State’s Office will feature some arguments in favor and against the ballot initiative on a voter pamphlet that it mails to all Idaho households ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
Arguments related to the Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act are due by 11:59 p.m. Mountain time on Friday, July 31, the Secretary of State’s Office announced in a news release. Submit arguments online at https://forms.sos.idaho.gov/pro-con/. Learn more about Idaho’s ballot initiative process online at voteidaho.gov/initiatives-amendments/.
This year’s voter pamphlet will include information on two constitutional amendments, proposed by the Legislature. Here’s a primer on those:

One proposed amendment, through House Joint Resolution 4, would allow only the Idaho Legislature – and not Idaho voters – to have the authority to legalize medical cannabis, recreational marijuana or any other drug. A proposed ballot initiative to legalize medical marijuana failed to qualify for the ballot this year, election officials announced last week.
Another proposed amendment, through House Joint Resolution 6, would declare English as the state’s official language.

A committee of legislative leaders last month approved language to describe those two proposed constitutional amendments on ballots. 
The voter pamphlet will also include information on an advisory question for voters to designate a state gun for Idaho. Lawmakers approved the advisory question this year through House Bill 932.

title: Stockard on the Stump: Congressional candidate says he’ll drop Chinese military stocks
description: Tennessee Sen. Brent Taylor held Chinese military stocks as part of his investment portfolio even though he says President Donald Trump endorsed him in the Republican primary for the 9th Congressional District seat because he’ll be tough on China. Taylor reported owning between $1,000 and $15,000 worth of stock in three companies connected to China, […]
text:
State Sen. Brent Taylor reported owning between $1,000 and $15,000 worth of stock in three companies connected to China, two of which are designated by the Pentagon as “Chinese military companies.” (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Sen. Brent Taylor held Chinese military stocks as part of his investment portfolio even though he says President Donald Trump endorsed him in the Republican primary for the 9th Congressional District seat because he’ll be tough on China.
Taylor reported owning between $1,000 and $15,000 worth of stock in three companies connected to China, two of which are designated by the Pentagon as “Chinese military companies.” They are Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., Tencent Holdings Ltd. and Prosus N.V. ADR, which holds a large stake in Tencent, according to his federal financial disclosure.
In response to questions from the Lookout, Taylor, a Shelby County Republican, said the president knows he has a “record of holding China accountable.” Trump and numerous Republican leaders and candidates have gone back to a tough-on-communism mantra as election season heats up.
Taylor explained in a text message to the Lookout that a broker handles his portfolio and independently moves his funds in and out of investments. 
“Nonetheless, I recently instructed my broker to review my holdings and sell any associated with Chinese businesses,” Taylor, a former funeral home owner, said in the text message.
The senator, as he is wont to do, joked that his broker doesn’t bury dead people and he doesn’t trade stocks.
Starbucks is opening a corporate office in Nashville. (Photo by Karen Pulfer Focht/Tennessee Lookout)
But Taylor doesn’t bury dead people anymore after selling his funeral home business to a company that broke ties with him. Yet his disclosure form shows it continues to pay him a tidy sum, $35,000 last year and $17,500 so far this year.
Taylor also holds stock in Starbucks, which has come under scrutiny for — gasp — liberal leanings after receiving a $30 million state grant to open a corporate headquarters in Nashville. Taylor didn’t answer the Lookout’s questions about those two matters.
He’s going up against Republican state Rep. Todd Warner for the 9th District seat after the Tennessee Legislature split the majority-minority district in Memphis and diluted it with white, rural voters stretching all the way to Williamson County, since they have so much in common. The idea is to give Republicans a clean sweep of Tennessee’s congressional delegation following a U.S. Supreme Court decision that dismantled a key provision in the 1965 Voting Rights Act.
Warner’s disclosure form isn’t quite as exciting as Taylor’s. He has some loans on farm equipment and bank notes on his Chapel Hill property.
He entered office a few years ago on a not-so-high note, when the feds introduced themselves at his house early one morning as part of the investigation into former House Speaker Glen Casada and his ex-staffer Cade Cothren, who were subsequently convicted of multiple counts of fraud involving a secretive company that tapped into lawmakers’ state funds for constituent mailers. 
After a painful four-week trial, Casada and Cothren received full presidential pardons — as if it never happened.
Rep. Todd Warner in his legislative office at the Cordell Hull Building with a life-size Donald Trump cutout. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Considering Warner has a life-size cutout of Trump in his office and continues to use Cothren for campaign work, you’d think the president would endorse him. But alas.
Despite the feds’ invasion before he took the oath of office, Warner was never indicted. He did catch the wrath of neighbors last year after starting a mining and quarry operation on his farm, which he claimed was an agriculture operation.
At the Capitol, he bucked House Republican and Senate leadership a couple of times and fought Gov. Bill Lee’s private-school voucher program. It didn’t work, but he garnered attention. He even teamed with ultra-liberal Rep. Aftyn Behn — OMG — for legislation that would move sexual harassment investigations from the legislature’s control to the attorney general.
Also running in the Republican primary for the 9th District seat are perennial candidate Charlotte Bergmann of Memphis and Jeremy Thompson of Fayetteville.
The winner is likely to take on Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson or state Sen. London Lamar, either of whom would face an uphill fight in a district designed to guarantee a Republican winner. Other Democrats in the race are LaTroy A-Williams of Memphis and Jim Torino of Columbia.
Pearson and Lamar are still running to hold on to their state seats, though, so they’ll probably be hanging out in D.C. or Nashville next year. Never fear.
Gubernatorial primary heats up
The Republican race for governor appears to be tightening as U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, nearly crowned early this year, lobs attacks at U.S. Rep. John Rose.
The Blackburn campaign accused Rose this week of falsely claiming that Blackburn is attacking him, when it was really an outside group.
To back up their argument, Blackburn’s campaign provided evidence that Rose voted as a Democrat in three primaries, including the 2002 and 2004 presidential primaries, donated money to Democratic candidates and committees and was appointed to the Tennessee Heritage Conservation Trust by former Gov. Phil Bredesen, a Democrat.
Further, Blackburn’s people challenged Rose’s claims that he co-founded Transcender Corporation, saying his friend, Aneel Pandey, really started the company before Rose joined him when they were law school students at Vanderbilt.
Rose campaign spokesperson Chris Devaney responded by saying it’s “rich” that the Blackburn campaign is claiming it isn’t attacking Rose when PACS are doing exactly that on Blackburn’s behalf.
As for the founding of Transcender, which Rose sold for a pretty penny, Devaney said if Blackburn had done anything “besides being a career politician, she would understand that starting a business involves more than just filing paperwork with the state.”
Meanwhile, Rose is calling for Blackburn to explain the results of a Senate Ethics Committee investigation into claims that she used taxpayer resources for political campaigns. NewsChannel5 reported on conversations by Blackburn’s staffers that they were worried about being asked to violate the Hatch Act by working on her campaign while on federal time.
Final votes are to be cast Aug. 6 in the Tennessee primary.
Photo op at the Capitol
Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn poses with Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson and a large group of young people in the House chamber of the Tennessee Capitol. (Photo via Blackburn’s campaign Facebook page)
Sen. Blackburn’s Facebook page contains a March 28 picture of her and Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson in the House chamber of the Tennessee Capitol with a large group of young people. Some of them, including Johnson, are wearing “Marsha Marsha Marsha” stickers.
Blackburn doesn’t appear to be sporting her own campaign slogan, potentially enabling her to circumvent prohibitions on using the Capitol for political campaigns.
In fact, state law says it’s illegal for any elected or appointed official of the state to display campaign literature, banners, placards, streamers, stickers, signs or other campaign items or political advertising on behalf of any party, committee or agency or any candidate for political office on the premises of any state building or land. 
Johnson, of course, is wearing a “Marsha Marsha Marsha” sticker, but Blackburn was comfortable enough with the picture to put it on Facebook. That must make it OK.
More than a bad look
A week after writing an op-ed about questionable teachings at a police use-of-force seminar, Memphis District Attorney Steve Mulroy declined to pursue charges against a U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency agent who shot and killed a Memphis Burger King worker. 
Mulroy then released brief videos used to make the decision in connection with the shooting death of Darrin Pigram, 41. The videos don’t exactly match the claims that Pigram pulled up his shirt and showed a gun when members of the Memphis Safe Task Force entered the restaurant to serve an arrest warrant. The footage has several gaps.
What the video shows is disturbing and shocking. Pigram is gunned down as co-workers watch.
And for what? He wasn’t wanted on a drug-related charge.
The Lookout reported that Pigram had one misdemeanor conviction in Memphis for threatening his stepfather. The arrest warrant feds served on him was for aggravated assault, aggravated burglary and employing a firearm in commission of a felony in connection with an accusation that he threatened neighbors with a gun over loud music in January.
In that case, deadly force has to be justified?
If you fully support the task force’s actions and the Mulroy decision, though, consider this: According to the Lookout report, the task force members couldn’t find Pigram at home, so they went to Burger King.
They couldn’t wait until he got off work and went home. Thus, someone came up with the bright idea for DEA and other agents to go to Burger King where folks were eating, working and going about their day when officers wearing military garb and carrying rifles took over the place and killed a man who got mad about loud music?
Done with it
Sen. Ferrell Haile is dropping out of the race for Tennessee Senate speaker, leaving it to Johnson and Sen. Paul Bailey to grapple for the top position, the Tennessee Journal reports.
Haile told the Lookout this year he decided to enter the field to replace outgoing Senate Speaker Randy McNally after several people asked him to get involved.
Speculation was that Johnson and Bailey weren’t lighting anyone’s fire, so Haile could bring a steady hand to the race. Haile’s candidacy clearly didn’t excite enough people to garner a majority in the Senate Republican Caucus, which will choose the speaker, who also serves as lieutenant governor, second in the line of succession in Tennessee.
The caucus has 27 members, so it’s going to take a lot of cajoling and maybe some arm-twisting to line up the votes for a win. They have until December to get it done.
