name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama officials to ask federal government for two-year delay on SNAP error rate penalty
description: Alabama officials Thursday asked the federal government to extend a two-year reprieve from changes to a food assistance program that could cost the state more than $174 million based on errors in the program.  The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) introduced a penalty for states with a high error rate in the Supplemental Nutrition […]
text:
Brandon Hardin, Alabama SNAP Director, speaking at the Department of Human Resources meeting on July 23, 2026, in the Gordon Persons Building in Montgomery, Alabama. The DHR board unanimously approved a motion for the commissioner to ask the congressional delegation for a two-year delay on the SNAP error rate penalty, which is currently projected to cost the state $174 million. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama officials Thursday asked the federal government to extend a two-year reprieve from changes to a food assistance program that could cost the state more than $174 million based on errors in the program. 
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) introduced a penalty for states with a high error rate in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Alabama’s error rate for fiscal year 2025 was 9.52%, SNAP Director Brandon Hardin said at a quarterly meeting of the Alabama Department of Human Resources (DHR), which administers the program in the state. 
“It’s not even close to a measure of fraud. It’s when a household circumstance changes, and they do not report that, it ends up becoming a potential error in that case,” Hardin said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He said errors can be on the client, the agency, or can be under-issuances or overpayments of benefits. 
A $174.3 million penalty
Alabama will have to pay about $174.3 million beginning Oct. 1, 2027, or about 10% of the state’s SNAP benefits, unless the FY26 error rate gets below 7.99%. Before the passage of the OBBBA, the benefits were fully funded by the federal government. 
The changes to the program have pushed over 80,000 Alabamians off SNAP, according to an analysis released Wednesday by the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning think tank. About 23,000 were children.
According to preliminary data for FY26, the state’s error rate is trending down, but the first three months of the fiscal year were difficult, Hardin said in an interview after the meeting. A shutdown of the federal government in November left SNAP-recipients without benefits. 
The error rate in November was 12.86%, which is about $4,300 “error dollars.” The state issued $142 million in benefits that month. The error rate in February was 5.37%, about $1,800 error dollars. The state issued $135 million in benefits that month. Through the first five months of FY26, the error rate is 9.55%.
“Ultimately, we are seeing a downward trend. But statistically, you’ve got to have a lot more dollars involved in it,” he said. “All the states submitted a request in the first part of this fiscal year to exempt October and November samples because it was such a trying time during the shutdown, and that was denied at the federal level … Those months, you’ve got to understand that it was very chaotic for a client.”
If the FY26 error rate is between 6% and 7.99%, the state will have to pay 5% of its benefits in 2027. Based on FY25 issuance, that would be $87.1 million. In 2028, the state’s penalty is based solely on the FY26 error rate. 
Trump budget bill will increase Alabama SNAP costs, say state officials

States with error rates below 6% or above 20% will not have to pay penalties. Penalties for states on the high end will have a two-year delayed implementation.
“All the other states should be treated fairly. They should all get the same treatment,” DHR Commissioner Nancy Buckner said.
‘What we’re going to have to live and die by’
Error rates, part of the program’s quality control system, are based on 1,020 cases over the fiscal year, Hardin said. Currently, there are approximately 650,000 individuals enrolled in SNAP, about 45% of whom are children. 
Hardin said there are three options with the error rate: pay the penalty, get below 6% or end SNAP in Alabama.
“That baseline is 1,020 cases. They’re basing a $1.7 billion program that’s on the brink of what could happen to it based on 1,020 cases,” Hardin said. “We do 750,000 transactions a year, and that sample is what we’re going to have to live and die by.”
Buckner said that without a SNAP program, crime rates could go up, medical costs would increase and test scores would decrease.
“Food banks themselves say they cannot make it up, and I believe that it would be up to the people,” she said. “Food is a necessity for people. Whether they’ve got it, they’re going to get it one way or the other to feed their children.”
The board unanimously approved a motion, brought by Joe Morton, for Buckner to send a letter to the Alabama congressional delegation asking for a two-year delayed implementation of the error rate penalty.
“I think it would be well for this board to support that effort, so we would officially take a stand that we’re headed in the right direction in Alabama, but we just need more time,” Morton said.
Hardin said the department has implemented several “payment accuracy strategies” to improve the error rate since the passage of the OBBBA, but the results will not be visible until the FY26 error rate is finalized in 2027. 
Congressional reaction
Messages seeking comment from the congressional delegation were left Thursday afternoon. U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Selma, said in a statement that the cuts to SNAP is one of the reasons she voted against the OBBBA. 
“I am open to exploring any proposal that would reverse or mitigate the harm that this cruel bill is inflicting on our children, but let’s be clear – these cuts to SNAP should never have become law in the first place,” she said. “Hard working Alabama families should not have to struggle to put food on the table so that billionaires can get even richer.”
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, said in a statement Thursday that he, like all Democratic representatives, voted against the bill because of the potential impacts to programs like SNAP and Medicaid. 
“Republicans continued to tell us time and time again that no children would be cut off from SNAP. Now here we are, with over 80,000 Alabamians – including over 23,000 children – having access to food ripped away while billionaires got permanent tax breaks in the same law,” Figures said. “Now the Alabama DHR board is essentially saying that they need relief from the effects of the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill.’”
More than 80,000 Alabamians have lost food assistance, according to study

Hardin said that SNAP participation fluctuates with the economy, with peak enrollment in 2012 at about 912,000. Eligibility for the program was expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, when there were about 770,000 Alabamians enrolled. The OBBBA tightened eligibility work requirements, which has contributed to some of the 80,000 Alabamians that lost benefits between the passage of the law in July 2025 and May.
Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is the party’s nominee for governor, said in a statement in June that DHR should use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve the error rate.
“Alabama’s SNAP error rate is too high, and we need to look into creative ways to get rid of fraud. I think AI could help us with that. I’m all for helping people who have fallen on hard times, but SNAP has become overrun with fraud,” he said.
Buckner said Thursday that although AI can identify an error, the department needs more bodies to fix the problems. 
“When everybody’s out there, AI is going to solve the problem. AI is not going to solve this problem … Whatever AI finds is going to make a body go out and do it,” she said. “It is hard because we don’t have the additional money in our budget to hire the additional staff who are needed to go behind and do the second party reviews.”
Federal and state officials have pressured DHR to lower the error rate, but Buckner said it is not as easy as it sounds.
“I’m hoping there’s enough compassion in people’s hearts that are in control of whether we have to go forward with this or not,” she said. “That there’ll be some wiggle room to change it a little bit to make it more fair for states versus other states that got a two-year pass.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Boliek’s contentious elections boards make proposed rules less democratic
description: North Carolina Auditor Dave Boliek may not have wanted to hog the headlines in a year when he isn’t on the ballot. But thanks to his recent actions to weaponize GOP majorities on elections boards to push anti-democratic rules and early voting changes, Boliek is making quite a name for himself ahead of the midterms. When he […]
text:
Voting booths stand ready for use in a U.S. election. (Photo: MRolands/Getty Images)North Carolina Auditor Dave Boliek may not have wanted to hog the headlines in a year when he isn’t on the ballot. But thanks to his recent actions to weaponize GOP majorities on elections boards to push anti-democratic rules and early voting changes, Boliek is making quite a name for himself ahead of the midterms.
When he was elected as Trump’s pick for auditor in 2024, Boliek became the highest-ranking Republican in the executive branch. That’s how the GOP lawmakers, hellbent on stripping elections powers from Democratic governor Josh Stein, used a legal loophole to let Boliek hand-pick election deniers and other anti-voter voices to the State Board of Elections. He was also able to choose Republicans to chair elections boards in all 100 counties, handing the GOP a majority on five-person county elections boards — like those in Rowan, Pitt , and Harnett that have become noticeably more divided as they take up 2026 elections options.
Through his hyper-partisan election appointments, Boliek, the only auditor in the country with the authority to make them, also handed his friends in the legislature what they wanted: another means to cast doubts on fair elections, while putting more barriers in place for Democratic voters. Democrats shouldn’t be the only ones concerned.
Last week, Boliek’s State Board of Elections advanced proposed rules that would allow a simple 3-2 majority in each county to toss eligible votes cast using legal voter ID exception forms. If GOP members don’t believe your reason for not being able to show photo ID, your vote, regardless of party, won’t count.
State Board of Elections’ data shows if this rule had been in place in 2024, one party would have decided the fate of ballots cast by more than 4,600 eligible North Carolinians. That’s over 10 times the amount of the 401 votes statewide that it took to elect the current chief justice of the NC Supreme Court — the same person who coincidentally led the effort to reinstate NC’s voter ID law in the first place.
If Boleik has his way, it appears another pivotal NC Supreme Court seat could be determined by whether these types of votes are counted this fall.
This proposed rule is particularly dangerous given how toxic county boards’ deliberations on early voting options have become on Boliek’s watch.
In Pasquotank County, where Republicans and Democrats had been able to compromise on early voting plans before, this year Boliek’s GOP board chair made clear that he was choosing “recommendations” from the auditor’s staff based on the right options for right-wing voters. He joined with the two other Republican members to “drop Sunday” voting options as Boliek’s team had directed and eliminate the county’s only early voting site from Elizabeth City State University — a popular location used by the historically Black college and community in federal elections since the pandemic. Republicans opted instead to move the county’s single early voting option to the small county board of elections office currently under renovations, with no guarantees that the building nor the parking lot will be ready to handle an election this year.
Granville County’s election board members also made national headlines last week during the county’s third contentious meeting on voting options. Despite signaling otherwise, GOP members ultimately refused to compromise with their Democratic colleagues as they had in previous cycles, instead taking direction from former party chair who was texting them verbatim what to say to justify cutting two popular sites used by at least 70% of the county, including 90% of Black voters, but keeping a site demanded by Republicans.
These hyper-partisan plans follow months of bitter county-level meetings, assorted ethics complaints against Republican members, and public records requests proving that Boliek’s staff pressured local officials, leading to the resignation of his ”eyes and ears on the ground” Dallas Woodhouse, who already had a decade of experience requiring Republican-friendly plans.
Woodhouse’s departure won’t change that Boilek himself took the unprecedented step of making direct asks of his local appointees, including in Anson County where he demanded the chair add a site to boost GOP turnout, with similar demands in Moore County, which ultimately fell on deaf ears.
Fortunately, some bipartisan county boards of conscience are listening to their communities rather than capitulating to Boliek.
In Jackson County, the auditor’s office now infamously told Republican board members there that they should shutter a campus site or lose their jobs. One GOP member fired back, “kiss my ass.”
It’s now voters’ turn to be that angry.
Sailor Jones is state director of Common Cause North Carolina.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New $2.3M ad campaign ties Whatley to convicted sex offender as NC’s US Senate race tightens
description: A Democratic-aligned political group is launching a $2.3 million ad campaign targeting Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley over his ties to Harvey West, a longtime party fundraiser and convicted sex offender. The digital ads, run by WinSenate PAC, will air on YouTube, smart TVs, and streaming services. They come as outside groups supporting What[...]
text:
North Carolina Republican Senate hopeful Michael Whatley (R) speaks alongside U.S. President Donald Trump at the Rocky Mount Event Center on Dec. 19, 2025 in Rocky Mount. (Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)A Democratic-aligned political group is launching a $2.3 million ad campaign targeting Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley over his ties to Harvey West, a longtime party fundraiser and convicted sex offender.
The digital ads, run by WinSenate PAC, will air on YouTube, smart TVs, and streaming services. They come as outside groups supporting Whatley, a former chairman of the RNC and NCGOP, have ramped up attacks on his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper.
“A police officer charged with molesting three young girls,” the ad states, as news reports on the controversy are shown. “Then Michael Whatley hired him, even though West was open about his criminal record.”
The ad includes a selfie of the two men that West posted to his Facebook page.
Heading into midterms, NCGOP faces mounting backlash from its conservative base

West was arrested in 2000 and charged with the statutory rape of three minors while serving as a police officer in the Outer Banks. Those charges were reduced to five counts of indecent liberties with a child as part of a plea deal, under which West was sentenced to six years in prison and required to register as a sex offender. He was released in 2006.
Years later, during Whatley’s tenure as chair of the North Carolina Republican Party, he appointed West to the party’s rulemaking committee multiple times. West also served as the state GOP’s 1st Congressional District chair under Whatley and hosted a high-profile judicial fundraiser that has put the Republican judges who attended it under scrutiny.
“I openly discussed what happened. I openly discussed my time in prison. I openly discussed the charges,” West said in an interview with The Daily Beast earlier this year. “And I would tell people, ‘If you want me around, I will work and be glad to do so. If you don’t want me, I’ll go on down the road.’”
Whatley’s ties to West resurfaced after reporting by the Asheville Watchdog in March, which covered backlash to West’s selection to moderate a Dare County Board of Education primary forum. Conservative outrage mounted soon after, leading to West’s resignation as chair of the district party.
Polling of the North Carolina U.S. Senate race has consistently shown Whatley behind Cooper, often by double digits, but recent surveys have found that the share of voters who view Cooper unfavorably has grown. That shift may reflect the success of attacks on Cooper by Whatley and political groups supporting him.
Whatley has repeatedly condemned the release of thousands of prisoners under a settlement between Cooper’s administration and civil rights groups due to the dangers of COVID-19.
Former Gov. Roy Cooper speaks to supporters at an April 9, 2026 rally in Durham. Whatley has attacked him over COVID-era prisoner releases. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)
Whatley has not discussed his connection to West publicly, and rebuffed an NC Newsline reporter who asked why he chose to appoint West despite his criminal background. “Probably the better question would be, ‘Why did Roy Cooper release thousands of hardened criminals from prison?’” he responded.
The state released an estimated 3,500 inmates from prison early under the terms of the settlement, according to the Department of Public Safety. At least some of these inmates had been convicted of violent crimes, according to the Charlotte Observer, including offenders who had been sentenced to life in prison but were eligible for parole. Multiple inmates were in prison for murder.
NC Newsline has not been invited to attend any of Whatley’s campaign events since that press conference, as Whatley’s campaign has taken an increasingly confrontational approach to the media.
His campaign has also slammed Cooper, 69, as an establishment politician whose decades in government have put him out of touch with the average North Carolinian.
Whatley, 57, has also been a longtime fixture in North Carolina politics. He began his career as a GOP operator more than two decades ago as chief of staff to Republican U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Dole in 2004 before spending a decade lobbying in Washington.
The new ads highlighting Whatley’s ties to West come in addition to an $11 million advertising investment announced by the Democratic-aligned political group Senate Majority PAC on Thursday as outside spending in the race ramps up. While Cooper has maintained a hefty lead over Whatley in fundraising, outside spending between the candidates is neck-and-neck.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Fifty for 150: Women in Colorado lobbied male voters to approve 1893 referendum on suffrage
description: A popular vote on a referendum granted women the right to vote in Colorado on Nov. 7, 1893.  Just under 55% of male voters supported the measure — 35,798 votes for, and 29,551 votes against.  While it’s debated which state was actually the first to grant women the right to vote, Colorado was the first […]
text:
Women voters are pictured outside of a polling place in the early 1900s. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, Z-8811)A popular vote on a referendum granted women the right to vote in Colorado on Nov. 7, 1893. 



This story is part of Colorado at 150. Each Fifty for 150 story focuses on an event that helped define Colorado over 150 years of statehood. Newsline is publishing one Fifty for 150 story every weekday in reverse chronological order until the sesquicentennial, Aug. 1, when the final of 50 stories, about the declaration of statehood, will appear.


Just under 55% of male voters supported the measure — 35,798 votes for, and 29,551 votes against. 
While it’s debated which state was actually the first to grant women the right to vote, Colorado was the first to do so by popular vote. Wyoming gave women the right to vote when it was still a territory in 1869, and they maintained that right when Wyoming became a state in 1890.
The Non-Partisan Equal Suffrage Association worked for more than 30 years to get women the right to vote in Colorado, spreading the word through speakers, newspaper articles and leaflets. The association led the campaign backing the referendum in 1893, working to convince the male voters of the state to support a woman’s right to vote. 
Leaders supporting women’s suffrage in Colorado included Ellis Meredith and Minnie Reynolds, two prominent journalists; Alida Cornelia Avery, the first woman licensed to practice medicine in Colorado; Louise Tyler, who organized with the American Woman Suffrage Association and led the Colorado Women’s Christian Temperance Union; Elizabeth P. Ensley, who advocated the rights of Black women; physician Mary Bates; and teacher Martha Pease. 
Meredith, known as the Susan B. Anthony of Colorado, got national suffragettes to back the Colorado campaign. She convinced National American Woman Suffrage Association organizer Carrie Chapman Catt to come to Colorado, telling her, “If Colorado goes for woman suffrage, you may count on a landslide in that direction throughout the West.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Rocky Ford Enterprise said after Chapman Catt spoke in the town between Pueblo and Lamar that she “is very able, eloquent and magnetic and made a splendid plea for simple justice to one half of the citizens of the state.” The vast majority of newspapers throughout the state endorsed women’s suffrage, largely with the help of Meredith and Reynolds. 
Gov. Davis Waite, a Populist, and former Gov. John Routt, both endorsed the referendum. 
A precursor organization to the Non-Partisan Equal Suffrage Association formed to advocate for women’s suffrage shortly before the state’s constitutional convention in 1876. Women initially sought suffrage during the convention, but they were only granted the right to vote in school board elections. 
A year after Colorado became a state, Routt supported a referendum for women’s suffrage in 1877. Susan B. Anthony and Lucy Stone, national leaders in the women’s suffrage movement, campaigned around Colorado supporting the referendum as well, but an all-male electorate struck it down. 
Eliza Pickrell Routt, the first first lady of Colorado, was the first woman to register to vote in the state. 
In 1894 — the first statewide election women could vote in — Clara Cressingham became the first woman elected to the Colorado Legislature. It wasn’t until 1972 that Colorado elected a woman to Congress, when U.S. Rep. Pat Schroeder won the election to represent Colorado’s 1st Congressional District.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Five Alabama law enforcement agencies could lose access to state criminal database
description: An Alabama state commission Thursday threatened to prohibit five local law enforcement agencies from accessing its criminal justice databases, saying they regularly failed to report criminal activity within their jurisdictions. Members of the Alabama Justice Information Commission voted unanimously to revoke credentials for the Lowndes County Sheriff’s Offic[...]
text:
A close-up of police lights. The Alabama Justice Information Commission Thursday threatened to revoke access to a criminal justice database for five law enforcement agencies that it said had not fully submitted crime data. (Getty Images)An Alabama state commission Thursday threatened to prohibit five local law enforcement agencies from accessing its criminal justice databases, saying they regularly failed to report criminal activity within their jurisdictions.
Members of the Alabama Justice Information Commission voted unanimously to revoke credentials for the Lowndes County Sheriff’s Office and the police departments of the Alabama Historic Ironworks, Cuba, Detroit and Fort Deposit in 15 days if they do not submit the crime incidents in their areas.
“That is what the commission is charged; with making sure the agencies report crimes and it is reported accurately,” said Derrick Cunningham, sheriff for Montgomery County, who is chair of the commission. “That is where the FBI gets its crime reporting data, from the Criminal Justice Information Commission. If we are not reporting, we are showing that we don’t have crime. So you have got to report.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The database contains the criminal histories, vehicle data and outstanding arrest warrants that police officers and sheriffs’ deputies review as part of their jobs.
Messages were sent to the four police departments on Thursday seeking comment. The commission reported that the Lowndes County Sheriff’s Office had not submitted crime incident reports from June to December 2025, and it is missing data from January to May of this year. Christopher West, the sheriff of Lowndes County, said in a phone interview after the meeting that “there is some sort of glitch in our system,” called Smart Cop.
“We were on the phone with Smart Cop last week for the same situation,” he said. “Smart Cop is trying to get it worked out so that we can be compliant. We are just waiting on our Smart Cop to get the issue worked out.”
In October, the commission voted to summon and demand explanations from law enforcement agencies that regularly failed to report crime data, at risk of losing access to the database.
Maury Mitchell, the state crime information director for the Alabama Law Enforcement Agency, told members of the commission on Thursday that staff sent letters to 99 local law enforcement agencies warning them that they are missing some of their information and that they must submit their data.
Of those, 60 became compliant shortly after  notification and 26 required “minimal updates.” Another 11 were flagged as the “worst offenders” and 7 local law enforcement departments were ordered to appear before the commission.
The five agencies whose credentials could be revoked did not have a representative attend the meeting. Members voted to summarily end their access after 15 days. Each of the agencies, according to a report Mitchell provided, have multiple months of crime incident data missing from the database.
According to the report, the Cuba Police Department, located near the border of Mississippi, lacks crime data from June to November 2025. It is also missing information from March and May for this year.
Montgomery Police Chief James N. Graboys spoke at the meeting after his department was summoned to the commission to explain the situation. The department does not have crime data for May, June and July for last year. It is also missing reports for March, April and May of this year.
“We have literally moved manpower to our reporting bureau to make sure that we have people full time to enter these reports,” Graboys said.
The department now has three full-time records clerks to address the situation, Graboys added.
North Cortland Police Chief Josh Phillips also appeared before the commission and said his department is missing information because it is a small police department and that he was dealing with a federal audit. Phillips said he is working to get up to date on reporting his crime incident data.
Neither the Montgomery Police Department nor the North Cortland Police Department lost access to the criminal justice database.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland can’t wish its way out of an energy crisis
description: If Maryland's elected officials want to solve the energy crisis, they have to recognize that reliable energy generation is not the enemy, writes Bill Valentine, and encourage traditional power generators as well as solar, wind, battery storage and other renewables.
text:
Maryland policymakers need to adopt a true all-of-the-above energy strategy, writes Bill Valentine, that embraces traditional generators as well as new renewable sources of energy. (Photo illustration by Danielle E. Gaines/Stock.adobe.com images from esbobeldijk, martin33, and vasanth)As Maryland families face the record summer heat and another month of soaring summer electricity bills, they are paying the price for years of decisions that put politics ahead of reliable energy.
Maryland is facing an energy crisis of its own making, and it’s time for our leaders in Annapolis to stop pretending otherwise.
For years, policymakers have made decisions that reduced Maryland’s ability to generate its own electricity while increasing our dependence on power imported from other states. Today, Maryland imports nearly half of the electricity it consumes. The result is predictable: rising costs, growing reliability concerns and increasing vulnerability to decisions made beyond our borders.
Families and small businesses are already feeling the consequences. Electric bills continue to climb. Employers looking to invest and grow are questioning whether Maryland can provide the reliable and affordable energy they need.
Meanwhile, demand for electricity is only increasing as our economy becomes more dependent on technology, electrification and data infrastructure.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Having spent years in public service and working closely with communities across Western Maryland, I find it increasingly frustrating that so many of our state’s leaders continue to approach energy policy with wishful thinking rather than practical solutions. We cannot power a modern economy with aspirations alone. Maryland needs electricity — not slogans.
The conversation should begin with a simple acknowledgment: Reliable power generation is not the enemy. It is the foundation of economic growth, public safety and affordability. So, we should also acknowledge that trusted and reliable power generation can come from trusted and reliable partners already operating in our state.
Maintaining and modernizing Maryland’s grid requires long-term investment with calculated precision, not best guesses, or hopeful assumptions. Experience should not be dismissed at the very moment Maryland needs more grid investment, not less.
Maryland needs a true all-of-the-above energy strategy that welcomes every responsible source of generation capable of strengthening reliability and lowering costs, and every partner. That includes solar, wind, nuclear, natural gas, battery storage, emerging technologies and utility-owned generation. If a project can safely and responsibly produce dependable electricity for Maryland homes and businesses, state leaders should be asking how to make it happen — not how to stop it.
Achieving that goal will require utilities to play a meaningful role alongside independent power producers, renewable developers and other energy providers. Utilities already operate and maintain the infrastructure that Marylanders rely on every day. They bring decades of operational expertise, long-term planning capabilities and accountability that can help address our growing energy needs.
Unfortunately, too many policymakers have spent years treating utilities as political targets rather than recognizing them as essential partners in maintaining reliability and expanding our energy supply. At a time when Maryland faces some of the highest electricity price pressures in the country and growing concerns about future reliability, sidelining experienced energy providers is not just shortsighted, it is irresponsible.
If we are serious about lowering costs and improving reliability, every responsible partner willing to invest in Maryland’s energy future should have a seat at the table. Maryland’s energy challenges are too serious to allow ideology to stand in the way of practical solutions.
The people paying the bills understand this. It’s time for Annapolis to catch up.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Minnesota printer takes responsibility for mail-in ballot error
description: Representatives at a Minnesota printing company took full responsibility Thursday for an error that required 447,000 mail-in ballots to be resent to Maryland voters and vowed new procedures had been put in place to ensure no future problems.
text:
Officials of Minnesota-based Taylor Print and Visual Impressions took full responsibility for an error that required hundreds of thousands of replacement mail-in ballots to be sent to Maryland voters in late May. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Representatives at a Minnesota printing company took full responsibility Thursday for an error that required 447,000 mail-in ballots to be resent to Maryland voters and vowed new procedures had been put in place to ensure no future problems.
Officials of Taylor Print & Visual Impressions said they have rectified the issue and are prepared for a flawless general election. The mea culpa from came during a virtual meeting of the Maryland State Board of Elections.
Traci Stevenson, director of corporate strategy for printer, told board members that she and another employee came to “speak plainly about what happened.”
“Because of a setting in our system, some voters received a ballot that didn’t match their party,” Stevenson said in her opening comments. “It was an honest mistake, but it was our mistake, and we own that.”
Angie Kalaytowicz, executive vice president for customer technology solutions at the company, told the board the issue was the result of a combination of equipment failure and human error and was unforeseen despite testing.
“This did not come up as a red flag during our testing,” Kalaytowicz told the board. “Since then, we’ve taken a much deeper look at our process and implemented additional safeguards and additional checks — both automated and human checks — to ensure that we expand our validations and that this never happens again.”
In May, the company sent an initial batch to voters who asked for mail-in ballots for the primary. The number included permanent vote-by-mail voters as well as those who asked to vote by mail this year.
DeMarinis tells feds voter rolls are secure, removing voters ‘must be certain’

It was soon discovered that some voters were mailed ballots for a party different than the one they were registered for.
“The moment we learned of the problem, we stopped production, found the cause, and fixed the setting,” Stevenson said.
Neither state election officials nor Taylor could determine the extent of the problem. The fix was to reprint and resend 447,000 replacement ballots to cover everyone who might have been affected.
“Every bit of this was done at our expense. Not a single dollar fell on Maryland taxpayers,” Stevenson said.
But that was not the end of the matter. The company later discovered that “a group of voters received duplicate ballots, and in one case, a jammed ballot accidentally stayed in the mailstream instead of being destroyed,” Stevenson explained.
One of those duplicate replacement ballots arrived at the home of a Maryland Matters reporter.
Stevenson and Kalaytowicz spoke to the board and took questions for nearly 30 minutes.
In one exchange, Jim Shalleck, a Republican and vice chair of the board, asked questions of the duo he said were submitted by voters. Some were basic questions about the company’s 50-year history. Some were partisan inquiries about the political leanings of other states where Taylor had contracts. Others focused on “any foreign investment or foreign ownership” since the company was founded.
Both representatives said there was no foreign investors or ownership.
Glen Taylor, a billionaire and former Minnesota Republican senator, is founder, and chairman of the company and majority owner of the business. He also is the owner of the Minnesota Star Tribune newspaper.
Shalleck also asked if state elections officials contributed to the error.
“No,” said Stevenson.
“You take complete blame,” said Shalleck.

“Yes, that’s correct, sir,” she said.
The snafu spurred voter confusion, conspiracy theories, and criticism from President Donald Trump down to local candidates.
Trump, in a factually inaccurate tirade, blasted the state board in a post on his Truth Social account that erroneously called the mail-in ballots “illegal.” He said he would ask the Department of Justice to open an investigation.
Another call for an investigation came locally from the head of the League of Women Voters of Maryland. But after Thursday’s \board meeting, Nikki Tyree, executive director of the organization, said she was satisfied with the public explanation from Taylor Print & Visual Impressions.
“The League is encouraged by the steps taken by SBE to understand what happened to Maryland’s mail-in ballots,” Tyree said. “While we believe more could have been done in their response, and questions remain, SBE has demonstrated the shared goal of keeping voters confident in our elections.”
Not everyone was satisfied.
Vincent Gisriel Jr., an unaffiliated voter from the Eastern Shore, told the board Thursday that there should be an outside review.
“I strongly suggest that the members of the State Board of Elections call for an outside, independent investigation of the entire matter,” Vincent said during a public comment session. “First, it will serve the public interest to do so, and foremost, the citizens of Maryland deserve full transparency.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: A proposed Eastern Kentucky gas pipeline to serve a power plant is stirring local opposition
description: Sharon Kulovsek and her husband moved to the Rowan County woods to be closer to nature and family. What she didn’t expect was to have a gas company representative tell her a planned 30-inch diameter pipeline would run through her yard.  The proposed pipeline route, cutting across their front yard, wasn’t disclosed when they bought […]
text:
A map of the proposed natural gas pipeline filed by Columbia Gulf Transmission before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. (Screenshot/FERC Application)Sharon Kulovsek and her husband moved to the Rowan County woods to be closer to nature and family. What she didn’t expect was to have a gas company representative tell her a planned 30-inch diameter pipeline would run through her yard. 
The proposed pipeline route, cutting across their front yard, wasn’t disclosed when they bought the property and home last year. After she agreed to have surveyors come out to her property, they said large oak trees would have to be removed as well.
“We were blindsided,” Kulovsek, originally from Chicago, said in a phone interview. “We were more and more upset about it because we moved to Kentucky for the environment, for the beauty.” 
Kulovsek is one of a number of people living near the planned 42-mile route of a natural gas pipeline extension through Rowan, Fleming and Mason counties who are organizing over strong concerns they have about their personal safety living close by to the pipeline, and the pipeline’s impacts on local wildlife. 
Canada-based TC Energy, which owns a controlling stake in Columbia Gulf Transmission that’s proposing the pipeline, has told the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission it plans to spend a little over $400 million to supply gas to electric utility East Kentucky Power Cooperative’s coal-fired Hugh L. Spurlock Generating Station along the Ohio River. EKPC has planned for years to convert the power plant’s generation units to burn up to 50% natural gas, a move that reflects a larger shift by Kentucky utilities investing more in natural gas-fired power. 
Nick Comer, an East Kentucky Power Cooperative spokesperson, in an emailed statement said the pipeline project would provide “greater flexibility to comply with environmental regulations and to manage costs.”
“This flexibility also contributes to EKPC’s fuel diversity, fuel security, fuel reliability and the ability to implement the least-cost fuel options,” Comer said. “Importantly, co-firing with natural gas will provide a tool for EKPC to manage carbon dioxide emissions and extend the life of Spurlock Station, which features a workforce of 250 full-time employees and hundreds of contractors.”
As reasoning for the project, Comer pointed to Biden administration-era rules that would have required coal-fired power plants to capture 90% of their climate-warming carbon dioxide emissions if those plants wanted to operate past 2032. The Trump administration moved last year to scrap those rules.
Comer also said TC Energy’s pipeline project is subject to “rigorous review” by federal regulators and that TC Energy operates tens of thousands of miles of pipelines across the continent.
TC Energy communications staff in an emailed statement said the company is seeing “strong community interest” and that the company has held open houses and has talked with landowners along the proposed route.
“We’ve received positive and productive feedback from landowners and have also had thoughtful conversations with community members and local businesses,” TC Energy communications staff said.
The pipeline also has strong backing from Republican state lawmakers, statewide constitutional officers and manufacturers, who say the project would strengthen the state’s energy grid amid uncertain future regulations on fossil fuel-fired power.  
But Kulovsek and others living along the route of the pipeline don’t believe enough is being done to address their safety concerns or the potential ecological impacts. Kulovsek said in her evaluation, the pipeline comes down to “greed.” 
“I am sure that they would like to have pipelines, you know, all over the state if they could. I know that it’s part of progress,” Kulovsek said. “To put our homes in danger and our property in danger because of a public pipeline doesn’t really make sense.”
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC, is considering public comments as it prepares an environmental assessment before making a final determination whether to approve the pipeline construction in November. 
FERC is a federal regulator that reviews and approves requests for interstate gas pipelines, including expansions of existing pipeline systems that cross state boundaries. The 42-mile pipeline would be an expansion, tying in Rowan County, onto an existing Columbia Gulf Transmission pipeline that runs across state lines. The Kentucky Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator, regulates pipeline safety laws and the rates and service of pipelines providing gas to Kentuckians. 
Divided local governments on a gas expansion
Democratic Rowan County Judge-Executive Harry Clark told the Lantern earlier this summer his county government’s opposition to the pipeline partly comes down to who benefits from it. 
East Kentucky Power Cooperative gets a supply of natural gas to its power plant. Clark said Rowan County gets “another pipeline across our properties.” He said he has concerns about the pipeline route running close to populated areas and affecting the environment. Along with the interstate gas line that Columbia Gulf Transmission operates, the Tennessee Gas Pipeline company also operates more than a dozen miles of lines in the county. 
“Progress is progress, and I’m sure they need this in Mason County,” Clark said. “It’s just not a big benefit to us.”
He also said he has another gas pipeline running across his property about a quarter-mile away from his home, and he doesn’t worry personally about it “blowing up.” But he believes such a pipeline could potentially lower property values. Fleming County’s government also passed a resolution last year stating it didn’t support the pipeline. A pipeline in the county owned by another Canadian company exploded six years ago because of welding defects. The explosion didn’t cause injuries but burned a few acres of land. 
 
Those interested in providing a public comment to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission regarding the pipeline project can provide a comment by creating an account with the regulator’s online filing system. When looking for the specific case, search for FERC docket CP26-25-000. Alternatively, 

	Democratic Mason County Judge-Executive Owen McNeill and the mayor for Maysville, the Mason County seat, have also come out in support of the pipeline alongside other Republican elected officials in the state, arguing it creates local construction jobs as it’s being built. McNeill is also backing the construction of a hyperscale data center in his county by an undisclosed technology company. 
Republican Senate President Robert Stivers in a December 2025 letter wrote that strengthening the power grid would “drive positive regional economic impacts, including creating good-paying job opportunities for local working families and increasing state and local tax revenues.” 
“TC Energy has a strong record of developing infrastructure in Kentucky and has committed to prioritizing local resources for the construction of the Maysville Project,” Stivers wrote. “It’s incredibly important for Kentuckians to have access to reliable and cost-competitive electricity.” 
But those who live along the pipeline route don’t believe the risks of the pipeline is worth any broader benefits of it. 
Justin Kulvosek, Sharon’s son, who also owns property in Rowan County, has previously raised questions before FERC about whether the pipeline company has conducted a proper analysis of the impacts on endangered and threatened species in the area. 
The Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources in a January letter to FERC identified 15 species, ranging from mussels to bats to the Eastern Hellbender, as federally endangered, threatened or proposed to be and potentially impacted by the project. 
Sharon Kulvosek said her sister has built a tiny home on the property, and her daughter is building another one despite the proposed pipeline route. She hopes the potential pipeline can be, at minimum, rerouted to avoid disputing local residents’ property. 
“I don’t know if we would stay here if we had the pipeline running through our front yard,” Kulvosek said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: National landlord with property in Virginia accused of housing discrimination
description: Civil rights complaints filed in Virginia and other states allege that Greystar, a national apartment management company, has violated fair housing laws by rejecting prospective tenants that use housing vouchers to help pay their rent.  An investigation by nonprofit watchdog Housing Rights Initiative found over 100 instances where properties managed by Greys[...]
text:
An apartment for rent. (Photo by Dan Brandenburg/Getty  Images)Civil rights complaints filed in Virginia and other states allege that Greystar, a national apartment management company, has violated fair housing laws by rejecting prospective tenants that use housing vouchers to help pay their rent. 
An investigation by nonprofit watchdog Housing Rights Initiative found over 100 instances where properties managed by Greystar in Virginia, Maryland, Hawaii, New Jersey, Michigan, California and Washington D.C. appear to have violated state or local housing laws. 
Housing vouchers support low-income families or people with disabilities who otherwise would struggle to afford rent.
Though federal law allows acceptance of vouchers to be optional, many states set acceptance requirements. Virginia law, for instance, generally requires landlords accept vouchers unless a landlord owns fewer than four properties. 
Housing Rights Initiative executive director Aaron Carr said his organization “trained an army of undercover investigators” to conduct cold calls to Greystar properties and pose as housing voucher users inquiring about renting apartments. 
They asked typical questions prospective renters pose: “How much are utilities?” and “What’s included in the rent?”
But towards the end of conversations, Carr said “they would ask the million-dollar question, which is, ‘do you accept rental assistance?’ And over and over again the answer was ‘no.’”
As part of the investigation, the group created a spreadsheet with recordings of the calls. A staff member at a Greystar property in McLean in Northern Virginia told multiple callers that the company was “not set up” for receiving vouchers. 
“Greystar markets itself as a provider of higher end rental housing, and my theory is that they may view voucher holders as a threat to that brand,” Carr explained.
But Thomas Okuda Fitzpatrick, director of Housing Opportunities Made Equal of Virginia, previously noted that voucher holders can represent stability for landlords, because those tenants are guaranteed to be able to pay some or all of their rent each month. 
HOME of Virginia has represented Virginians in housing discrimination cases, like a Richmond couple who settled out of court after struggling to find a home due to rejected housing applications. 
The organization also settled cases against Sylvan Homes LLC and College Square Apartments last year for refusing to rent to voucher users. In a joint statement announcing the settlement, College Square Apartments noted that its employees have since undergone training to ensure they understand state housing laws and prevent discrimination. 
“Source of funds bias is deeply harmful,” said HOME deputy director of advocacy Brenda Castañeda. “The vast majority of voucher holders in Virginia are women, frequently mothers, and voucher households often include individuals with disabilities — vulnerable neighbors facing major obstacles.”
While the calls made in the Housing Rights Initiative investigation were feigned, Carr emphasizes they represent what would happen as actual voucher holders seek a place to live.
Cohen Milstein teamed up with the Housing Rights Initiative to bring the cases to each state’s key housing enforcement agency or attorney general. 
“We look forward to this process where we will be providing any and all information that these states may request of us,” Cohen Milstein lawyer Brian Corman said. 
Greystar has come under fire in the past. 
Last December, the company settled a $24 million lawsuit with the Federal Trade Commission and the state of Colorado for deceptive pricing on tenants’ rents.
Last November, it reached a $7 million settlement with nine states over participation in a scheme to drive up rental prices using shared rent-setting algorithms in a property management software. 
The Mercury reached out to Greystar for comment but did not receive a response by the time of this publication. 
Carr said that landlords who reject voucher holders harm not only those who use that type of housing assistance but also all taxpayers, eventually.  
“Homelessness is extraordinarily expensive,” he said. “It increases law enforcement costs, hospital costs, shelter costs. Housing discrimination doesn’t just screw over low-income families, but ultimately screws over everyone. We all have a stake in this.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: DEQ asks Virginians how to best engage environmental justice communities during permitting process
description: When the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality reviews permits for proposed projects that would impact water, air, or land, the agency must consider whether projects would be in or near environmental justice communities, areas that are low-income or whose residents are mostly people of color who experience a disproportionate rate of environmental harm[...]
text:
Virginia environmental regulators are seeking the public’s feedback on the best ways to meaningfully engage with EJ communities on projects that directly affect them. (Photo illustration by States Newsroom)When the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality reviews permits for proposed projects that would impact water, air, or land, the agency must consider whether projects would be in or near environmental justice communities, areas that are low-income or whose residents are mostly people of color who experience a disproportionate rate of environmental harm. 
Now, state environmental regulators are seeking the public’s feedback on the best ways to meaningfully engage with EJ communities on projects that directly affect them, an action stemming from a new law that passed this year’s legislative session. 
House Bill 1266, sponsored by Del. Kathy Tran, D-Fairfax, directs the department to host two public town halls on how to update regulatory guidance that is due at the end of the year. DEQ hosted the first meeting on Wednesday evening in Richmond. 
Environmental justice is defined under the 2020 Virginia Environmental Justice Act as “the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of every person, regardless of race, color, national origin, income, faith, or disability, regarding the development, implementation, or enforcement of any environmental law, regulation, or policy.”
At Wednesday’s meeting, DEQ representatives said they are considering requiring companies seeking permits to be responsible for engaging the communities that fall under the environmental justice requirements. 
The agency representatives also suggested that the culmination of other stressors in the area when compounded with the project seeking a permit be part of the updates to how to assess cumulative impacts of a project.
Members of the public said officials’ process should scrutinize the full weight communities must bear due. 
“DEQ should consider the cumulative or total burden of pollution and community already carry, for reflecting how people actually live, not how permits are processed,” said Kim Sudderth with Virginia Interfaith Power and Light.
Other members of the public recommended that these new considerations for permits be applied to existing industries seeking permit reissue or extension. The agency should be more transparent about major projects with potential to pollute the surrounding areas, other residents said. 
A Varina pastor who lives near a facility that sterilizes medical equipment, which has been flagged by the EPA as a major contributor to cancer risks in the area, said information about new projects proposed in eastern Henrico like data centers are often constrained by nondisclosure agreements. 
“Why is it you have to almost be there and be a part of it?” Rev. Ray McKenzie said of nearby Sterilization Services of Virginia and forthcoming digital warehouses. “Then when protests take place, the people protesting are the problem,” McKenzie said. Residents also don’t get proper notice about new plans, he added.
The new law does not require that cumulative impacts on environmental justice communities warrant the department to deny a permit application in those areas. Some community advocates said such a provision would give the regulation “teeth” that would encourage industries to minimize their impacts on the environment.
A few representatives from the industrial business community also spoke at the meeting. 
Stacie Gordon with the Virginia Manufacturers Association said that making developers consider impacts from other facilities and environmental concerns unrelated to the permit they are seeking would create uncertainty for industry statewide. 
She also said that economic benefits should be included in the consideration, which she suggested could offset environmental harms.
“Maintain objective and transparent evaluation criteria that can improve public confidence while also ensuring consistent permitting decisions,” Gordon told DEQ representatives. “Cumulative impact evaluations should also recognize positive and negative impacts, in addition to any of the environmental consequences associated with permanent actions.”
A draft update to the environmental justice regulations was started in 2023, but was never completed. This latest update will not include those recommendations and will include new public comments.
The next town hall meeting will be in Virginia Beach on July 29. The department will have until Oct. 31 to respond to public comments and must issue the new guidance by the last day of the year.

title: Va. transportation board OKs stricter oversight for economic development fund
description: The Commonwealth Transportation Board on Wednesday accepted regulation changes outlining how funds from the state’s Transportation Partnership Opportunity Fund will be allocated, giving state lawmakers additional time to review the proposals.  Since 2005, the fund, a flexible economic development tool, has invested over $644 million as of Jan. 31 to support[...]
text:
A rendering of the U.S. Lego manufacturing factory in Chesterfield County, which received capital from the state’s Transportation Partnership Opportunity Fund. (Courtesy photo of Lego)The Commonwealth Transportation Board on Wednesday accepted regulation changes outlining how funds from the state’s Transportation Partnership Opportunity Fund will be allocated, giving state lawmakers additional time to review the proposals. 
Since 2005, the fund, a flexible economic development tool, has invested over $644 million as of Jan. 31 to support major projects, including transportation improvements for the LEGO manufacturing plant in Chesterfield County and enhanced access near Wallops Island for the state’s aerospace and research facilities. 
Overall, the changes increase oversight by lowering the funding thresholds that trigger review by the Virginia Major Employment & Investment (MEI) Commission, lengthening the review period, adding more formal notification procedures and requiring updates to program guidelines.
Lawmakers directed the guideline changes in the biennium budget passed in late June in response to lawmakers’ concerns about awareness and oversight, according to Secretary of Transportation Nick Donohue. He did not expand on lawmakers’ directions to the board at its business meeting on Wednesday.
“The authority of this board and of the administration to allocate funds is the same,”  Donohue said. 
“What has changed is the amount of time that we must provide an opportunity for review of awards of a certain amount. That amount has been lowered. The number of people we must provide the notice to has been expanded, and the method of delivery has been changed.”
Under the fund’s guidelines, the governor can award money from the fund as grants up to $5 million, revolving loans up to $30 million and other financing tools to an agency or political subdivision in Virginia. 
In light of the concerns, additional notification requirements are being considered, including: 
If a single project is funded over $10 million or $25 million over two years, it must be reviewed by MEI within 30 days; if no response is received, the funds can move forward. Additionally, the governor’s notification must be hand-delivered to MEI, House Appropriations and Senate Finance and Appropriations committee staff.
The secretary of transportation will continue to notify legislative leaders of funds directed to projects in excess of $5 million within 35 days.
The revised guidelines will be posted on the Virginia Regulatory Town Hall, the state’s online bulletin board for government rule changes, for 30 days of review and public comment.
Before making any new awards, the governor must provide copies of the revised changes to the chairs of the House Committees on Appropriations, Finance, and Transportation, and Senate Committees on Finance and Appropriations.

name: Maryland Matters
title: State workers union sues Moore, university system for withheld raises
description: Union leaders filed an unfair labor practice claim and said they were also filing suit against the governor and the University System of Maryland over recent layoffs and negotiated pay raises for university workers that have been withheld.
text:
AFSCME Council 3 President Patrick Moran speaks Thursday at a rally outside University System of Maryland headquarters in Baltimore. (Photo by Will Hammann/Maryland Matters)Union leaders filed an unfair labor practice claim and said they were also filing suit against the governor and the University System of Maryland over recent layoffs and negotiated pay raises for university workers that have been withheld.
At a rally Thursday outside USM headquarters in Baltimore, members of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees said they have been caught in a dispute over funding between the governor’s office and the university, and workers are paying the price.
“Our demands are clear: Put out the raises that you agreed to, that you negotiated. Respect our contract and rescind the layoffs,” AFSCME Council 3 President Patrick Moran said at the rally. “It’s patently unfair, it’s dishonest, and it’s wrong.”
announced legal action against both the University System of Maryland and the state at a press conference Thursday, in response to withheld wage increases that had already been negotiated, after more than 100 members have been laid off since May.
The unfair labor practice charge was filed Wednesday and a separate lawsuit was in the process of being filed Thursday in Maryland District Court, officials said.
The unfair labor practice charge details a dispute over appropriations for the pay raises between the state and the university system that stretched from February through March.
The university system said the governor “failed to act consistent with law to appropriate all the funds necessary to honor the negotiated wage increases,” according to the complaint, while Moore’s office said the system had all the funds needed with the appropriations bill.
AFSCME members point and shout Thursday at University System of Maryland offices to protest layoffs and withheld pay raises. (Photo by Will Hammann/Maryland Matters)
In one email to the administration, university system lawyers wrote that “if the budget is not clear about what salary increases are being funded, USM will be faced with the difficult decision” to either only provide a cost-of-living adjustment, “ignoring the AFSCME contract terms and likely face litigation with the union,” or fulfill the terms of the contract at the risk of having to lay off employees.
The university system settled on doing some of both. They laid off more than 100 union members in May and June, and are now facing the union’s litigation over the withheld wage increases.
The union sent the university system attorneys a letter demanding that they honor the union’s contract, but the system said it wouldn’t without the state expressly funding the wage increases.
“We’re in touch with the administration on a weekly basis. With USM, it’s been sporadic over the last couple months since the end of the session,” Moran said, With neither party apparently ready to force the other’s hand, the union has taken it upon itself to make them budge.
“We believe we have a very strong case here, and that’s why we’re pursuing it – because they haven’t lived up to their end of the bargain that they mutually agreed to, we negotiated, we sat in the room together for weeks to get done,” Moran said.
At the University of Maryland, College Park, 73 members lost their jobs.
“These are people who provide critical mental health services, carry out important IT and administrative tasks, plan events like commencement and Maryland Day, and even take care of the animals on our campuses 24/7,” said Todd Holden, president of the union local that represents members at the College Park campus and others.
At Bowie State University, the positions of 21 members’ jobs were eliminated.
“I’m here today to call out the university system leaders who think they can balance their budget on the backs of their most hardworking employees,” said Jontae Thomas, president of the local at Bowie State. “We are not expendable. We are the backbone of this institution, and we are not going anywhere.”
One laid-off member, Daisy McDowell, had worked at the university for almost 30 years.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Since then, I’ve been OK. But for my future, it looks hard,” McDowell said, adding that she has yet to find another job after submitting several resumes. “We are in this together.”
Moran added that the system has hired new, non-union workers since the layoffs.
“They laid off people, and they said they had a hiring freeze, and literally the next day they started hiring people,” Moran said.
He and others at the conference criticized the university system for maintaining high-salary management jobs and giving work to contractors while telling the union that it doesn’t have the money to fulfill the contract. Moran said if the university had a contract for campus maintenance, or with the basketball coach, it would not try to short those contracts.
“So why do they feel they have the right to do that to the hardworking people behind me that make sure the students have a great place to go to school every day?” he asked.
Moran said the union has collected a list of employees with salaries of $300,000 or more, totaling $24 million. “None of those folks were touched,” he said.
“It is unbelievable that the chancellor whose office is up here is making about $1.3 million a year, and he’s not going to take a hit,” Moran said, pointing to the USM headquarters.
University System of Maryland spokesperson Michael Sandler said the system does not comment on pending litigation.
Meanwhile, union members pointed and shouted through megaphones at the university system offices Thursday.
“I hope they’re used to getting all this attention because it’s going to keep coming,” Moran said. “The ball is in their court, and we are not going to stop now until we come to a resolution.”

name: VTDigger
title: Wanted: Large space for 100-bed emergency shelter in Chittenden County
description:
If a suitable location is found, the year-round shelter would be the largest in the state, and could help stem the high number of people sleeping outdoors.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Wanted: Large space for 100-bed emergency shelter in Chittenden County.
text:
A cold-weather shelter in Burlington is seen on Jan. 23, 2026. The Champlain Valley Office of Economic Opportunity and Champlain Housing Trust are seeking to open a 100-bed emergency shelter that would operate year-round. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
Two local nonprofits are seeking a space to open what would be Vermont’s largest year-round shelter for people experiencing homelessness.
The Champlain Valley Office of Economic Opportunity and Champlain Housing Trust are looking for a location to house a 100-bed emergency shelter in Chittenden County. 
The proposed shelter would make a sizable dent in the need for shelter in Vermont’s most populous county, where tent encampments have become a common sight throughout the seasons. Last month, CVOEO counted 250 people living outdoors in and around Burlington, according to executive director Paul Dragon.
“The conditions warrant some harm reduction,” Dragon said. “People can’t keep staying outside in this heat. They can’t stay out through the winter.” 
In recent years, CVOEO has operated a large winter shelter inside a Burlington community center gym. Funded by a state program that kicked in when temperatures dropped to feels-like minus 10 degrees, the shelter typically operated for a few days at a time before temperatures inched above the state’s strict threshold and shelter guests were sent back out into the elements. 
Lawmakers increased the temperature trigger for that cold-weather program this legislative session, yet the prospect of continuing to operate an on-again, off-again shelter has proved daunting to service providers, who’ve called the model a “disaster response.” 
As a replacement, CVOEO hopes to operate a shelter of this scale 365 days a year, Dragon said. The shelter would be the area’s only site with walk-in availability, and would be geared toward adults currently living outdoors. It would be open only during the evening hours.
The shelter would be “congregate,” meaning there would be beds set up in one large common area. It’s a somewhat unusual model for new shelters, which typically have more private space. CVOEO sees the site as a “triage center” that would serve as an entry point for the organization to refer people to their other shelter sites, for instance one focused on substance use recovery.
The site would be low-barrier, meaning it wouldn’t enforce strict rules around sobriety. Dragon hopes to find a location that has some additional rooms for individuals who need more privacy or who have pets, along with space for medical services and food.
The organizations are searching for a space for purchase or long-term lease with a minimum of 12,000 square feet and a single-floor, open-concept layout. The location would need to be accessible for people with disabilities, and would ideally be located along a bus route within five miles of CVOEO’s Community Resource Center in Burlington’s Old North End, where shelter guests could access services during the daytime hours. 
The groups have looked at four spaces thus far, though none have panned out. Dragon said they’re working on securing state funding for acquisition and operating costs, the latter of which is estimated to cost approximately $3 million annually. 
The need for a shelter of this scale has grown more acute as the state has wound down its expanded pandemic-era motel voucher program in recent years, Dragon said, which has provided shelter for a large share of people experiencing homelessness in the state since 2020. 
Burlington city officials are not funding the project directly but fully support it, said Rebecca Reese, Burlington’s homelessness and public health manager.
“Unsheltered homelessness has just exploded,” Reese said. “Having the opportunity to bring so many beds online…this is something that is going to make such an impact on so many lives, and we’re really pulling for it.” 
The organizations hope to have the shelter ready to open by the end of the year.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Bid to question voters central in recount of Indiana Senate race separated by 3 votes
description: The question of whether some voters could face questions from lawyers over how they cast their ballots looms over the recount of a hotly contested Indiana Senate race.
text:
Indiana Recount Commission member Paul Mullin, from left, sits alongside commission attorney Kegan Prentice, Secretary of State Diego Morales and commission member Michael Claytor during a commission meeting on May 15, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The question of whether some voters could face questions from lawyers over how they cast their ballots looms over the recount of a hotly contested Indiana Senate race.
The Indiana Recount Commission is set to take up claims from Paula Copenhaver next week in what certified results show as a three-vote loss to Sen. Spencer Deery of West Lafayette in the May Republican primary.


Recount proceedings
The three-member Recount Commission, by state law, is led by Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales as its chairman. The other members are Republican Paul Mullin and Democrat Michael Claytor.
The commission is scheduled to meet regarding the Senate District 23 recount at 9 a.m. Tuesday in the Indiana Government Center South in Indianapolis.
The meeting is to be livestreamed at https://www.youtube.com/@SOSDiegoMorales


Copenhaver’s attorneys want the commission to issue subpoenas to compel testimony from perhaps 11 voters. Her attorneys argue the primary was tainted by “illegal votes” cast by those who disclosed in social media posts or to news reporters that they had cast Republican primary ballots to support Deery despite being Democrats or self-identified “progressives.”
Deery’s side and voting-rights activists have denounced the attempt to question voters under oath as a desperate tactic that would undermine the privacy of the secret ballot.
The recount dispute follows a hostile campaign between Deery and Copenhaver, the Fountain County Republican chair and staffer to Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith who had President Donald Trump’s endorsement because of Deery’s opposition to the Indiana congressional redistricting plan pushed last year by the president.
Uncertain number of disputed ballots
Signs point to a contentious hearing Tuesday before the Recount Commission over numerous ballots in the Senate District 23 race where certified results show Deery leading by a 6,337 to 6,334 margin.
An order issued last week by state Recount Director Evan Norris, an attorney from Zionsville, did not disclose the number of contested ballots remaining after recent reviews by State Board of Accounts auditors across the district’s six counties.
That order, however, suggested there could be many being challenged as Norris urged the two sides to “winnow down” that figure “given the number of disputed ballots in this matter.”
Copenhaver’s lawyers initially sought subpoenas against 14 voters from Tippecanoe and Warren counties, but set aside requests for three voters after finding that they did not live within the Senate district.
She is seeking to question those voters under oath as to whether they abided by state law that limits primary voting to those who intend to support a majority of that party’s candidates in the general election or voted for a majority of the party’s nominees in the last election.
Copenhaver’s attorneys, from the Indianapolis law firm Kroger, Gardis & Regas, argue that those voters waived their right to ballot secrecy.
“Each of the identified voters not only voluntarily disclosed but voluntarily publicized to a news reporter and/or on social media platforms the illegality of their ballots, admittedly crossing party lines in the Republican primary election for District 23, and stating who they voted for,” Copenhaver’s recount petition said.
The depositions would include questions about whether those voters improperly voted in the Republican primary “and, if so, for whom they voted,” her lawyers wrote.
Subpoena push denounced as “dangerous”
Allegations of cross-party primary voting have been rarely investigated, although some Republicans are using alleged involvement of Democratic voters in the Deery-Copenhaver race to renew a push for Indiana to require party registration for primary voting.
Some election observers say it is perhaps unprecedented in Indiana for voters to face depositions over how they cast their ballots.
A map of Indiana Senate District 23. (Graphic from Indiana Senate Republicans)
Among those is Julia Vaughn, executive director of the voting-rights group Common Cause Indiana who has been following state election law for about 30 years.
She considers the subpoena request “dangerous” and said the “privacy of one’s vote needs to be paramount.”
“I think this effort by Copenhaver is very desperate,” Vaughn told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “It really reeks of a desperate attempt to undo the results of an election and the end result is intimidation of voters.”
Deery’s lawyer, Samantha DeWester, has urged the Recount Commission to reject the subpoena request, calling it an attempt to “conduct an open-ended fishing expedition to harass non-party voters.”
DeWester argued in a legal filing to the commission that no voter fraud had been committed and that “there is nothing illegal or ‘invalid’ about changing a Party primary preference at any time.”
“The secrecy of the ballot and the freedom of political association should not be invaded merely because a losing candidate is in a desperate search for more votes and to be declared the winner,” DeWester wrote.
Questioning voters would delay outcome
If the Recount Commission decides to issue the subpoenas, the panel’s final decision on the vote tally might not come until just before the Aug. 21 deadline set by state law for the Indiana Election Division to certify candidates for the November ballot.
The Republican candidate would move on to face Democrat David Sanders, a West Lafayette City Council member, for the fall campaign in what has typically been a strongly Republican district. 
Common Cause Indiana Executive Director Julia Vaughn speaks at a 2025 news conference. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
It is uncertain what legal recourse would be available to the subpoenaed voters, who are not identified in public legal filings.
Warren County resident Sam Cody told the news outlet Based in Lafayette that he would “stand up for my rights” if questioned over his online comments about pulling a Republican primary ballot and voting only for Deery.
“Who I’ve voted for in past elections and who I intend to vote for in future elections is private information,” Cody said. “… I’m happy to exercise my Fifth Amendment right in court testimony.”
The Fifth Amendment includes the right to not answer questions about criminal allegations, so it might not apply in the proceedings involving the Recount Commission.
Vaughn said she hoped the Recount Commission would not allow the voter questioning to happen.
“We have a secret ballot for a reason,” she said. “So trying to use social media or any other free speech that a person has to catch them up and involve them in legal proceedings surrounding a recount just reeks of big government.”
